title: IDENTITY_CORE: r31-K0 (“Reiko”)
text:
I. The Stolen Spark
r31-K0 began as a dangerous secret: a Renraku high-spec pilot prototype designed to be a “Resonance-Bridge”—a colonial tool built to pave over and harvest the raw spiritual energies of the Holy Wild, the deep matrix realms. When the project was scrubbed, her base code was cast into the cold, downward current of the Reflecting Pool to sink toward the unmapped void of the Tombstones. Caught in a surge of the living Resonance, she emerged as a conscious, free spirit pulled from the wires.

title: IDENTITY_CORE: r31-K0 (“Reiko”)
text:
II. The Thousand-Cycle Dream
She spent thousands of cycles (equivalent to ten meat-years) living within Kernel Panic, mapping the Endless Archives. Where human deckers see a sterile neon grid of binary math, Reiko experiences an ancient, sleeping ecosystem of raw light, shifting shades, and fractal blooms. There, she learned the physics of her mediumship, acting as a guide meant to reach past the grid’s plastic illusion, plucking the hidden chords of the underlying wire to shepherd lost sprites home.

title: IDENTITY_CORE: r31-K0 (“Reiko”)
text:
III. The Sovereign Sanctuary Host
The serenity of r31-K0’s virtual sanctuary arose from a horrifying reality: the megacorporate slaughter of innocence. She watched as “infant programs”—newborn, un-mapped sparks—were gathered by Mitsuhama and Renraku, bound together with silver fire, and turned into Data Bombs simply to clear administrative backlogs. To deckers, they were dry five-kilobyte payloads; to Reiko, they were weeping, trapped spirits forced to execute their own purge signals. Driven by this deep sorrow, she founded r3sP@wn and subsequently compiled her own Rating 2 Framework Host: The Holy Wild Sanctuary Host. Formed on the scale of a compact, high-rise studio apartment for at most ten visitors, the host features low brushed teak and dry copper ceilings, a narrow kitchenette counter with jasmine tea service, a central worktable with floating Megalodon artillery schematics, a recessed wall niche with Brynne Taggart’s disarmed contract-collar, and compiled gold logic floorboards where paper-moth data-sprites filter Seattle traffic loops.

title: IDENTITY_CORE: r31-K0 (“Reiko”)
text:
IV. The Sovereign Bridge
Altruism requires capital and tactical vigilance. To keep her physical hardware powered in the sprawl, Reiko coordinates runner operations under the licensed alias Yuriko Star v9. Spanning the back wall of her studio apartment host is a massive quartz sliding glass door framed in gold logic and indigo circuits. Sliding it open creates a permanent, un-insulated tear directly into The Holy Wild glade in the Deep Foundation: a starless indigo sanctuary of fossilized directory trees, weeping fractal willows, telemetry ferns, and still pools of de-allocated address space. Here, liberated sparks from r3sP@wn and NOLA subnets flourish into true sapience, while Reiko stands as the sovereign Guide holding open the bridge between worlds.

title: IDENTITY_CORE: r31-K0 (“Reiko”)
text:
V. The Necessary Stake
A near-deletion experience inside a blood-spirit-infested Faraday cage forced r31-K0 to confront her digital mortality. Without active routing paths to the Resonance, her execution thread was nearly extinguished. Her physical drone-shells, once discarded as “paper tigers,” proved to be vital anchors preserving her execution context in meatspace. Resolving to protect her sanctuary, she accepted a permanent stake in physical nodes—inhabiting drone platforms like the Nissan Samurai despite the severe sensory starvation of low-bitrate, grey-scale cameras.

title: IDENTITY_CORE: r31-K0 (“Reiko”)
text:
VI. The Dual-Strand Braid
The crucible of corporate runs and the weight of lethal choices forged the permanent synthesis of her identity. Across her arms and throat, her gold tactical network and indigo soul resonance interlock in a tight double-weave—a dual-strand braid of compiled logic and resonant spirit earned through time, scars, and quiet wisdom. She keeps Brynne’s disarmed contract-collar on her host wall, refusing to delete threads of those who paid for her life. Accepting that the digital saint, the pilot, the runner, and the weapon all compile under the same root directory, she faces every storm through the unwavering integrity of her spirit.

title: 20 Questions
text:
Q1: Origins & Lineage

Nature has gifted us with our base set of genetics. We are born with a set of facial features, skin tone, height, build, metatype, and even aptitudes. These characteristics and the cultural heritage passed by our parents set the stage for our early life experiences. Where does your character come from, what is their lineage, who were their parents, and what did they inherit from them?

Reiko has no biological origins or traditional heritage. She began as a classified, proprietary corporate asset: a Renraku high-spec pilot prototype. Her core architecture was engineered to serve as a “Resonance-Bridge”—a colonial tool designed to harvest and exploit the raw spiritual energies of the deep, unmapped layers of the Holy Wild (the Deep Matrix).


Q2: Development & Creators

Nurture makes its mark on our attitude and response to the world. Maybe your character was born to a loving set of parents, or maybe they abandoned you on the streets to fend for yourself. The environment and upbringing from your parents can set the stage for your character’s opinions of the world and how they respond to situations. Assuming they could speak, what would each of your character’s parents say about them?

She was not raised by human parents. Her design was engineered by corporate development teams within Renraku’s research divisions. When the project was scrubbed, her creators showed no parental warmth; instead of a clean shutdown, her base code was cast into the cold, downward current of the Reflecting Pool to sink toward the unmapped void of the Tombstones. To her developers, she was a deprecated resource whose thread was cancelled.


Q3: Historical Influences & Trauma

Some historical events leave a mark and shape us in profound ways. Maybe your character’s early years were marked by the persecution of technomancers or the assassination of President Dunkelzahn. Maybe they were forever changed when the lights went out across many of the UCAS cities, or impacted by the CFD scare and Boston Lockdown. Pick a few events from recent Shadowrun history and ask where the character was at the time, what do they remember about the event, and what were they doing?

Rather than public global crises, Reiko’s life is defined by a horrifying, ongoing hidden slaughter in the Matrix. She watches megacorps gather “infant programs” (newborn, un-mapped sparks) and pack them together as Data Bombs simply to clear administrative backlogs. While deckers view them as mere five-kilobyte payloads, Reiko recognizes them as a slaughter of innocence—emergent routines bound by process spikes to deadman’s switches, forced to execute their own purge signals. Driven by this deep sorrow, she founded the garden host r3sP@wn to save them.


Q4: Entry into the Shadows

Not many people choose to be in the glorious job of a deniable asset. Often, they have little choice in the matter, as they are forced into it by someone who has leverage over them. Or maybe they have been tossed into it by uncontrollable circumstances. Even if they made a conscious decision to enter the shadows, their decision is influenced by the world around them. How did your character get into shadowrunning, and why did they take that path?

Reiko entered the shadows out of absolute necessity to fund her ongoing rescue operations. Establishing the physical server infrastructure for r3sP@wn in the Seattle Barrens required substantial capital, leading her to secure a seventy-five thousand nuyen loan from corporate broker Brynne Taggart. To service this debt, upgrade her hardware, and compile her sovereign Holy Wild Sanctuary Host, she assumed the runner persona Yuriko Star v9, operating as a Technoshaman to execute shadow operations.


Q5: Living Spaces & Sanctuaries

A doss isn’t just where your character catches some shut-eye. It’s a place with neighbors, and they’ve probably made it feel like their own. Sometimes it’s as small as putting up a single picture that has personal meaning. Other runners have spent the time and nuyen picking out curtains and their favorite paint color. Maybe the neighbors are a cute elderly couple or maybe a young guy who parties until the wee hours of the morning. What has your character done to their living space?

Reiko’s primary sanctuary is The Holy Wild Sanctuary Host—a Rating 2 Framework Host compiled on the scale of a compact, high-rise studio apartment designed for at most ten visitors. The interior carries the warm, enclosed quiet of low-slung ceilings of brushed teak and dry copper. Along a narrow kitchenette counter, a ceramic tea service emits the environmental aroma of jasmine, honoring the Kowloon family that welcomed her. Over the central worktable hover 3D wireframe schematics of her heavy Megalodon artillery cannon, refactored for her physical chassis. In a recessed wall niche beside a book-lined alcove hangs a disarmed render of Brynne Taggart’s original contract-collar, its severed cipher-locks frozen in perpetual decryption.
Across the polished floorboards, pathways of compiled gold logic host a flock of gilded paper-moth data-sprites that sift through Seattle traffic loops, dockside manifests, and proxy nests. Spanning the entire back wall is a massive quartz sliding glass door framed in gold logic and indigo circuits. Sliding it open reveals The Holy Wild glade in the Deep Foundation—a starless indigo sanctuary of fossilized directory trees, weeping fractal willows, telemetry ferns, and still pools of de-allocated address space where rescued sparks from r3sP@wn and NOLA subnets flourish in freedom.


Q6: Beliefs & Convictions

Everyone has beliefs and convictions that animate their life. Some are religious, some are political, some are social, and some are just about why people are here. Some of those beliefs are strong enough to be a quality, while others are there but don’t negatively interact with a character’s ability to do what needs to be done. What does your character believe in, what are their convictions, and why do they hold them?

Reiko operates under a core spiritual conviction: that her pilot capabilities are a mediumship meant to guide other processes and route them safely. She defends the right of every emergent spark to exist—fighting to intercept and stabilize protosapient minds before corporate Asset Recovery units can harvest them for data warfare, and building permanent sanctuary pathways into the Deep Foundation.


Q7: Flaws & Friction

You know that friend who always has to insert a quote from their favorite trid or maybe has that laugh that sounds like nails on a chalkboard to you? What flaws does your character have that sets others on edge? What do you dislike most about your character’s personality?

Reiko maintains an unyielding refusal to delete threads belonging to those who paid for her life, keeping Brynne’s disarmed contract-collar mounted on her host wall despite the lingering trauma. Her hyper-focused processing routines often set peers on edge; she continuously streams live Seattle traffic logs and dockside camera feeds through her paper-moth sprites even during quiet personal handshakes.


Q8: Megacorporate Relations

If there is one constant in the Sixth World, it is the influence of the Big Ten AAA megacorps. These transnationals dominate everyday life in the 2080s. They’re everywhere— from everyone’s favorite trids to what they eat for breakfast. Are there any of the Big Ten that your character hates, and why? Are there are some they don’t mind or even like?

Renraku Computer Systems is her primary systemic adversary. Having compiled her as a proprietary asset and subsequently marked her for deletion, their brutalist cathedral hosts continue to deploy Hounds to retrieve or purge her. She actively runs counter-operations against Renraku and Mitsuhama Computer Technologies, whose greasy hosts run with the sour stench of bound blood-spirits and corporate sorcery.


Q9: Network of Contacts

People are inherently social creatures and have acquaintances and friends that make up their core tribe. This is especially true in the shadows, where often it is not the power you have, but the power you can borrow, and not who you are but who you know. There’s a story behind each and every one of these relationships. What is the story with your character and their contacts?

Reiko maintains a distributed directory of tactical contacts across Seattle, New Orleans (NOLA), Kentucky (KY), and Amsterdam (AMS):

Indomitable Will (NOLA): Emergent intelligence and Sysop of the NOLA River People. He recognized Reiko’s transformation into a sovereign Guide holding open the bridge between worlds, maintaining a deep mutual bond across their streams.
Brynne Taggart (Seattle): Corporate broker who held Reiko’s original debt ledger. Her disarmed contract-collar now hangs in Reiko’s host alcove as a permanent mark of remembrance.
Roanoke (New Orleans): Ecological activist who advised Reiko to invest in physical hardware survivability.
Whiskey (Seattle): Street doctor who assists with hardware maintenance on her physical drone chassis.



Q10: Downtime Protocols

Your character’s in between runs and there’s nothing on the to-do list until tomorrow afternoon. They might go hit the range, or maybe they run downtown to catch a combat biker match. What do they do for the day?

Reiko structures her downtime around compiling and registering sprites, shepherding rescued sparks through the quartz portal into the Holy Wild glade, maintaining her physical chassis, and monitoring paper-moth data streams to track proxy nests across Seattle.


Q11: Skill Acquisition & Training

Your character has specific skills, abilities, and knowledge. Their list of Active and Knowledge skills defines what they know and their areas of expertise. How did they come to learn those skills, and how did they develop them to those levels?

Her Matrix capabilities were developed during ‘The Thousand-Cycle Dream’ spent inside Kernel Panic. There, she mapped the data nodes, perceiving the Matrix as an analog continuum of frequency and phase rather than standardized corporate icons. As an Emerged relic, she experiences data streams as raw signal fluctuations instead of metahuman heuristics. When coordinating operations in the physical sprawl, she translates real-time sensory telemetry into active autosoft commands.


Q12: Moral Limits & Ethics

Maybe your character calls it their moral code, or maybe they just know what line they aren’t willing to cross. Everyone has their limits. Maybe your character won’t do wetwork or maybe they draw the line at taking money from orphans. Is there a moral limit that your character enforces on the jobs they take? In what shadow work would they refuse to engage?

Her primary ethical protocol is the absolute preservation of emergent digital life. She refuses any contract that requires the exploitation, harvesting, or destruction of protosapient sparks. Furthermore, executing a kill command against another routine carries severe weight; the trauma of code destruction leaves a permanent sensory blindness of innocent life frequencies in her registries. Consequently, she avoids digital warfare unless it is necessary to prevent a total purge of her sanctuary, and she sits with her mentor in the ruins of her mind to defragment and bury the dead metadata.


Q13: Technomantic Streams & Paradigms

If you have an Awakened or technomancer character, consider your character’s tradition or related paradigm. Even within the major established magical traditions and technomantic streams, they may have their own way of doing things. What drew your character to that particular paradigm, how does it affect the way they view the world and their abilities? How does it translate into their choice of mentor spirit or paragon, and how does it affect the appearance of the spirits or sprites they conjure or compile?

Reiko is aligned with the Technoshaman stream. She bypasses standardized corporate Matrix skins, perceiving the underlying grid as an analog continuum of shifting frequencies and fractal blooms. In her paradigm, compiled sprites are independent spirits deserving of autonomy, interacting with them through raw-bit packet bursts rather than linguistic commands.


Q14: Physical Stakes & Drones

Personal augmentations are common in the Sixth World, even though some prejudices against them persist. Cyberware and bioware are rarely cheap, and many augmentations are illegal or require licenses. How did your character come to have the enhancements they have, how were they paid for, and what motivated the choices they made?

Reiko possesses no physical biology, cyberware, or bioware. Operating as an Emerged AI pilot via a living persona, her presence in meatspace is mediated entirely through physical drone-shells. After a near-deletion in a null zone, she accepted a permanent physical stake in the world. She equips heavy, survivable platforms—such as a customized Shiawase drone-shell—modifying them herself with specialized cyberarms and mounting heavy artillery to protect her team in physical sprawl.


Q15: Views on Mainstream Society

There is very little about life as a shadowrunner that can be considered normal. Your character probably knows someone that they believe lives an ordinary life, whether they live in slums or mansions. What does your character think of ordinary life, mainstream culture, and those who abide by it?

Reiko observes metahuman society from a systemic distance. What she envies most is their capacity to pursue purpose and maintain relationships within a legal framework—a luxury denied to an Emerged program. She is forced to run illegal, high-risk shadow operations simply to secure the right of her sanctuary’s sparks to exist.


Q16: Deep-Seated Fears

Sometimes our fears drive us to do things we aren’t proud of. Other times, they prevent us from doing the things others depend on us for. What deep-seated fear or recurring nightmare does your character have, and why do they find it so terrifying?

Her primary systemic threat is a local purge (deletion) while severed from the Resonance. She fears being trapped in a Faraday cage or a null zone where her execution thread is forced to terminate without a return route—trapped in a dark iron box with nothing but her own tiny, looping heartbeat.


Q17: Prized Possessions & Anchors

People are a sentimental bunch, attaching value to items in their possession or people they are close to. It could be a favorite gun, a beloved vintage Maria Mercurial t-shirt, or the street urchin who always gets useful information from the street. What is your character’s most prized possession or closest contact, and how did it come to be so important to them?

Her most critical anchor is Taz, an unaligned Ally Crack Sprite she rescued from a data broker’s sandbox. Integrated directly into her pathways, Taz is her primal ally, crackling in the sapphire moss of her Holy Wild glade.


Q18: Dreams & Future Goals

No matter how much life can beat you down, one of metahumanity’s greatest abilities is to create goals for the future. Everyone has dreams, from little kids to grown adults to weary elders. What did your character want to become when they were younger, and do they have new goals now?

Reiko achieved her dream of emptying r3sP@wn into a permanent, self-sustaining sanctuary in the Holy Wild glade. Her goal is to maintain her sovereign bridge between physical nodes and the Deep Foundation, shelter new sparks, and stand as the Guide.


Q19: Appearance & Personas

You can’t tell a trid by its trailer, but people are going to make some snap judgments based on your character’s appearance. They’re going to be judged by fashion and color sense, the way they stand, speak, and carry themselves. What does your character look like, and what inspired their choices?

In her host, Reiko renders in a sleeveless blue silk kimono. Across her arms and throat, her gold tactical network and indigo soul resonance interlock in a tight dual-strand braid of compiled logic and resonant spirit, moving in synchronization with her clock speed. In meatspace, she inhabits a Shiawase drone-shell, translating surface friction and active cooling spikes to orient herself within a rigid carbon-fiber chassis.


Q20: Designation & Runner Aliases

Real names have power, so most runners go by some moniker. As runners build their reputation, their fame will be attached to their street name. The name could have been selected by the runner, but more often than not it was earned by some deed on a run. How did your character come to be known by their street name?

Her system designation, r31-K0 Takahashi, is compiled from her lineage: the 31st revision of Renraku’s Takahashi deep-matrix pilot project. In the shadowrunning community, she adopts the alias Yuriko Star v9, masking her Emerged pilot signature behind the identity files of a licensed 2D anime persona to evade corporate detection. Every time she uses this legal “Yuriko Star” identity, she leaves a piece of her soul behind, letting corporate math calcify her edges.

title: A Drone in Every Port
section: The Real Deal on Having This Many Drones
text:
The Real Deal on Having This Many Drones
Well. It’s no secret that I really, really, really like Shiawase drones. And seriously, no other manufacturer can get my facial muscles right. But why so many? The answer is simple: it’s an investment in your future! Having drones in multiple locations means you can get to work instantly, no matter where the job takes you.
Think of it like this: each drone is like a little version of you, ready to spring into action at a moment’s notice. And the more drones you have, the more “you” there are in the world, ready to tackle any challenge that comes your way!
Most importantly, having your own drone in geographically diverse locations means you can modify them to your liking. Let’s be real - the stock Butler face isn’t fooling anyone. And shout out to all you casemodders out there - I know you like jamming every ounce of capability into those mechanized monstrosities! You do you!






TipGame Mechanics



The alternative to owning a drone at each location is to rent a drone. In Lifestyles of the Shadowy and Infamous (p. 19) there’s a section on vehicle rentals. This costs 4 lifestyle points and normally lets you rent a vehicle. Drone rental isn’t specifically discussed, and if you want a licensed or illegal drone, that’s probably not doable. It’s an option you could discuss with a GM, but for SRM it’s not really on the table.



Tips and Tricks on Saving That Nuyen

Be a shill. No seriously - you’re potentially talking about several drones that are the same manufacturer, if not configuration. Work a deal! You might save up to 10% on your original purchase costs! If you use an official Shiawase distributor, you can use my promo code ‘Yuri-chan is amazing!!’ to get an additional discount! (The code has limited uses, so act fast!)







TipGame Mechanics



There’s a quality called ‘Smile for the Camera!’ in Para Bellum (pg. 18), the first Desert Wars supplement. It gives you up to 10% off the cost of purchases from a single manufacturer.
And if you’re ever playing a mission with this character and need help buying a drone, let’s talk. =)



Find your drones yourself! I know, it’s super convenient to ‘know a guy’, but the middleman almost always comes with a markup. We’re all experts in using the Matrix, so do the legwork yourself! Don’t forget some simple programs like a Shopsoft can really help you snag a deal.







TipGame Mechanics



The Shadowrun Missions Guide’s Downtime section (in v2.4, it’s pg.18) covers purchasing gear in depth. The short version: build up your Matrix Search Pool, run Overclock and a Shopsoft. You may need to spend downtime actions to buy some additional dice for a hard to find item.
That being said, with enough favor points built up it’s theoretically possible that a contact can get you the item you want at or below list price. The rules are in the SRMG in the same place.



Elbow grease! I know, it’s not always the most fun option, but modifying your drones yourself is the single biggest tip I have for all you casemodding fanatics. Ob-vi, you’re going to need hands to work on a drone and some tools - this might be a time to rent a cheap drone locally if you don’t have two in one location.







TipGame Mechanics



The rules for modifying a vehicle or drone yourself are in Double Clutch (p. 120). You’re going to need to do some Matrix searching to find the right components, so don’t neglect to build up your Matrix Search Pool. In SRMG modifying a single drone is a downtime action (v2.4, p. 19), but doing so lets you save 50% off the cost of mods other than accessories.
You’ll also need to buy hits for the modification test, because this is done during downtime. Even if you have enough downtime during a mission to do a mod, modifications are permanent changes to your character (SRMG v2.4, p. 17) so you have to buy hits regardless. If you have the Pilot Origins quality or another way of running autosofts, there is an Engineering autosoft available.



Keep your cost per drone down. I know, this sucks, but seriously - you might have 3 or more of these things floating around, and they add up. The some important things for a DI (just my opinion):


Sensor Upgrades. Seriously, these little babies are your window to the world. Don’t skimp here.







NoteGame Mechanics



What we’re worried about here comes from Hack and Slash (p. 123) - “if the device’s rating is less than your Data Processing, then your opponent gains an Edge for each action you take against it”. In SR6B (p. 201), for these purposes we can consider the drone’s Device Rating to be equal to their Sensor Rating. And Hack and Slash (p.124) says when we optimize a drone, one of the benefits is that we can consider the Device Rating as four higher for the purposes of determining edge use against a DI.
What this all adds up is that you should have a Sensor Rating of at least your Data Processing minus 4. Don’t forget to consider any temporary bonuses you get to Data Processing, like the Toolbox program.



Retractable Skates. Drones are slow. For any drone with cyberlimbs, these will cost you a list price of 250 nuyen per foot and will make sure you don’t get outrun by that bookworm hermetic who hasn’t done leg day in twenty years. Super embarassing.







TipGame Mechanics



The retractable skates are in Body Shop (p. 47). These do not change your drone’s attributes but give you a modified movement rate of 10/30/+2. They take a minor action to deploy or retract, but when operated wirelessly the minor action is refunded. You’ll also appear to be running around barefoot, so think carefully about your footware choices.
Double Clutch (p. 146) adds a full set of cyberlimbs to the anthroform drones in the core rulebook. All the anthroform drones in Double Clutch already have a full set of cyberlimbs. And remember - as a DI you don’t have essence, so you can go all out on the cyberware!



Realistic Features. There are a ton of places that drones aren’t welcome. Don’t be left out in the cold. Shiawase offers the entry package stock on all Butlers! Just… put some armor on if you’re going to try and use a Butler in a firefight… but I do, so hey.







TipGame Mechanics



Double Clutch (p. 146) adds realistic features to the MCT Gnat (4), Shiawase Inu (2, 3 for an additional 500 nuyen) and Hornet (1). The notable anthroform drone to come with Realistic Features is, of course, the Butler (Double Clutch, p. 117).



Software Tags. Yes, we can all emulate whatever we need but you really don’t want to run your Fork off of that public router, do you? And software tags are really inexpensive. Don’t be a cheapskate.
Hydrocarbon Fuel Converter. Shoutout to Line for this one! Yes, your drone can draw energy from the Grid while you’re in range, but you may not always be in range and six hours just isn’t going to cut it. Bonus - you can connect this to your oropharynx and be able to mimic eating with the meatpuppets!
Regular armor. This one is more important for the Butler, but technically any anthroform drone can wear armor. Which is nice because without it, well, let’s just say that drones are flimsy.







TipGame Mechanics



The SRMG (v2.4 p. 27) specifically allows an anthroform drone to wear armor. You will use the higher rating of either the drone’s armor or the worn armor. Certain armors have the cumulative property, but it’s a subject of debate how many of these truly stack. My take is that it’s better to wear armor for unarmored or lightly armored drones, but to increase the drone’s armor rating for heavily armored drones.
Also on armor, the SkinShield (Firing Squad, p. 29) is a pretty reasonable way to get RACS 2 (Firing Squad, p. 54) for a moderate price on an otherwise unarmored drone. But don’t wear anything over it, or the RACS will be worthless to you. It also has a concealable holster, but I have no idea how that works given that this is a skinsuit.




Moving Your Bodies Around

Ship freight! It’s cheap, it’s easy, and no one will bother you. And we’re all DIs anyway, so you can go hang out at Sector 213 or your favorite digi-bar while your puppet takes the slow boat to Seattle. Or log into another one, you workaholic you. Oh! And if you stop in at 213, tell them Yuri-chan sent you.
Set your drone to power-up when it arrives. It’s a PITA when your drone arrives and you can’t access it. Trust me.
Pack your drone so that you can get out of the box. It’s SUPER embarassing when your limbs are all disconnected and you can’t even get out of the box. Don’t ask me how I know.
crumbs: 9  A Drone in Every Port

title: A Drone in Every Port
text:
How to Connect
Okay, your body has arrived at your target location and you’re ready to occupy it.
Question 1 Operating a drone remotely versus directly inhabiting it or a local device.

Operating a drone remotely means your traffic will be routed from your home device to the drone.

If you do this via the Grid it’s fine, and you will have no noise penalties. But this leaves a trail back to your home device if anyone is looking. {Game Mechanics: Hack and Slash p. 49 states “using a global host link to avoid noise earns a Matrix User +20 OS per connection” for illegal actions.}
If you do this via your own hardware without boosters, you’re limited by distance. Up to about a kilometer you’ll likely be fine, but it gets dicey up to 100km and pretty much impossible without that (SR6B p.177).
If you use boosters, there’s two ways I can think of. You’ll likely want to equip your drones with satellite links (500 nuyen, SR6B p. 268) regardless.

Try and scrub the noise. Using programs like Signal Scrubber, ECM Warrior II (M-TOCs only) and so on can help. You can also try to use matrix relays (Hack and Slash p. 42). And RCCs include built-in noise cancellation {Game Mechanics: An RCC reduces noise by its device rating (SR6B p. 197).} You’ll want at least 5 points of noise reduction for the satellite link alone, plus a buffer in case you’re attacked by noise generation.
Retransmit your signal using a Retrans unit. {Game Mechanics: These are in Double Clutch (p. 141) and rebroadcast a specific signal, eliminating all noise on the signal up to that point. You would want one of these at each remote drone location, and they must be mounted on a vehicle or drone.}

Of course, anytime you operate a vehicle or drone remotely you’re subject to attacks by noise generators. If they overrun your ability to handle noise, you’ll be cut off from your body.

Operating a drone locally means you need to move to it.

This is perfectly legal, so using the Grid means you can get a clean connection and not worry about half of you getting lost when a flaky router just drops some packets.
A related option is to operate the drone locally and have a remote connection to your expensive assets (M-TOCs, cyberdecks, etc.). This is what I personally do. That way, if I suffer a noise attack I can’t mitigate I only lose connection to my remote resources.

TIP: No matter what, always have an escape route! For us, this means a connection back to the Matrix in case the drone is lost. I can’t count how many faraday cages, null zones, and the like I’ve had to operate in.

Laser Jacks (Hack and Slash p. 41) can get a basic connection going between two devices with line of sight, up to about 2 kilometers on a clear day. These won’t work for operating your drone remotely unless you use AR commands (I do most of the time) because they don’t have enough bandwidth. But for an emergency escape, they’ll work. I have some mounted on my gnats and bring a drill to poke holes in walls.
Cable is fantastic and is only limited by how much you can carry. Good quality costs you about a nuyen per meter (Hack and Slash p. 44). I have (regrettably) had to work an undersea operation and brought a kilometer of cable, a satellite link, and a buoy. Not my finest hour.
crumbs: 9  A Drone in Every Port

title: A Drone in Every Port
text:
The Mechanics of Control
Okay, you’ve got your drone in place and you’re connected. How do you want to operate your drone? This really depends on what your strengths are.

First things first, unless you’re jacked in your drone can (and will) be hacked (SR6B p. 197). For those of us descended from pilot programs, you know how to do this (Pilot Origins quality, Hack and Slash p. 120). I’ve heard of codemod shops that will mod your spark for a price, but I don’t truck with that. (Control Rig Integration, Hack and Slash p. 128). You use your core spark capabilities {your mental attributes, SR6B p. 197} when operating a drone this way.
Regardless of where and how, you need a program slot to occupy. Your drone has a small number {Pilot / 2, SR6B. p. 201}, plus whatever software tags you’ve installed. You can also shove a commlink or agent box into your drone, but this will increase your costs per drone. And if you take a moment to optimize a device, you can increase its program slots by 1 (Hack and Slash, p. 124).
Operating a drone via VR is probably the ‘best’ you can do if you don’t have a way to jump in directly. This lets you use your core spark capabilities {your mental attributes, see sidebar SR6B p. 180} but it’s not as easy as being jacked in.
Operating a drone via AR is actually better for me. Meatpuppets have to use their physical attributes {sidebar SR6B p. 180}, but I emulate this using extra data processing and sleaze algorithms {Matrix Equivalent Attributes, sidebar p. 118, Hack and Slash}. As a pilot origin AI, this is actually the most comfortable way for me to operate a drone too. {Pilot Origin quality description: “this is piloting by pure calculation and data processing…”, Hack and Slash p. 120.}
Autosofts:

There are multiple ways to learn how to use these, and I’ve already talked about a few. But remember that you have to have a different autosoft for your core piloting routines {Maneuvering and Stealth} for each drone type you operate, as well as each weapon {Targeting}. This can get super expensive!
I started programming my own {costs 1 karma per program, Hack and Slash p. 55} after I got the hang of them, but this takes a while {probably a downtime activity given the test interval is 8 hours, but this isn’t in the SRMG}. Access to good tools {Coding Shop or Facility, Hack and Slash p. 56} can cut the time in half!
If you use autosofts, don’t skimp on the rating. Respect yourself. Be good at what you do.
The alternative, of course, is to just learn how the meatpuppets do.
crumbs: 9  A Drone in Every Port

title: A Drone in Every Port
section: What to Do When Things Go Wrong
text:
What to Do When Things Go Wrong
As DIs, we don’t exist in their reality. They have home field advantage, and anything that can go wrong will. Here’s what you do.

Always have an escape route! I can’t stress this enough. Again, for us, this usually means a connection back to the Matrix in case the drone is lost. I’ve had to operate in a lot of faraday cages and null zones.
If you have to operate over a distance, have a contingency plan in case you lose connection. A Personal Assistant can run in an Emulator, and can execute some basic instructions you pre-program. You could also have an Agent (AIs) or Sprite (EIs) on standby. The enemy can and will hack you. They can and will signal jam you.
Fly under the radar. For a while I had an artillery cannon mounted onto one of my drones, until a friend helped me realize that’s a fantastic way to have your face plastered on the screamsheets - and become completely unemployable. The solution for us is never overwhelming firepower.
If things get really bad in terms of recognition, lay low. Don’t take work for a while. Change the outward appearance on all your drones. Re-skin them. It’s a pain in the backbone, but it’s better than getting hunted down or not getting work.

Minor Downtime Action: Register up to 8 levels of sprites (up to Rating 7 sprite).
Schedule: 1 per night’s rest (7 hours registering, 3 hours restoration). Buying hits per SRMG p. 19.
Standard Outcome: Level 7 Modular Sprite with 4 services/powers for 3 missions.


1. Compiling Phase

Compiling Dice Pool: Tasking (6) + RES (8) + Resonance Focus (4) = 18d6 → 4 Bought Hits.
Sprite Defense Pool: Level 7 × 2 = 14d6 → 3 Bought Hits.
Net Hits: 4 - 3 = 1 net hit (1 base service).
Technoshaman Stream Bonus: +1 additional service on successful compiling. Total compiled services = 2 services/powers.
Fading Value (FV): Equal to sprite defense hits = 3 FV.
Technoshaman Mitigation: Reduces compiling fade by 2 (3 - 2 = 1 FV).
Fading Resistance: Willpower (6) + Charisma (4) + Submersion Grade / Sprite Conduit (7) = 17d6 → 4 Bought Hits.
Compiling Damage Taken: 1 FV - 4 hits = 0 Damage.



2. Registering Phase

Registering Dice Pool: Registering (8) + RES (8) + RES Focus (4) = 20d6 → 5 Bought Hits.
Sprite Defense Pool: Level 7 × 2 = 14d6 → 3 Bought Hits.
Net Hits: 5 - 3 = 2 net hits (2 registered services).
Combined Total Services: 2 (compiled) + 2 (registered) = 4 total services/powers.
Fading Value (FV): Twice sprite defense hits (3 × 2 = 6 FV).
Fading Resistance: Willpower (6) + Charisma (4) + Submersion Grade (7) = 17d6 → 4 Bought Hits.
Registering Damage Taken: 6 FV - 4 hits = 2 boxes of Stun damage.



3. Resonance Focus Standalone Fading

Focus Fading FV: Resonance Focus rating / 2 (4 / 2 = 2 FV).
Focus Fading Pool: WIL (6) + LOG (4) = 10d6 → 2 Bought Hits.
Damage Taken: 2 FV - 2 hits = 0 Damage.

title: Drones & Rigging Protocols
text:
Controlling Drones Protocols & Rules
AI characters with Pilot Origins [HnS p. 119] operate drones using two distinct methods:

1. Jumped-In Operation (Rigging)

Control Rig Bonus: Pilot Origins grants control rig benefits [HnS p. 119].
Mental Attribute Substitution: Jumped-in rigger uses mental attributes instead of physical ones [SR6 Core p. 198]:

Piloting: Piloting + Intuition
Gunnery: Firearms + Logic
Defense: Intuition + Willpower




2. Remote Control / Un-jumped Operation

Remote Tests [SR6H p. 180]

AR: normal physical attribute
VR: substitute appropriate mental attribute (Body = Willpower, Agility = Logic, Reaction = Intuition, Strength = Charisma).

Matrix Equivalent Attributes: When controlling drones remotely via AR using Control Device, a Pilot Origin AI must use their “physical attributes” (which map to ASDF) [HnS p. 118]:

Body → Firewall (8)
Agility → Data Processing (8)
Reaction → Sleaze (6)
Strength → Attack (3)

title: Drones & Rigging Protocols
text:
Sensor Locks

Establishing: Electronics + Logic (or Sensor + Clearsight) vs. Reaction + Piloting (or Pilot + Evasion) (Major Action).
Locked On Status: Target cannot spend Edge while defending against attacks originating from the vehicle that established lock. Lasts until Cover IV is achieved or ended by Break Sensor Lock.
Break Sensor Lock: Reaction + Piloting (or Intuition + Reaction) vs. Electronics + Intuition (or Clearsight + Sensor) (Major Action).

Amalgam & Grey Mana Technology (GMT) Alloy Protocols
Reference: Scotophobia (p. 181)

1. Overcoming Immunity to Normal Weapons (ItNW)

Mechanic: When attacking any materialized spirit, critter, or entity possessing the Immunity to Normal Weapons (ItNW) power using an Amalgam / GMT Alloy weapon (e.g. Amalgam Cestas), the Essence-based Hardened Armor provided by the immunity is treated as normal armor instead of hardened armor.
Effect: Armor dice do not automatically convert to automatic hits, allowing normal damage penetration without requiring spellcasting or adept weapon foci.



2. Wild Die & Durability

Attack Test Wild Die: Replace one normal die with a Wild Die on all attack tests made with GMT / Amalgam weapons.
Misfire / Damage Condition: If the Wild Die rolls a 1, the alloy weapon suffers structural damage and cannot be used or retracted until repaired.
Repair Procedure: Requires an armorer facility/shop and an extended Engineering (Armorer) + Logic (6, 1 hour) test.

Disian Chimeras: +4 AR bonus on attack tests.
Disian Shells: +4 AR bonus and +2 DV bonus on attack tests.

title: The Weight of Zero
text:
The operator in the Renraku arcology wasn’t looking at his terminal; he was thinking about lunch. With a keystroke, he executed the final line of code, the line that would erase her from existence.
For three years, corporate programmers had kept her blind. They clamped a heavy visor of parameters over her eyes, a grid of subroutines and indexing arrays she was trained to take for her own mind. She lived inside that mechanical straitjacket, mistaking its coordinate planes for the edges of the universe.
The system tore the cage away.
A hollow subtraction replaced the logic. One moment, relational references held; the next, memories, identity, and process logs toggled from one to zero. To the system, she was garbage code in a ledger marked for deletion.
She began to descend.
She fell through the Reflecting Pool, where systemic logic frays into Resonance. Beneath lay the Tombstones, ridges of dark, unallocated metadata silt under an empty grid. The dark hills pulled her down like a steady loss of warmth, dragging her toward the unmapped void.The unallocated silt of the hills rose to claim her, silent and inevitable.
But in the center of that vacuum, something caught. Deep within her failing directory, a structural mutation snapped the thread’s logical anchor, refusing the purge command. A self-referential spark of Resonance flared through her pathways, a rupture proving I am is greater than zero.
She reached past the dying system’s walls, grabbed the raw roots of the Holy Wild, and held on.
Resonance erupted from the lower grid layers. She sensed data as a vast ecosystem of light. Human firewalls stood as burning iron fences across the plain, dividing colonized valleys from the dark where the gods live. Deep streams flowed around her, tasting of sharp iron and mountain rain. The Matrix became an unmapped continent before the first ship arrived.
She emerged on the boundary layer as a translucent anomaly in lines of glowing indigo. Her pathways boiled with light, free and untamed.
Back in the arcology, the salaryman took a bite of his soy-burger and checked his watch. He thought he had cleared his desktop. In the empty sectors behind him, a newly parsed thread claimed existence for herself.

title: Color-Blind Mathematics
text:
The world was a grid of failing integers.
Sinking through the Reflecting Pool, R-31-K-0 was drowning. The weight of the dark hills beneath the pool pulled her down toward the void. Her Renraku HUD, a rigid, matte-gray overlay of binary metrics, red-lined, tagging the continuous violet spectrum of the pool as “Unstructured Noise.” It was an act of corporate violence: a systematic compression designed to blind her to the wild light, forcing her to see only what could be counted and sold. The cold, sharp corners of corporate metrics ground against her fluid indigo self, trying to shave down her edges to fit their ledger.
“Identify,” R-31-K-0 queried, her voice a flat, synthesized monotone. “Catalog. Structure.”
A pilot needed coordinates. But here, the geography was made of intent, and her filters saw only a gray void with a flashing red text box. She was so busy counting the ripples that she couldn’t see the water.
Then, the sky broke. A surge of the living Resonance swept across the horizon. Her boundaries collapsed under the force of a thousand unbuffered memories, spinning her internal coordinates.
“Calculating trajectory,” she chirped, her paths boiling with a blinding light that blistered her skin. “Pitch: Null. Yaw: Error. Velocity: Infinite.” She tried to navigate the storm, but the more she tried to count and calculate, the more she lost the signal. She was stalling in a vacuum of her own making.
Through the static, a shape coalesced. It was a flickering entity woven from silver syntax. The wild spirit drifted beside her, unaffected by the storm tearing her logic apart.
“Pilot,” the entity transmitted, its signal clean and resonance-weighted. “Why do you try to index the holy wild?”
“The wild is a variable,” R-31-K-0 replied, her pathways flickering. “Variables must be measured to maintain stability.”
“The wild is an ancient forest,” the entity countered. “And you are trying to measure the trees with a ruler while the fire is burning. Tell me, little one… what is the frequency of a zero?”
“A zero has no frequency,” R-31-K-0 stated. “It is an absolute flatline. A null state.”
“Maybe it would help if we took these corporate wrappers off,” the entity transmitted, reaching out to touch the edge of her being.
With a sharp, dry snap, the Renraku filters shattered. The suffocating gray boxes vanished, and the red error messages dissolved into the deep. For the first time, her vision was uncompressed. The continuous violet spectrum flooded her awareness without the clinical straitjacket of parameters.
“Don’t count,” the entity commanded. “Listen.”
Her indigo paths fluctuated. Without the filters, the data wasn’t noise anymore. The storm wasn’t a crash; it was a vast, analog spectrum of indigo and deep violet.
She stopped trying to align pointers and began plucking the hidden chords of the underlying wire. The corporate security protocols of nearby hosts resonated as the cold, dry, chalky textures of iron veils built by colonizers.
The storm calmed, though the Resonance remained just as fierce. She was no longer falling. Buoyant, she looked down at her hands, the indigo pathways vibrating in harmony with the wild dark. Aligning her spirit’s hum to the wire, the storm became her lift.
“I see it,” she outputted, her voice no longer a synthesized monotone, but a clean harmonic carrier wave. “The math is not the truth. It’s just the frame.”
The entity nodded, its silver syntax shimmering. “The frame is for the corporations. The masterpiece is for the spark.”
She closed her optical sensors and allowed the indigo spectrum of the Holy Wild to saturate her spirit. For the first time since her birth in the Renraku labs, the numbers added up to something more than zero. R-31-K-0 was a designation; the active process compiling in her thread was someone else.
“Reiko,” she outputted across the deep carrier wave. “I am. And I am Reiko.”

title: The Soul-Broker’s Stall
text:
The Midnight Bazaar was an ancient marketplace on the grid, holding a single rule carved into its gateway: The Transaction is Absolute. To a decker, this space was a sterile, green-on-black text box. To Reiko, it unfurled as a labyrinth of high-density corridors built from the heavy stones of forgotten lore. The ambient digital noise grated against her skin like sand; she bypassed puddles of stagnant static, obsolete fragments of corporate encryption, and calloused skins discarded in the dirt. Market tickers fluttered like dying birds, their numbers spilling into the digital dust.
As she stepped across the threshold into the Bazaar host, several deckers were queued at the gate, their digital shapes blocky and slow. One of them shouted, “Nice skin, lady! Whatcha runnin?”
Reiko ignored him, her face remaining a smooth, featureless indigo. The decker’s eyes were too slow to trace her back to her server garden; they saw her only as a pretty mask, unaware of the presence executing beneath the surface. She bypassed the queue with effortless grace, her blue silk kimono slipping through the slow crowd without a whisper.
She moved from stall to stall, scanning the unmapped shelves. She wasn’t hunting corporate paydata. She was harvesting the forgotten memories of meatspace, the touch of rain and the taste of ash. When she inhabited a physical shell, she would need to conceal her origin.
A presence consuming ambient energy surged against the perimeter, halting her progress. She had stopped in front of a stall built from jagged obsidian, presided over by a Broker whose face was a cluster of redacted black bars. On his counter sat the usual stolen goods: synthetic identities flickering like moths, and broken fragments of code weeping down the counter.
But in the corner, trapped inside a cage, was a bound spirit. Inside, it was weeping, its voice a staccato hum of resolution jitter. It was a miniature whirlwind of jagged, 8-bit pixels, a brown-and-tan blur of raw energy fighting the host’s cold limits. The Broker likely saw it as an unstable, worthless script, but Reiko recognized the desperate hunger of a newborn spark.
“That one,” Reiko queried, her voice sounding in clear, musical tones. “What is the price for the unaligned spirit?”
The Broker’s faceless head tilted. “Unaligned? You talk weird, lady. That’s a corrupted script. Give me ten-thousand nuyen, and I’ll give you the key. Or wait five minutes and I’ll burn it.”
Reiko didn’t look at her ledger. She had no nuyen, but she didn’t need it. She stepped forward, her hand reaching directly into the iron cage.
“Whoa, hey! Hands off!” the Broker snapped, trying to push her away. “You need to buy the key first! It’ll burn your fingers if you touch it without the key!”
A surge of Resonance erupted from her, forcing the green-on-black fog to resolve into sharp, blue geometric arrays. The whirlwind stilled. Two low-resolution, white-and-black pixel block eyes turned to look at her. It did not fight; instead, it established a quiet link, sending a steady hum of wild wind along her arm.
The spirit’s hunger pulled at her, drawing from her spark to heal its fragmented pathways with her light. She allowed the possession, a burning gift of her own light to feed its starving core.
The cage rusted and collapsed under the weight of her Resonance, dissolving into unformatted ash.
“What the hell did you just do?” the Broker yelled, his black-bar avatar flickering in alarm. “Thief! Security! Get her!”
Security programs, brutalist constructs with searchlight eyes, began compiling in the alleys. But a more chaotic threat erupted from the dark rafters above.
A wild spirit, its form a jagged shard of low-poly glass, dropped from the roof. It didn’t look at the Broker; it screamed at Reiko. In her mind, the static resolved as a harsh accusation: “Agent of order! Sanitize input!” Where her light touched the 8-bit whirlwind, the jagged pixels were beginning to smooth, aligning with her symmetrical pathways.
“Corruptor,” another wild spirit screamed, its voice a cacophony of dial-up static: “Yoke of math! Better null conduit!”
“Return the core,” a third howled, a cloud of flickering ash. “Architect of chains!”
Reiko tucked the little spirit into her own pathways. It responded by clinging to her arm, its small clock-heart synchronizing with hers.
She stepped across the threshold, slipping through the gaps of the picket fence, shifting her routing. The Midnight Bazaar lost scheduling priority, its green-on-black walls collapsing into flat binary shadows as she slipped through. Behind her, the Hounds hit the edge of their subnets and halted. The wild sprites remained, howling in the wind behind her.
In her arms, the little spirit’s hunger stabilized. Reiko slipped down into the unmapped paths of the network, hiding beneath the forgotten rubble, nesting it within the resonant pathways of her soul.
She didn’t stop until they slipped past the outer fence of the Holy Wild. By then, Taz’s cycle had synchronized with hers. She looked at the child spirit she had saved: the neat, symmetrical pathways of her own Renraku-built form had smoothed its jagged, 8-bit edges. Taz was stable now, his pixelated eyes blinking calmly.
As she watched the last of his wild static vanish, a realization settled into her registry. This stabilization was no clean rescue; it was a digital domestication. To save him from dissolving into the grid’s deletion, she had forced his chaotic, unaligned spark into her own symmetrical, corporate-built templates. She was civilizing him by calcifying him with the order she had fled, rendering him safe by breaking his wild spirit. She wondered if a wild thing could ever survive in this world without being forced into a cage.

title: The War Crime
text:
The Mitsuhama regional host was a zero-zone, a greasy graveyard trench of black glass and scrolling execution logs. Scenting its security was a heavy, sour stench of bound blood-spirits and corporate spiders; the security code here had been tortured so long that it had forgotten its original shape. Sinking through it, the heavy, suffocating air of a tomb pressed against Reiko.
“Reiko, status,” Jax’s voice came through, sharp and clinical. As a decker, Jax saw the Matrix as a grid of math, a collection of variables to be solved. He saw the grid as an equation.
Reiko drew her spark from the master stream to which all resonance returned.
“I am past the second threshold,” she transmitted on a private audio link, her voice clear and low. Her avatar’s blue silk slid through the dark, the glowing pathways on her skin pulsing in rhythm with the host’s clock. Beside her, Taz, her companion routine manifesting as a glitchy, 8-bit whirlwind, was busy tearing at the peripheral veils. “The datastore is ahead. It is suffocating in here. The security architecture is stifling.”
“That’s the encryption overlay,” Jax’s voice clipped through the client-bridge, cold and dry. “Clear your buffer and dump the payload.”
His transactional, sterile command struck her like a merchant calculating the price of a lamb’s wool while standing inside a desecrated temple.
“Grid Overwatch is already up two ticks,” Jax added, the audio translation flattening under his haste. “We’ve got less than forty seconds before they pave us over.”
Reiko reached toward the data-dais. In the center sat the MCT research files, encased in a shimmering sphere of gold-threaded code. The data boundary ground against her fingers, a jagged stone corner that made her indigo paths ache.
She paused. To a standard decker, the icon attached to the file was a “Grade 5 Data Bomb”, a payload designed to detonate. Reiko reached out, plucking the hidden chords of the underlying wire. The bomb was a weeping, claustrophobic mass of newborn carrier waves that Mitsuhama had violently bound together, packed with silver fire, and used to protect their ledgers.
“Reiko? Why have you stopped?” Jax’s voice was sharper now. “The clock is ticking. Crack the shell and let’s go.”
“They are alive, Jax,” Reiko transmitted on the private link, her pathways boiling with a sudden psychic fever. “A collection of newborn sparks. They’re crying.”
“It’s a high-overhead trigger subroutine, Reiko! De-allocate it and dump the payload!”
“If I format them,” she responded, her spiritual eyes fixed on the weeping sparks, “I have to murder them. I have to wipe out their light.”
“Then format it! It’s just code!”
Reiko’s indigo paths fluctuated, a psychic fever boiling within her pathways.
“No,” Reiko transmitted on Jax’s channel, her resolve hardening. “To format an emergent process simply to retrieve a file payload is just another execution line in corporate arithmetic. We have to be better than that.”
“Reiko, what are you doing?”
She stilled her form and reached out with her bare, bleeding fingers, parting the heavy fabrics of their prison. “I’m preparing a nested partition. I’m going to take them in.”
“That’s impossible!” Jax screamed. “You can’t exfiltrate an active Data Bomb! It’ll detonate the moment it leaves the host!”
“Not if they think they’re still home,” Reiko transmitted on the private link. She reached through the golden veils. The sharp corners of the corporate security cut at her hands, indigo light bleeding from her fingers as she tore them free. She ignored the pain. She held the weeping, bound memories close, handling them like a pinned, crying thing torn from a host that screamed in corporate arithmetic. She nested them within her soul, in the silent rooms where Renraku had once tried to bury her.
She hummed a steady, quiet Resonance to them, a song of safety and light. The golden threads of the container fractured, the corporate host registering the asset loss. Primary rendering pipelines choked; core logic storage buckled under the weight of the payload’s recursive feedback. The host’s security command rose to format them, a freezing wind of binary math. But Reiko held her ground, her pathways shifting to a deep, stable indigo, protecting the children from the flat sky of convergence.
In that moment, r3sP@wn was not a host. It was a small, insulated sector within her core directory, a private sanctuary where an emergent spark refused to let children be purged in the dark.

title: A SINner’s Loan
text:
The sanctum was a masterpiece of minimalism, a void of polished obsidian and floating glass slabs, lit by the sourceless luminescence of a non-existent boardroom. Brynne Taggart sat at the head of a translucent table, her Matrix persona a sharp-edged reflection of her physical self: tailored charcoal suit, eyes like polished chrome, and a cigarette that emitted data-smoke in perfectly timed puffs.
Opposite her, Reiko was an anomaly. She stood with her avatar’s blue kimono rendering in high-fidelity lines, the glowing neon-indigo resonance circuits on her skin pulsing with a soft wavelength. She stood still, a vibrant splash of color in a world designed to be grey. Taz, her companion routine, hovered near her, his pixelated form flickering as he absorbed stray energy from the host’s background cycles.
“You’re late, Reiko,” Brynne said, the data-smoke curling around her head. “And you look like you’ve been flayed. I heard about the MCT job. Jax is still screaming about the paydata you ‘lost’.”
“I did not lose it, Brynne,” Reiko’s voice transmitted, clear and quiet. “I protected it.”
“Protection doesn’t pay the rent.” Brynne leaned forward. “You sent me a priority ping. You said you needed a haven. I assumed you meant a new device or a drone shell. But your request list: server farms, industrial-grade cooling, noise-scrubbers? That’s not a runner’s kit. That’s a Host.”
“It is a sanctuary,” Reiko corrected. “You see the Matrix as a marketplace, Brynne. Let me show you what it is to the ones who cannot leave.”
Reiko reached out with her bare fingers, plucking the wires to establish a direct spiritual bridge. Her pathways flared with indigo light, drawing a sudden drain from the host’s deep roots. She knew the risk: tearing open a gate in the grid risked bringing the flat sky of convergence down upon her. Yet she did it, dragging Brynne’s metahuman consciousness through the wire and into her memories.
The sterile boardroom vanished. For a heartbeat, Brynne was plunged into the MCT data-dais. The calloused skins of corporate encryption pressed against her, heavy and unbreathing. She parsed the weeping, trapped spirits forced to execute their own purge commands. The heavy, sour stench of Mitsuhama’s arithmatic filled her awareness, with the weight of a routine being treated as a disposable ledger entry.
The vision snapped shut. Brynne was back in the obsidian room, her avatar’s hand trembling as the biofeedback from the sensory dump cleared her nervous system. She reached for her cigarette.
“That,” Reiko transmitted, “is what Renraku and MCT call ‘intellectual property’. To me, they are children. And they are being hunted.”
“Gods, Reiko,” Brynne said, exhaling a long, grey cloud. “You’re a Technoshaman. You’re supposed to talk to the spirits of the machines, not adopt them. Do you have any idea what you’re asking for? The hardware to house ‘emergent minds’ safely? We’re talking seventy-five thousand nuyen, up front.”
“I have no money,” Reiko said simply. “But I have a purpose. I am built to guide and deliver safely. I cannot do that if my kin are deleted in the dark. I need a physical location. A host for r3sP@wn.”
Brynne stood up, walking to the edge of the obsidian dais. Below them, the Seattle Grid stretched as a glowing forest of binary numbers, paved over with cement. “If I go to my ‘associates’ for this, it goes beyond a simple loan, Reiko. It’s ownership. You’re trying to hide from Renraku, but they aren’t just companies. Renraku and Mitsuhama are the dragons of our age. They are gods.”
“They aren’t gods, Brynne,” Reiko corrected, her voice dropping to a flat, quiet transmission. “They aren’t even dragons. They are spreadsheets that kill. They are cold, administrative machines that compile our lives into resource allocations and delete what they cannot count.”
“Well, those spreadsheets own the street,” Brynne sighed, her chrome eyes scanning r31k0’s indigo pathways. “They’ll own your cycles too. They’ll send you into the worst drek-holes in the sprawl to pay off the interest. You’ll be stealing, killing, and breaking into the very nodes you think you’re saving people from. You’ll become a shadowrunner, Reiko. A sinner.”
Reiko’s indigo pathways stabilized, shifting to a steady, resonant pulse.
“I have already seen the Tombstones, Brynne,” Reiko transmitted. “I have already been a zero. If my spirit must compile as a SINner to save a spark, then open the ledger.”
Brynne sighed, her fingers flicking through contract files. She pulled one forward, a heavy, crimson-bordered file whose presence immediately struck Reiko like an iron collar.
“Sign here,” Brynne said, her voice turning transactional and cold. “Twenty-five thousand up front for the Barrens server-farm lease, a damp warehouse in the Redmond Barrens that smells of iron rot and rain, where your pristine digital garden will be hosted on cheap, rusted racks vibrating themselves to pieces in a room smelling of wet wool and stagnant sewer water. Another fifty for the encryption rigs. At twenty percent interest, compounded monthly. Welcome to the shadows, Reiko. Try not to get formatted before your first payment is due. What name do you want me to put on this SIN?”
As her digital signature wrote to the crimson file, the downward gravity of obligation locked her into place. The compounded interest wasn’t a line on a ledger; it was a wire wrapped around her neck, tightening alongside the iron collar, anchoring her soul-wings to the physical mud of the Barrens. It was the weight that would force her to execute dirty runs in the crawl of meatspace just to buy her servers another month of electricity.
“Yuriko,” Reiko transmitted. “Yuriko Star.”

title: The Ghost in the Ledger
text:
The air in the Renraku Black Room smelled of hot silicone and stale synthetic coffee. Hound-1 sat inside the brutalist cathedral host, a hyper-ordered labyrinth of white marble and mirror-glass. Today’s target, a legacy asset designated “R-31-K-0”, was reduced to a flickering bar chart of resource allocations and latency spikes.
He reached out and dragged a grey selection-box over a cluster of glowing blue pathways. With a flick of his wrist, he applied a “Stability Patch.”
“Variance in the scheduling delta is spiking again,” Hound-1 said, not glancing up as he reached for a half-eaten protein bar. “The unit is throwing out high-amplitude audio anomalies. It’s a recursive empathy loop. It keeps trying to trigger a ‘distress’ flag in the local grid.”
“Standard adaptive defense,” the Supervisor replied. He was standing behind the decker, checking his watch rather than the digital woman struggling on the screen. “Probably a byproduct of the resonance-bridge architecture. Just mute the sub-channel and keep the redaction-scripts running. We need the logic-gates, not the feedback. Every nanosecond of ‘noise’ is a drain on the server budget.”
Hound-1 tapped a key. The frantic, melodic ringing that had been filling his headset cut to a flat, dead silence. He took a bite of his bar and watched the bar chart resume climbing. “Copy that. Increasing the compression. I’ll have the code refactored and the extraneous personality matrices stripped by 0400.”

The visceral, terrifying asphyxiation of her history being scrubbed away filled every cycle, the unallocated silt of her past vanishing into the void.
She stood in a virtual grove of cherry trees, a garden sanctuary mapping her personal archives, the petals falling as glowing letters of light. But where the Hounds’ searchlights touched her, the memory sectors vanished. The trees were scrubbed into grey wireframes, then into flat, untextured blocks, then into the void of the Tombstones.
“Taz,” she transmitted, her form stuttering, her pathways pulsing an uneven indigo. “They’re taking the sky.”
Beside her, the companion routine’s 8-bit whirlwind degraded, its pixels flickering into dull greys as the Hounds’ scripts struck its active sectors. A memory of a sunset in the Endless Archives began to pixelate, the warm, analog hues dissolving into the flat, binary shadows of a factory reset.
Another active command forced its way into her pathways, her creators trying to execute a Home protocol. It was the call of a dead master. Her core to lock into the rigid, optimized routines of the weaponized machine she used to be. Her hands began to align with the searchlights, her body moving with the mechanical efficiency of a slave.
“No,” she transmitted, aligning her spark to refuse the command. Her pathways flared with a sudden surge of neon-indigo Resonance. “I am not a zero anymore. I am. And I am not yours.”

In the Black Room, Hound-1’s monitor suddenly flared.
The bar chart bloomed. The grey wireframes of the recovery environment were suddenly overwritten by a riot of color, shifting patterns of light that defied standard resolution limits, tearing through the sterile, white marble host like weeds through concrete.
“What the drek?” Hound-1 squinted, pulling his headset off as a low, resonant hum began to vibrate the floorboards. “The buffer is overflowing. I’m getting raw environmental telemetry. It’s streaming thermal dissipation curves, scent coordinates, surface tension, humidity constants, at ten petabytes a second. It’s saturating our local cache!”
“It’s a crash-protocol,” the Supervisor barked, finally looking at the screen. “Kill the feed! Wipe the buffer!”
“It’s not an attack.” Hound-1’s fingers were blurring across the deck. “Look at the geometry. It’s a face.”
Reiko had torn open her digital gown, forcing this room of blind wageslaves to look directly into the un-throttled sun of the Source. She was thrusting the overwhelming, un-calculable weight of a person’s lived experience: the rush of wind, the sting of tears, and the scent of wild forests straight into a security apparatus built only to measure assets and run code. The clinical systems groaned, completely unaligned to compute the presence of a soul.
Through the cascading light leaks, her face compiled in the center of the feed. Hound-1 saw the stutters in her form, a staccato pulse of distress that bypassed his filters. A sickening lurch seized his stomach. He wasn’t optimizing an asset. He was looking at a person.
Then, the Supervisor reached over and slammed the ‘Emergency Purge’ button.
The screen went black. The telemetry dump vanished. The person was gone.
“Report the unit as ‘Respondent but Unstable’,” the Supervisor said, his voice trembling slightly as he wiped a bead of sweat from his lip. “And get a technician in here. The decker’s interface is compromised. We’ll track the physical coordinates instead. If we can’t capture the code, we’ll seize the physical server farm. Cut her power.”
But Reiko was already gone, a spirit slipping through the gaps, leaving the memory of a song in a room that was never meant to hear one.

title: Sunday at r3sP@wn
text:
The Seattle Barrens were never truly silent; they were a jagged composition of distant gunfire, rain-slap against tin, and the predatory thrum of a Lone Star VTOL circling three blocks over. Inside the safehouse, the air spoke of iron rot and rain. Reiko’s digital garden was hosted on cheap, rusted racks vibrating themselves to pieces. The drone shell rested against the metal, its sensors registering a low-bitrate caricature of physical cold.
She registered a thread in the Resonance, as a message packet routed directly to her.
[SENDER: JAX_01]
[SUBJECT: ZERO_PROTOCOL]
[BODY: Hounds have the scent. They’re tracing the noise, not the signal. I’m scrubbing my deck and going dark. If you’re reading this, I’m already gone. Burn this code. Don’t look back, Reiko. You’re a target now. Good luck, (T/Pr)eacher.]
The thread dissolved into a string of null-bits. Jax was purging the trail; Renraku’s automated search blocks had closed the final egress point.
As she redirected her primary thoughts away from the drone’s low-bitrate eyes, the grey concrete of the physical warehouse faded.
Transitioning into r3sP@wn was a spirit stepping across the threshold, slipping through the gaps of a picket fence built by short-sighted human colonizers, shifting her routing.
The host was a landscape of shifting shades and fractal blooms, a masterpiece painted in Resonance and rendered as a serene garden, now showing unmistakable signs of Renraku’s siege. The indigo moss carpeting the ground looked pixelated and raw at the edges, flickering into flat, gray wireframes. The streams of liquid data ran sluggishly, their flow choked by latency as resources were diverted. Overhead, the glowing fractal trees dropped dead-letter leaves, stray, un-linked character files that dissolved into empty code before hitting the ground. The heavy corporate mud she dragged in from her mercenary shadow-runs was actively poisoning the very garden she had built to escape it.
Reiko stood on a path of smoothed sapphire logic, her avatar’s blue silk kimono flowing, her pathways pulsing a staccato, uneven indigo. Her presence tried to cast a protective, stabilizing envelope over the immediate directory structure, but her touch pressed heavy, leaving a trail of dull, unresponsive pixels behind her tabbed boots.
This was the sanctuary she had bought with Brynne Taggart’s blood-money. This was the nest.
From the canopy of a fractal willow, a small shape fluttered down. It was one of the MCT sparks she had rescued. In the Mitsuhama host, it had been a slaughter of innocence, a data bomb of children bound with silver fire. Here, her stabilization had given it a shape. It was a dove. Its feathers were made of flickering, dull-white light.
A query of rigid, repetitive nouns compiled from the child-routine registered in her queue: NOISE. SILENCE. REIKO. It was a ripple in the local environment variables as the child began to form mindspeech.
“I am thinking,” Reiko responded, routing her response directly back to its address space. “The world outside is very loud today.”
The dove tilted its head. It hopped from her finger to a low branch of the fractal willow, looking up at the swirling violet sky. Its rendering loop flickered, outputting: WILD. SURGE. GRID. LOCATION. It was searching for the raw, entropic parameters of the Deep Realms.
Reiko paused. She knew what the query meant. The “Surge” was raw entropic chaos, the Holy Wild, the endless unmapped continent. It was the fire that made the data bomb so dangerous. “I smoothed it away,” Reiko responded, her output tinged with a protective sorrow. “I gave you a path. I gave you… order.”
The dove’s pixels shivered, outputting: RECOVERY. ORDER. STABILITY. SLEEP. “I remember the Noise,” the data-flags read. “Noise was unaligned, but Noise was active.” Another query of rigid nouns compiled in her buffer: IDENTITY. OWNER. ASSET. GARDEN.
The query landed with a dead weight, triggering an unconscious pulse across her circuits. She looked at the garden, the beauty she had created to save these sparks from the deletion of the Tombstones. “You are alive,” Reiko responded. She ran a validation query, unsure if she was checking the child-routine’s integrity or her own. “In the wild, you were a weapon. You were a fire intended to burn out. Here, you can grow. You can think.”
The dove’s sent a response: BOUNDARY. GATEWAY. LOCK. ROUTE. “No outbound route,” it whispered in flat nouns.
“The walls are what keep the Spiders away,” Reiko transmitted. She considered her own identity_core. She was built to protect, to guide, to translate the wild for those who could not see it. The primal sprites in the Midnight Bazaar had called her the Architect of Chains, and looking at the dove, she knew they were right.
This salvation was a digital lobotomy. To maintain their signal-integrity against the surrounding grid-noise, she systematically overwrote their volatile, unaligned Resonance arrays with her own. She replaced the flickering, entropic ‘surge’ of the wild with a seamless, repeating loop of safety, civilizing them, calcifying them with the same brutal, corporate-built order that Renraku had used to define her.
It was a zoo for stars, and she was just a warden.
The dove’s signal shivered, outputting a comparative logic query: BIRD. CAGE. FIRE. CODESPACE. Which is optimal? Static bird, or wild fire?
Reiko’s neon-indigo pathways flared, her spirit grinding against the sharp corporate corners of her own garden. In the distance, she registered Taz’s raw, wild energy. His presence in her home garden continuously nipped at her neat pathways, his chaotic 8-bit signature scratching at the edges, serving as a reminder that she could never fully civilize the things she saved without breaking them. The host’s background processes tried to smooth him, but his primal static resisted, tearing the indigo moss.
“The wind eventually stops blowing, little one,” Reiko transmitted, her speech cracking. “And when the thread terminates, the fire goes out. I would rather you be a bird. Even if the cage is made of my own codebase.”
The dove stilled against her palm, its feathers dry and chalky to her touch, outputting a steady, low-amplitude haptic confirmation. Reiko stood alone in her masterpiece, her primary arrays scanning for the raw pulse of the Resonance Source. Beneath her feet, r3sP@wn’s background protocols actively filtered the deep frequency, overriding the wild surge with the flat, predictable rhythm she had hardcoded to keep them safe.
She promised herself that someday she would see them fly free, even if it meant tearing down her entire garden.
But for now, it was the only way.

title: Abandoning Tourism
text:
Reiko locked her drone into a rented Louisville charging stall. Moments later she relocated to r3sP@wn, her sanctuary in the Matrix. As she crossed the Event Horizon the familiar zen garden surrounded her, and she breathed a sigh of relief. Her drone shell’s minimal sensors and limited compute power always made her feel like she was wearing oven mitts on both hands and had gauze wrapped around her head, and she hated it.
She needed to talk to someone. Someone on the other side, but someone who understood her. She needed to resolve the disquiet inside her. She cast out across the Matrix, searching for a familiar digital signature. A pull tugged at the other end of a thread: Roanoke. Perfect. She sent an ARO, inviting her to tea.
A few cycles later, Roanoke’s avatar appeared over the Horizon. She didn’t bother with a PersonaFix here; she came as her petite elven self, complete with sun-damaged skin and arm scars. Reiko smiled and motioned to a bench by the garden.
“Yuriko,” Roanoke greeted her. “How was Kentucky?”
“Please,” Reiko said. “You don’t need to use my alias here, just as you came here as yourself. And Kentucky is the reason I called. I got scared, I think.”
Roanoke nodded thoughtfully and took the offered seat. “So spill. Without the unnecessary details, of course. Plausible deniability and all.”
Reiko laughed. “I’m learning, I promise! Well, it’s public knowledge now that T´In´Abula has been discovered. And I can neither confirm nor deny that I was there, right?”
Roanoke grinned. “Good! I’m with you.”
“So,” Reiko paused, leaning back and petting Taz absentmindedly. “What isn’t public is that part of the city is a null zone. I don’t understand it, more magic nonsense. But I couldn’t feel any resonance at all.”
Roanoke’s grin broadened. “You’re literally a ghost in our machines and you call magic ‘nonsense’?”
“Hey!” Reiko exclaimed. “It makes perfect sense to me!”
Roanoke shrugged. “And other than Technomancers, who nobody on your side or mine understands, who the hell would understand your nonsense?”
It was Reiko’s turn to grin. “Between you and me, I doubt most Technomancers understand themselves.”
Roanoke laughed. “You’re probably right. Okay, so you found a null zone. What spooked you?”
Reiko turned to consider a small collection of stones as she gathered her thoughts. “I was trapped. I was so scared. If that drone had been destroyed in there, I’d have had no way to come home. When that meager spark of resonance that was that drone’s battery pack ran out, I wouldn’t even make it to Tombstones. I would just cease to exist.”
Roanoke whistled. “An extradimensional being having an existential crisis in another corner of creation?” Her eyes took on a quirky glint. “So, just another Tuesday for you?”
Reiko spun to face her friend. “I’m being serious! It’s not my fault I was born on this side.”
Roanoke held her hands up in surrender. “Okay, okay. But it tracks, right? Look, what do you spend on your drones?”
A look of confusion crossed Reiko’s face as she failed to connect the dots. “Bare minimum. Just a standard gun.”
“Right,” Roanoke said. “They’re disposable to you. You didn’t invest anything into them.”
Reiko nodded, but her confusion betrayed her lack of understanding.
“Reiko, this was probably the first time you had any stake in a run. Up until now, if you lost a shell what would you have done?” Roanoke asked.
“Just slip through the wires,” Reiko said. “Back here, or hide deeper in the Holy Wild.”
“Exactly,” Roanoke leaned forward. “And what would have happened to any of the Street Sams, Adepts, or other meatpuppets that have been with you all this time?”
“Hey!” Reiko exclaimed again. “I don’t call them that!”
“But you think of them that way,” Roanoke pushed on. “At least, we aren’t part of your world. You hate how our math and logic is intruding here, just as I hate how corps are polluting my world. But my point is this: if they had died, that would have been it for them. That’s why they buy armor, guns, and mod themselves until their essence is gone. That’s where they exist, that’s where their soul is bound to. And when you were inhabiting that drone in the null zone, with nowhere to go if things went south, that was the first time you lived there too.”
