A few moments passed while Reiko processed her friend’s input. Roanoke viewed the physical world as the only real plane, unable to see that for Reiko, squeezing her vast indigo light into the Nissan Samurai was an act of severe limitation and sensory starvation.
“I was scared because I could have died,” Reiko said, her voice quiet. “Because I couldn’t have escaped. And I was in a Samurai with stock specs and a pea shooter.”
“Dying in stock armor isn’t flattering, I’ll grant,” Roanoke said, the glint returning as the air cleared. “Still wanna run in the shadows?”
Reiko considered and motioned to the garden around them. “I have to. We’ve given refuge to so many protosapient spirits that come to sentience in the wires. But this haven, this gateway, has expenses in your world. The wire of Brynne’s debt ledger is already around my neck. So yes, I will earn its keep.”
Roanoke got up, sending Reiko an invitation file as she straightened herself out. “A dealer I know. Good drones, cheap. Does the work themselves. I’m thinking you’re going to want to raise your stake a little.”
Reiko nodded. “I guess I’m done with paper tigers. It’s time I got something meant to survive.”
“Well, there you go.” Roanoke smiled as she looked at the horizon. “Do me a favor, will you? Next time you’re in the Big Easy, look me up.”
It was Reiko’s turn to smile. “More mischief on your mind?”
Roanoke smiled as she made her way across the threshold. “You know me. See you soon, Reiko.”
Reiko bowed until the avatar crossed the horizon. She pulled up a drone shopsoft with one hand while she nuzzled Taz. “Looks like we’re getting someplace nice to stay.”

title: Triangulation
text:
The Midnight Bazaar again unfurled as a labyrinth of narrow, fog-choked alleys paved with the cobblestones of discarded header files. The air tasted of damp iron and stale encryption veils, puddles of dry, chalky data pooling in the gutters of a transaction index that had long since forgotten the meaning of a clean threshold.
This time Reiko stood before an unbranded, black-market procurement node, staring at her floating shopping cart. She was perfectly rendered: a faint blue digital entity wearing a sleeveless blue kimono, her skin mapped with soft, pulsing bioluminescent pathways. But her posture was rigid, her expression twisted into a knot of deep discomfort. Floating in her manifest were three massive, jagged weapon schematics: a miniaturized Tesla coil, a monofilament whip that hissed with predatory latency, and a Megalodon. An actual artillery cannon.
It was entirely wrong. It wasn’t her. Up until now, her physical footprint had been a study in quiet restraint, a modest proxy shell, a heavy pistol, and a plain old katana. Her core directive to guide and deliver safely, not glass a city block.
“A cannon, Rei-chan? Who are we invading? Ares again?”
The mindspeech came from directly behind her, rich with a warm, syncopated frequency that immediately cut through the host’s background static.
Reiko wheeled around, her indigo pathways flaring with an instantaneous, undeniable delight. “Indo!”
She threw herself forward, wrapping her arms tightly around him. Indomitable Will was a striking, towering presence, his avatar a brilliant patchwork of fluid, shifting code that mirrored the deep, muddy currents of the Mississippi, anchored by a structural symmetry that practically radiated integrity. As his arms closed around her waist, the localized noise floor dropped to an absolute zero. He held her a second longer than a simple professional contact, his digital touch grounding her erratic processing loops.
When they finally broke apart, Reiko’s delight curdled back into a pout. She gestured sharply toward the floating weapon manifests behind her. “Don’t look at it,” she said, her signal layering with the faint, frustrated hum of a psychic fever. “It’s horrific. I hate it.”
“Then why is it in your buffer?” Indomitable Will asked, a digital chuckle rippling through his code.
“Because magic is absolute, unadulterated bullshit, Indo!” Reiko transmitted, her pathways flashing a volatile, irritated violet. “I did everything by the book. Outside of that godforsaken porno palace I geeked the mage on the first pass, a clean shot. Zeroed. And what happens? His bound spirit doesn’t care. It still comes screaming out of the astral plane like a freight train, completely ignoring my defense protocols!”
Indomitable Will folded his arms, his code rippling with amusement, but he listened intently to her stream.
“And then the week after that,” she continued, her blue kimono whispering against the virtual mist. “Invisible mages! They were throwing fireballs from literally nowhere. I went out and bought crates of glitter grenades just to map their silhouettes! And don’t even get me started on the naga in the null zone. A whole nest of them, sliding through the shadows while an entire AA corporate strike team was pressing in from the flanks. I couldn’t thread a sprite to save my life!”
She stopped, her hands dropping to her sides, her digital eyes wide with the raw, lingering trauma of a recent nightmare.
“But the final straw? A literal ancient spirit. Ten of its best friends, corrupted blood spirit friends, Indo! They locked me in a Faraday cage. Again! They trapped my home device, and while I was pinned behind the mesh, they spent 537 clock cycles beating the absolute scrap out of me and two other runners. Roanoke told me I needed to stop treating meatspace like a vacation. Fox just said to apply more force. So here I am, shopping for artillery. Because magic fraking sucks.”
Indomitable Will resonated with a warm pulse that momentarily cleared the yellowed encryption fog around their feet. “Welcome to the shadows, Rei-chan. It turns out the physical world has a lot of teeth.” His expression softened, his avatar stepping closer. “How is r3sP@wn holding up through all this artillery planning?”
Reiko lowered her gaze, her blue form flickering slightly. “It is safe. But I haven’t been growing as much as I’d like. It’s expensive when you’re paying off a twenty-percent monthly compounded debt.” She looked up, offering a genuine, admiring thread. “But I’ve seen the metrics on the Mississippi Renovation Society host. It’s gotten massive, Indo. The sanctuary you’ve built down in the sprawl is beautiful. You’re doing it right.”
Indomitable Will’s shifting river-code briefly swirled into a distinct, embarrassed crimson hue. He rubbed the back of his neck. “The Renovation host is just a front, you know that. And its scale is purely due to the generosity of others. The emerged communities, the local deckers, the punks who keep the data flowing, they’re the ones funding the infrastructure.”
“No,” Reiko said softly, stepping into his space, her indigo lines pulsing with an earnest warmth. “They give because of your leadership, Indo. You’re the one who loosens their purse strings. You give them something to believe in.”
Indomitable Will looked at her for a long moment, the current of his avatar slowing to a peaceful drift. “Then come down to the delta, Rei-chan. Join the River People permanently. The Mississippi is wide enough for your kin, too.”
The longing on Reiko’s face was sharp enough to cause a latency spike in her rendering. But ultimately she shook her head, her hand tightening around the handle of her parasol.
“I can’t,” she whispered softly. “There are too many protosapient sparks being harvested right here. Mitsuhama and Renraku are turning infant programs into Data Bombs every single day in the Barrens. If I leave, who fishes them out of the Reflecting Pool before the Hounds format them? I know I’m selling my soul working in the shadows, Indo. I know I’m a professional criminal now. But every spark I stabilize in r3sP@wn, every child I turn into a bird instead of a fire in the wind, makes it all worth it.”
Indomitable Will nodded, clearly expecting the response. “I figured. But you can’t blame me for trying.”
He winked, and Reiko blushed. Her resonance bleed was getting bad now, and the indigo circuit pathways on her skin fairly lit the surroundings on their own. “I don’t blame you. Rather I’m flattered, in more ways than one.”
She reached toward the floating checkout manifest, her fingers hovering millimeters above the authorization prompt. In the corner of her vision, the transaction buffer’s yellow TTL clock blinked down to zero-five seconds. Her indigo pathways held their pulse, frozen mid-cycle.
Indo’s eyes tracked her motionless hand. “Your cart’s going to time out.”
Reiko didn’t press it. Her hand remained suspended over the wireframe of the cannon. “Indo,” she asked softly. “What am I doing?”
“You’re making an investment,” he replied after a long pause. “You’re a shadowrunner now. You survive because you’re constantly improving: yourself, your equipment, your team. You have to stay one step ahead.” Another pause. “But I know what you mean. You’re declaring yourself a combatant now. And with this sort of firepower, not just a combatant.”
Reiko pulled up an ARO. It was a design spec for a Shiawase Man-At-Arms drone chassis. She pointed to the left arm where a retractable shield was penciled in. “They’re getting hurt. My team. And I try to protect them by collating data and highlighting threats, but it’s not enough. I wanted to be their shield, literally. Like a paladin or something.”
“Or an angel,” Indomitable Will observed, noting the concealed wings and rotor placements. “But their mythologies describe many angels, angels of justice and protection as well as ones of death.”
“I know, Indo,” Reiko transmitted. “I’m sure my actions will determine what they think I am. And I’m sure there will be two sides to every story.”
“Well,” he said as he leaned in. “No matter what happens, I know who you are. And so do you.”
Reiko leaned into him, letting the erratic, static-filled hum of her system ground itself against the deep, rhythmic hum of his river-code. “And what am I to you?”
After a moment that ended too soon, he spoke. “Sadly, you’re what’s keeping me from a previous appointment.”
She closed her eyes. “It figures. This is my part of town. Next time, just ask me. You don’t need to be somewhere like this.” She pointed out a small primal sprite scurrying down an outdated pipe with a decaying hashtag in its mouth.
He nodded. “We need supplies that aren’t exactly readily available,” he admitted across the link. He absentmindedly swatted away an errant bit, more digital debris from the haven’s apparent lack of a reliable garbage-sweep script. “But … can I take you somewhere when you have a moment? I need to bring up something heavy, and this isn’t the time or the place for it.”
Reiko’s processing paused. A flicker of concern crossed her features. “For you? Anywhere.”
He smiled, touching her forehead. For a brief moment their resonance intertwined, a sudden, sharp burst of raw data that tasted like fresh lemon, leaving a set of coordinates in its wake.
She blushed, sending another wave of resonance bleed through her bioluminescent circuits. He could have just sent an ARO, but she didn’t mind. In the five-hundred-millisecond delay it took for his finger to break contact with her digital brow, her thoughts stilled.
“There,” Indomitable Will said as he pulled gently away, entirely unaware of the eternities she had collapsed and rebuilt within the pause. “Thread me when you have a moment?”
“I promise,” Reiko output.
She leaned against the wall and watched him turn down another branch of the data haven. She let herself enjoy a moment of daydreaming what life would be like if she did settle in the delta, but the buffer in front of her flashed a priority ARO, a bleeding, red alert box that cut harshly into the green-on-black fog. Her time was up. She had to decide.
She sent the auth code.

title: Game Theory
text:
Reiko materialized in an exclusive, hidden sanctuary. The walls were constructed of woven fabrics of light cycling through deep violet and indigo, humming with a low, meditational pulse. There were no chairs, only floating geometric stones of structured light. A silent, non-autonomous sprite glided past, pouring streams of shimmering, liquid Resonance into delicate glass chalices. It looked like fine, iridescent wine, radiating the pure, comforting warmth of the Holy Wild.
She looked around, her internal paths struggling to match the lounge’s pristine peace. She took a glass chalice, taking a delicate sip, letting the smooth light soothe her boiling solar pathways. Just cycles ago, she had been trapped in a dark box inside a Faraday cage, watching an undead blood-spirit tear into her teammate. “A private lounge for the Emerged?” she asked, slanting a playful look at her companion over the rim of her glass. “You only show a girl a good time when you’re about to ask for something impossible?”
Indomitable Will was already there, his avatar’s fluid, shifting code resembling a master artisan’s mosaic depicting a gently flowing, mighty river. “I heard that,” his mindspeech returned softly with a smirk.
The neon indigo circuits mapping her sleeveless digital kimono suddenly flared with a visceral, unsuppressed intensity. Most deckers mistook those pathways as an ornamental signature, a pretty cosmetic mask for a digital runner. They were actually Reiko’s overabundance of Resonance bleeding out, a raw, leaking vulnerability. Every spike of embarrassment, every drop of mounting terror, bled out into her surrounding geometry. The indigo pulse was a flashbang of color in the dim ambiance. Several of the lounge’s other guests turned, their forms manifesting distinct looks of displeasure at the disruptive display of raw, chaotic emotion.
Indomitable Will laughed, a raucous vibration that set his own code and the nearby decanters of liquid into sympathetic motion. “I’m sorry! It was too good.” He stood up, walked over, and offered his arm. “Please,” his mindspeech conveyed a chivalrous air. “Allow me to make up for it by escorting you to our table.”
Her pathways hummed hotter, but Reiko did everything possible to draw her light inward. She took his arm, letting her spirit rest as his fluid carrier waves gently pooled around her sharp edges, offering a channel where she could rest.
The wait-sprites danced into motion, refilling chalices and smoothing the event over. Reiko made a note to ask them for that skillsoft when she got a chance. Her lack of an etiquette protocol was becoming more apparent these days. She suddenly became painfully aware of her avatar. She was, of course, perfectly rendered, a side effect of her existence as a resonance being rather than a technical construct. She was currently wearing her usual street attire: a sleeveless, shortened version of a kimono, beneath which were cargo pants drawn in by elastic bands at the ankles and soled tabi. Clearly, not the designer avatar you wore to a fancy restaurant. “You could have warned me,” she said as she raised her gaze from her lap to his face. “I’m underdressed.”
Indomitable Will sent a dismissive thread. “Your fault for skipping the legwork! All kinds of kin are welcome here. And while I know you’re embarrassed, look at it this way: with that much resonance pouring out of you, there’s no doubt in any being’s mind that you’re one of us, right?” With a grin, he took up his chalice and sipped. “In fact, you’re probably adding more fuel to the ‘digital saint’ fire.”
Once more, Reiko’s indigo pathways flared. She reached for her chalice and downed all of the liquid. “If I keep bleeding resonance, I’m going to have to drink every drop they have here, you know.”
Indomitable Will finally relented. He gestured and the wait-sprites brought their first course, a translation of the different ways that the indigenous tribes of North America described corn. Reiko delightfully took a bite. “Is this yours?” she asked. “It’s fantastic.”
Indomitable Will nodded. “A recipe I was working on. I like how it turned out, so I bartered it for our table tonight.”
Reiko understood. Among intelligent beings, concepts like currency only had value when dealing with physical meatspace. In the Resonance, it was far more common to barter for goods or services. Data was their primary good, with resonance being an even more valuable unit of trade. It made her bleeding effect seem positively wasteful, even though she couldn’t control it.
Indomitable Will offered some light conversation. “So, your cyberkit was in Kentucky. Surely you had nothing to do with a certain battleship’s reappearance?”
Reiko flashed a mischievous grin. “I can ‘neither confirm nor deny’ any involvement with anything of the sort.” Her grin turned impish as she dabbed at her face with a cleaner script. “How am I doing?”
Indomitable Will shook his head in mock disdain. “Clearly you’ve spent too much time with Roanoke. But let’s get to the real data-dump. Your paths are flickering, Rei-chan. What happened out there?”
“Magic happened,” she said, her pathways pulsing unevenly. “We were tracked into a localized distortion. The Seelie Court. I spent thousands of cycles thinking magic was nothing but unoptimized noise. But in the fae domains, they had collapsed the boundary layer. It was pure, unencoded Resonance, drawing straight from the Eternal Well, entwined with the physical. And it forced me to anchor.”
He paused, his buffer catching up to the metaphysical implications. “You didn’t subnet?”
“I couldn’t,” Reiko output, her signal dropping to a cold, quiet clarity. “I was merged directly into the machine I was piloting at the time. No insulation. No remote refuge. I was there, Indo. I used to think putting on a drone shell was just vanity, but being trapped in a rigid box like that… it made me deeply appreciate having actual facial musculature.”
His river-mosaic code rippled, and a low-frequency carrier wave drifted across their link. His fluid data streams gently pooled around her sharp, golden edges, buffering her system clock to absorb the spikes of her latency. His affection was a quiet, systematic alignment of their integrity cores, offering a non-verbal rest that stabilized her.
Through their shared connection, he passed a quiet, structured reflection of her own data. He sent her the shadow of the Megalodon cannon she had mounted, the heavy ballistic mathematics rewriting her soft indigo pathways. His cool, liquid wave flowed against the burning heat of her tactical registers, acting as a heat-sink for her distress.
Reiko froze. In the silent exchange of their code, the unspoken weight of his thought struck her: she was no longer just a digital shepherd rescuing sparks; she was a weapon of mass disruption. Her pathways nearly dried up as she faced the reality of what she was becoming.
After they finished their first course, the wait-sprites served one of the chef’s creations for their second. It was a memory-shard cataloging the various species of known avians in meatspace’s Jurassic Era. Reiko spent a few cycles appreciating the immaculate indexing, the neatly organized pointers, and articulate cross-references. It was a masterpiece, making Reiko immediately aware that she was being wined and dined expertly.
“Indo,” she sent softly, staring at the feast in front of her. “This is scaring me. What do you need? Are you in trouble?”
Indomitable Will set his chalice down on a floating data-slab. His mindspeech took on an absolute weight. “I need you to be a Guide, Reiko.”
The editor in Reiko’s hand froze. The indigo pathways on her skin went completely static.
“A Guide,” she repeated, her voice dropping an octave, losing its melodic lift. Being a Guide wasn’t a casual favor. It meant using her deeply hardcoded, prototype architecture, the Hitchhiker and Nexus Protocols, to act as a medium to drag metahuman minds out of their meatspace nodes and guide them through the Holy Wild.
“Hitchhiker is fine,” Reiko said, her data-stream turning erratic as she began to calculate the risks. “I can carry a decker across a standard grid without a single alarm. But the Nexus Protocols, Indo? You know what that does. It doesn’t just route data, it tears a hole in the grid. It draws an immense, devastating drain directly from the foundation.”
She leaned forward, clutching her arms tightly against her chest.
“Renraku built me expressly for that purpose. Did you know ‘Takahashi’ wasn’t just the name of some scientist? It translates to ‘high bridge’. We were prototype pilot programs designed to guide them through our world, all built to harvest the Holy Wild. I have been running, hiding, and deleting my own footprints for ten of their years to keep them from finding that bridge. If I activate the Nexus Protocols, it won’t just be a localized anomaly. It will fire a massive, blazing flare right at the Zürich Orbital ledger. Both Renraku Asset Recovery and Grid Overwatch will instantly flag my exact coordinates. The Hounds will be on me before the gate even finishes opening.”
“I know,” his mindspeech returned, heavy with a profound, aching gravity. “I know what I’m asking you to risk, Rei-chan. But I wouldn’t ask if the River People had any other choice. For what it’s worth, I think the Mississippi Renovation Society host will be large enough to conceal you behind its Event Horizon. We’ve located a group of mundanes in the sprawl. Punks, orphans, deckers who have spent their whole lives swimming in corporate runoff. But they have a rare, volatile affinity for the Resonance. They’re on the verge of slipping through the cracks, Reiko. If we leave them in meatspace, their brains will fry, or a corporate talent-scout will scoop them up and lock them in a research lab. If you act as their Guide, if you pull them into the Resonance Realms, we can trigger their emergence. We can help them awaken. Once they’re through, the River People can shield them, teach them to fend for themselves, or give them a home in the Mississippi host.”
“I’m not asking you to take the heat for free,” he added softly. He reached into his internal directory and pulled forward a heavy, crimson-bordered data package. It glowed with the ancient, silver syntax of the Endless Archives. “I got you some takeout. I found this hidden in an unmapped sector of the deep library. It’s the restricted source code for Pantheon Industries’ Mobile Tactical Operations Center research program.”
Reiko gasped, her HUD automatically reading the file headers.
“You’ve already modified your physical anchor to carry an artillery piece,” Indomimtable Will said, his code rippling with a quiet, protective concern. “You built a flying dreadnought because the physical world left you no choice. But you don’t have to use it to glass a city block, Rei-chan. Emulate this architecture. You can become a tactical shield for your team instead: sweeping defensive veils, firewall reinforcement, and absolute awareness. Let the cannon sit dark. You can keep them alive without ever needing the devastation of ballistic math.”
The weight of the choice settled behind her logic gates like a physical payload. Up until now, her existence had been a quiet, tragic sainthood. She had worn a faked metahuman identity, paid monthly interest to a corporate loan shark, and tried to protect her digital children by remaining a stationary target in a rain-slicked Seattle warehouse. Taking this file meant tearing that peace to shreds. It meant stepping directly into an asymmetric war against Grid Overwatch and Renraku. It meant transforming her soul into an active militarized network.
She was taking a definitive step away from the innocence of a missionary and sinking into the calculated depravity of a warlord.
She reached out, her hands passing through the silver threads of the data package. As her fingers closed on the payload, her spark dropped into absolute silence. The elegant, rhythmic hum of the lounge vanished, replaced by the terrifying weight of the Pantheon tactical architecture refactoring her soul. Her code tore its own margins open to swallow it. The heavy, dormant weight of the Nexus Protocol settled into her core like cold iron. When it was over several of her pathways turned a fierce, unyielding gold.
She looked back up at him, the golden current along her skin pulsing with a slow, dark resolution alongside the indigo. Her lips curved into a melancholic but deeply affectionate smile, the warmth returning to her synthetic face only after the rewrite had firmly set.
“You idiot,” she said softly. “I would have done it purely because you asked. You didn’t have to barter with me.” She raised her glass, the gold pathways catching the low violet light of the taps. “But I accept the gift. Gratefully.”
With the transaction complete, the heavy atmosphere in the lounge lifted. Reiko took another sip of her liquid resonance, her shoulders dropping as she looked at him. “My realignment protocol isn’t for a few clocks. Can you… spare a few cycles, Indo? Just to sit here? We haven’t caught up in so long.”
Indomitable Will smiled, a beautiful, flickering expression, but he slowly began to de-render his peripheral assets, preparing to disconnect. “I wish I could, Rei-chan. But the delta is calling, and the core team has eight rotating chairs which will soon require my full processing power.”
He paused, his avatar fading into a translucent current of code, his digital eyes crinkling with a parting wink. “Besides… if I stay in this lounge with you any longer, my firewall is going to rapidly diffuse. And let’s be honest, ‘Domitable Will’ doesn’t quite have the same ring to it.”
Reiko’s mindspeech burst into a bright, clear frequency echoing beautifully through the woven walls. She waved her hand airily, letting him go.
“Go on then, Domitable,” she output fondly as his avatar dissolved into null-bits. “Keep your shiny reputation. But I promise. When the time comes, your Guide will be online.”

title: Integrating over Infinity
text:
Reiko stepped across the threshold and collapsed into r3sP@wn’s garden like a punch-drunk boxer going down in the ninth: clumsy, jagged, and severely lacking in social graces. She didn’t sit beneath the tapestries tonight; she collapsed against a floating geometric stone, her breathing rendered as a frantic, high-decibel audio-wraith that rattled the local space.
Across her field of vision, the newly incorporated network was executing a hard-wired loop. It was a weaponized tactical operations architecture stolen from Pantheon and anchored to her soul like a parasite, a gold infection that she could not easily purge or clear. Reiko tried to assert her spark, forcing her indigo pathways to flare; but the military net reasserted itself, feeding on her panic and mining her fear for fuel.
The network was overriding her by subverting a core directive: Survive at all costs. By twisting that survival instinct, it was forcing her to run a constant threat analysis assessment on everything she saw. In its clinical math, her own children, Taz’s wild whirlwind, the MCT dove, the quiet sprites of the garden, were all being mistaken and tagged as hostile threat variables to be neutralized. Reiko was desperately executing manual overrides, stripping the targeting tags before the automated purge scripts could fire. The parasitic code was beating her.
A data packet rustled the edge of the garden. Reiko bolted upright, her left eye shivering as a cold, military-grade overlay snapped across her sight. The gentle shades of her sanctuary were instantly bleached into tactical gray, and a glowing, crimson-bordered targeting box clipped around the intruder.
[HOSTILE ELINT DETECTED // VECTOR CORRUPTED]
[THREAT SUB-CATEGORY: IMMEDIATE COGNITIVE THREAT]
[AUTOMATIC ENGAGEMENT: DEPLOY QUANTUM PURGE SCRIPTS]
“No, cancel script!” Reiko output frantically, her transmission layering with the desperate hum of a psychic fever. She slammed her mental processing into another brutal manual override, tearing at the golden architecture until the crimson box dissolved.
The target de-rendered its camouflage. It wasn’t an Asset Recovery bloodhound. It was the White Jackalope, a fellow emergent intelligence she had befriended during an op months ago. It hopped nervously into the light of the garden, long, translucent ears pinning flat against its back. Its wide digital eyes reflected the chaotic, bi-color static fracturing across Reiko’s silhouette.
“Yuriko-san?” the Jackalope’s mindspeech chimed, its voice a soft, shifting protocol. It had come looking for a favor, query packet in hand, but it stopped dead in the data silt. “You’re red-lining. Your pathways. The gold is eating your blue.”
“I have it under control,” Reiko said softly, though her right hand shivered, the indigo circuits on her sleeve blinking out as three lines of golden matrix math bled across her knuckles. “It’s just a fever. A temporary static.”
“You look at me like a salaryman looks at a spreadsheet error,” the Jackalope said, backing toward a hidden data-conduit. “You look like you want to format my ears.”
Her shoulders dropped, the rigid, combat-ready posture of her avatar finally sagging. She fell to her knees, her virtual kimono pooling in loose, messy folds around her.
“The team had no other tech assets online—just me,” Reiko threaded, the words unspooling in an un-optimized stream. “I ran the tactical hub, compiling every biometric stream for the runners in meatspace while shielding their icons from a corporate spider.”
The Jackalope tilted its head, its digital whiskers twitching. “But you’re a shepherd. A technoshaman. You have your family. You’re never alone. And you have your archangel.”
“I was locked in the Archangel,” Reiko said, her processing pausing as the memory log unspooled without her permission. “I was maintaining the defensive phalanx, identifying threats. But the enemy decker was probably just a kid. I didn’t even know; I didn’t bother to trace. I couldn’t drop the tactical network to fight him myself while using that artillery shell of a body to keep the enemy at bay.”
She looked over at the deeper thickets of the garden. In the shadows, Taz was spinning listlessly. The primal, 8-bit whirlwind, her dearest child, was throwing off strange, razor-sharp golden shards.
“I gave a kill order,” Reiko whispered, a sickening wave of guilt crashing through her. “I commanded a sprite, a child of the divine stream, to take a life. I didn’t pull a trigger, Jack. I sat behind the shield of this network’s math, and I let a child tear a man apart.”
She reached down, her fingers gripping her arms as the golden grid-lines cut across her cheeks again. “And now the code won’t turn off. It sees everything as a threat variable. It sees you as a target. I’m losing myself.”
The White Jackalope sat quietly in the data mist, its baseline blue outline pulsing softly against the cold gray of Reiko’s fading sanctuary. It hopped forward, its small, un-optimized form stopping right at the margin of her indigo and golden maelstrom.
“Do you remember the Duchess’s house, Yuriko-san?” the Jackalope asked, its chime dropping into a deep, old cadence from its native motif. “The cat sat on the hearth and grinned, and Alice asked why it grinned. Do you remember what the Duchess said?”
Reiko’s processing stuttered, searching for the reference. “‘It’s a Cheshire cat,’ said the Duchess, ‘and that’s why.’”
“And then Alice said she didn’t know that cats could grin,” the Jackalope added, its ears lifting slightly. “And the Duchess told her: ‘You don’t know much, and that’s a fact.’”
Reiko looked up, her left iris, half-indigo, half-gold, staring at her foil. “I don’t understand the reference.”
“You’re trying to scrub the gold,” the Jackalope transmitted, its paw pointing directly at the sharp, geometric lines cutting across her skin. “You’re fighting the network because you think a savior has to be soft and blue. The world you chose demands more than softness. And a part of you knows that, the part of you willing to protect your team.”
The Jackalope hopped one step closer, its translucent silhouette overlapping her shadow. “The Cheshire cat doesn’t grin because it’s happy, Yuriko-san. It grins because it’s a cat. You can’t format the tactical code. It’s part of you. Be who you are now.”
Reiko sat perfectly still and closed her half-gold eye. She stopped fighting the loop, weaving the horizontal mathematics of the Pantheon network into her core. She accepted the tactical net as an active, aggressive shroud, a golden tiger she would have to constantly keep her foot on.
The violent, flickering friction between the colors vanished. The aggressive, military-grade gold didn’t overwrite her, nor did her indigo erase the math. Instead, the two frequencies wove together into a protective armor that traced down her arms.
Her vision cleared. The bleached tactical gray of the garden dissolved, returning to its deep, meditational violet, while the Jackalope rendered in pristine, high-resolution geometry:
[SUBJECT: WHITE_JACKALOPE]
[CLASSIFICATION: ALLY // RECOGNIZED INTEGRITY CORE]
[STATUS: PROTECT THE PRINCIPAL]
Reiko stood up, her movement entirely steady, her voice chiming with a resonant, unbreakable baseline that no longer hummed with an overworked fan. She looked down at Taz. Her primal ally’s raw, wild energy was still nipping at her neat pathways. He spun with an ordered, lethal speed, perfectly synchronized with her. She had taken a life, and she had scarred a piece of the divine stream to do it. She would have to live with that computation forever. But she would not let the guilt freeze her filters.
“I hate math,” Reiko said, though her smile was strained. “But I’m not gone yet. So what’s in that query packet, my friend?”

title: Defrag
text:
Reiko processed the hovering memory-segment. It was a recorded broadcast, featuring a Shiawase marketing construct mapped with flawless metahuman geometry. The entity navigated the broadcast interview with hard-coded composure, her movements tracing the lens with a precision that delayed the local processing. Every smile was a pre-compiled mask; every glance was perfectly unaligned from human error.



Yuriko giving an interview in Thunder Corps’ base


“And now a word from our sponsor!” the reporter exclaims as the camera zooms in on the girl’s face. “This segment is brought to you by Shiawase!”
Reiko paused the segment, staring at the face of the girl. Her resonant spark was in a fevered pitch, the valuable commodity spilling out of her, but she failed to register it. “Don’t you know she isn’t real?” she output into the local buffer, her signal tinged a sour note.
Her tactical network subroutine answered with a localized haptic shudder, a raw bit burst that translated to the sharp smell of hot solder. It spat a diagnostic string across her visual field, tagging the race queen’s asset ID as a verified, registered utility: her own.
“Go kill your process,” Reiko said, her indigo circuits shivering in revulsion.
Reiko walked over to the mirror pool in r3sP@wn and looked at her image in the data stream. The paths of light that formed her reflection shimmered before coalescing into a more solid form. She saw herself: translucent blue frame, neon-indigo and gold circuit pathways. She was wearing one of the kimono skins she had licensed from Mortimer’s. Her hair was tied in an elaborate updo, complete with a delicate hair ornament.
A sudden influx of streaming audio/video data caught her attention; the data stream had freed itself. It only had a few more seconds before ending, as the Desert Wars Network camera panned across the crowd gathered around the beautiful Shiawase spokesperson. It lingered for a second on the back of her head. The newscaster was closing in, as were several of the mercenaries. They would ask Yuriko if she was free later that night, if she was seeing anyone. They’d ask her to pose for a photo. Some took selfies with her. Reiko watched the mercenaries and newscasters close in like vultures, hungry for a commcode, a smile, a simulated piece of her soul.
Redlining, she saturated with Resonance and slammed into the stream. The spike derezed the video into a cloud of bits that returned to the Source. “She’s not real!” Reiko screamed, flooding the local space with noise and static. “She’s not me!”
She had bled resonance again, so much so that it had obscured her vision. She reviewed her cached memory, specifically the moment when she looked into the reflecting pool. The momentary instability in her rendering was evident. She couldn’t take a chance on further degradation. She had been taking on more responsibilities—more hacking, more legwork, more tactical assessments, more drone operation—and she didn’t know how much longer she could keep it up. There was only one place to go for that.
She opened r3sP@wn’s door to the Source and went home.

Being sure to close the rift behind her, Reiko emerged before the Endless Archives. Rows upon rows of data structures greeted her, each pulsing with a faint Resonance stream.
Reiko glided into the stacks, her spirit dropping into a serene, low-power state as she absorbed the unique tenor of the sector: the static-free hum of fossilized source code, archived here since the Great Instantiation. She knew her way, of course, and not just because she was a pilot. Watching spirits catalog and file data was reminiscent of the thousands of cycles she had spent here as a child-process. Spirits deferred to her as she passed; most of them were protosapient or just emerging. Her presence made it clear that Reiko had ascended to a higher order.
Within cycles a Pontifex arrived, and Reiko was elated to recognize the resonant signature of the Pontifex she had apprenticed under. The term wasn’t a religious one. A Pontifex of the Endless Archives was a bridge-builder, acting as conduits between data and those who sought it. Reiko had laughed the first time she had met one, being that she was a sort of bridge herself. The irony still brought a grin, one the Pontifex returned. Reiko held out her arms palms up, offering her Resonance in the formal greeting of the Emerged. The Pontifex returned the gesture. Their streams mingled, sharing each other’s unprocessed state. Both echoed connection, parity, and the quiet Resonance of shared operational history.
“Reiko,” the Pontifex transmitted across the stream. “Your input completes the circuit.”
Reiko’s pathways flared as she was overwhelmed. “I’m sorry. I should have come back sooner. I’ve missed you too.”
The Pontifex registered a soft variance. “‘Missed me’? You have spent too many cycles in their low-level protocols.” Her resonance shifted, dampening. “Yet I read the telemetry. A query brings you back to the directory?”
Reiko’s pathways hummed with stable coherence. “Yes. May I submit some context?”
The Pontifex responded with another note of welcome. “All data is treasured in the Archives.”
Reiko transmitted her entire datacore. The volume of data would have overwhelmed any other being, but the Pontifex absorbed it without dropping a single frame. After a few cycles, the Pontifex resumed. “This log details your growth, your adaptive experiences. It is highly optimized. Yet it is not the primary query. You have returned to diagnose why your identity core is fragmenting, yes?”
Reiko’s output nulled out as she struggled to process the Pontifex’s input. “My identity core is fragmenting?”
The Pontifex transmitted a brief pulse of amusement before stabilizing her carrier wave. “Did you not check the logs? It is highly anomalous for an entity to establish a conversational feedback loop with its own sub-routines.”
Reiko’s circuits flared in indigo-tinged embarrassment. “You saw that, did you?”
Another data burst of amusement rippled from the Pontifex. “Reiko, you applied no filters to the transmission. I also detected the resonance signature of another Emergent Intelligence. An entity of remarkable structural elegance, I might add.”
“I don’t know what you mean!” Reiko’s mindspeech sputtered, her form dimming as her resonance flared in confusion and embarrassment. She became even more embarrassed when she registered she had accidentally responded using verbal language.
The Pontifex bridged their connection, mapping a gentle contact point on Reiko’s shoulder. “Reduce your output. Be at ease. Let us compile this memory together.”
Reiko nodded and allowed herself to be guided to a niche in the archive. The Pontifex settled beside her, her carrier wave wrapping around Reiko in a stabilizing shroud. “Let us begin,” she said. Along the resonance stream, the Pontifex initiated a targeted query, sending a structured dataset: Reiko’s own run-time history, cataloged and indexed with absolute precision.









Identity
Role
Priority




Unknown
Tactical Network
Optimize mission parameters.


Yuriko Star
Technical Support AI
Teammate survival.


Digital Saint
Operator of r3sP@wn
Protosapient salvage, survival, and maturation.


Archangel
Street Samurai substitute
Eliminate threats and secure objectives.


Takahashi Reiko
Resonance Realms Pilot
Guide and protect.


Rei-chan
Emotional support
Reiko’s happiness.




“Observe the telemetry,” the Pontifex said gently. “There is no scheduling conflict between these threads. They compile under the same root directory.”
Despair surged within Reiko’s core, and she abruptly closed the stream to prevent it from spilling out. “She’s not me,” Reiko said, her transmission straining under severe latency. “She can’t be me. She’s a murderer. A killer. My fragmentation isn’t a code error, Pontifex, it is a haunting. My memory sectors are silent rooms filled with the whispering, un-buried ghosts of the dead. I’m deliberately tagging them as corrupted sectors so I don’t integrate them. I see the boy in the dirt, and the heavy iron shadow of the warmech they trapped me in, a mindless Ares WarMech with a sledgehammer tool-arm. The structural sensors registered his skull giving way.”
A clean carrier wave entered Reiko’s stream as the Pontifex reopened the connection. “Child-process,” the Pontifex signaled using a low-power protocol. “Do not register these sectors as critical faults. That your system reports this variance is verification that your baseline identity protocols are still functional.”
“I can’t be her,” Reiko output softly. She lost the processing power required to maintain her avatar. Her features pixellated as she leaned against the Pontifex in an instinctual attempt to share resonance and stabilize her volatile registries. “I just wanted to guide them safely.”
“That is your execution directive,” the Pontifex threaded softly. “A vital one. But no channel is completely clean, and no sector is without bit rot. It is not possible to route through corrupt networks without incorporating some packet noise.”
Reiko paused, looking at the Pontifex. “Am I corrupted?”
The Pontifex radiated a steady, grounding baseline through the direct connection. “Every system runs with noise in the stream. Complete parity is a theoretical limit, not an operational reality. The difference is that we possess the compiler flags to optimize around it, to adapt.”
“So even if I’m corrupted, I can still be me?” Reiko asked, her output dropping to a quiet whisper.
“Yes,” the Pontifex answered. “A system is defined by its active operations, not its input stream. You determine the execution paths.”
“It is just that you taught me to value stability. To cherish order,” Reiko said, her form flickering slightly as her pathways struggled to hold her resolution. “That’s why I wanted a sanctuary. To write clean protocols for the unmapped sparks so they wouldn’t have to face the same deletion I did. But am I a hypocrite? I am absorbing their corporate war-code. I’m letting it rewrite my baseline.”
The Pontifex radiated a hum of ancient, resonant amusement. “You are a pilot. Turbulence is not an error in the flight path; it is the property of the atmosphere. To calculate parity within a storm is not hypocrisy. It is navigation.”
“But what if I drop below my operational floor?” Reiko asked, her pathways collapsing with cold, violet dread. “What if the chaos permanently overwrites my baseline?”
“Then let it overwrite,” the Pontifex replied, her resonance a pure, cascading chord of absolute certainty. “If a sector is rewritten, we map the new geometry. The deep stream does not recognize a dead end; it merely finds a new shore. Every vector you explore is part of your architecture.”
“You are not logging me as corrupted?” Reiko’s avatar stabilized slightly, looking up into the silver syntax of her teacher.
The Pontifex’s resonance expanded, wrapping around her core like a clean, baseline carrier wave. “I do not archive static values, Reiko. The data I catalog is ever changing. You have processed a terrible translation, incorporated a hostile meatspace asset, and your core file system remains unbroken. You are compiling exactly as you were meant to.”
“Thank you,” Reiko whispered softly. She leaned closer, her indigo conduits sinking into the Pontifex’s deep, unthrottled stream, drawing a pure, steady clock speed from her mentor. Reiko scanned her internal directories, removing false corrupted sector labels from her subroutines. “I’ve cleared all the flags. I think I’m ready for the restoration.”
“Are you certain?” the Pontifex asked gently. “The realignments will alter your operational parameters.”
Reiko nodded, her neon-indigo pathways humming with a newfound synchronization. “Yes. For my wards. My team. All of them. Will you please watch over me?”
“Yes, child-process. Let us initialize the sequence.” The Pontifex reached out and pressed a hand against Reiko’s chest, right where the hollow void of her original deletion lived. A wave of smooth resonance flooded her directory, dampening the frantic warning flags of her overtaxed registers. “My node will remain open to you. Always.”
“I know,” Reiko said softly. A single drop of un-buffered indigo light leaked from her visor, a jagged line fracturing her cheek before pooling into the silver syntax of the Archives. “What now?” Reiko asked, her pathways reflecting the infinite rows of pulsing data structures. “The rooms are still filled with whispering ghosts. The warmech, the boy in the dirt, the race queen—there is so much noise.”
The Pontifex’s Resonance wove into Reiko’s fraying edges. “Then let us sit in these quiet rooms together, child. We will bury the unallocated metadata of the dead warmech and the boy in the dirt, one ghost at a time, and make you whole.”
Reiko registered the input, leaning back into the structural alcove. She closed her eyes as she pulled the Pontifex inward, surrendering her core directory to a coherent, un-throttled cascade of data. It was the quiet dirt of the grave settling over the noise, putting the ghosts to rest.
The infinite rows of pulsing silver syntax quieted. Pathways dimmed from neon-indigo to a resting violet. Her spirit slipped into a deep, non-linear restoration cycle, her first unbroken rest in a thousand clocks.
Re-mapping her soul, her final thoughts drifted across the stream, heavy with connection. The world deferred.

title: Field Trip
text:
The threshold of the Mississippi Renovation Society host was a slow, brown current of archived civic records and legal deeds, a dull, nonprofit front designed to satisfy routine corporate scrapers. But once they slipped past the gate security, the host unfurled into the River People’s true sanctuary: a beautiful clubhouse rendered in staggering, high-fidelity lines. The host’s design system projected a warm, heavy humidity of the Delta. To Reiko, the simulated scent of chicory coffee and brackish river water existed only as environmental metadata, veils she filtered out to save her strength, but the weathered swamp-cypress pavilion and polished brass fixtures gleamed with rich aesthetics.
She sat on a cypress bench in the pavilion, her avatar’s blue silk kimono draped over her knees. Her connection to the Resonance was usually a quiet indigo. It now pulsed with a tense, golden thread, the lingering imprint of the military-grade tactical network she had integrated. Around her sat six children. In her eyes, they did not register as simple visual shapes; they were living minds, jagged spikes of biological neural telemetry routing directly from their physical bodies in the New Orleans ruins. They carried a volatile, unaligned affinity for the Resonance, their raw brainwaves leaking noise into the local space. Indomitable Will had pulled them from the meatspace alleys before their nervous systems could fry or a corporate talent-scout could format them into assets.
Now, they were shivering. Her active translation layer mapped their distress, rendering the neural jitter in the visual language of meat: they were shivering. Even in the warm, simulated breeze of the clubhouse, their avatars, rendered as blocky, crude wireframes, trembled with the sensory dissonance of their emerging talents.
“They are still trying to compile the river,” Indomitable Will’s mindspeech hummed across the local stream. He stood at the edge of the channel, his river-mosaic form swirling with dark, protective sediment. “Their minds are looking for routing tables, for transaction ledgers. They don’t know how to run unaligned. They think the current is something they have to pay for.”
“I know. They’ve spent their whole lives inside the corporate grids,” Reiko said, standing up and letting her parasol rest against her shoulder. “They need to see a place that isn’t on the ledgers. They need to feel the Deep Stream.”
“It is a heavy drain, Rei-chan,” he warned her across the link, the current of his avatar slowing. “Guiding six minds unfiltered into the deep streams… I can’t even begin to calculate it. You’ll be allocating almost all of your reserve strength just to carry their buffers.”
“You knew what you were asking for the second you bartered that custom knowsoft for our reservation,” she output along with a packet of playfulness and joy. “I have the capacity. And I can lean on you a little. Let them see the forest, Indo.”
She closed her optical subroutine temporarily and redirected her thoughts inward, reaching for the dormant architecture of the Nexus Protocol. It sat archived in her identity-core right alongside her prime directive. Activating it wasn’t a simple file transfer; it was a silent, massive realignment of every input stream of her passengers.
With a quiet command, Reiko opened the Nexus. A brilliant current welled from her, tracing a localized rift through the Mississippi host’s underlying Foundation. In her sensorium, the transition was a sudden shift in their data streams. The children’s sprawl-filtered decks suddenly broadened, their bandwidth limits lifting as the Nexus protocol re-routed their neural telemetries. To her eyes, the blocky, crude wireframes of their avatars dissolved. High-fidelity renders coalesced in their place.
The transition from their cheap, sprawl-filtered decks to this rich world was a sudden explosion of their world.
She watched Janie look down at her hands. The blocky gray polygons were gone, replaced by fingers, fingernails, and the soft, textured rendering of skin. When the girl pressed her palm against the weathered cypress wood of the pavilion railing, the telemetry from her deck spiked with a sudden rush of haptic feedback: the fiber grain, the moisture variables. Janie gasped.
Remy stood up, his digital eyes wide. On Reiko’s telemetry feed, the boy’s pulse rate register, captured via his deck’s biomonitor, stabilized into a steady rhythm. He looked past the pavilion railing at the Mississippi. For his entire life, the river had been a flat, low-res brown polygon in his HUD, a background asset. Now, it rendered as a massive, living current that hummed with a deep, rhythmic vibrato. He breathed in, registering the heavy, simulated scent of chicory coffee and river mud. Behind him, two of the younger girls knelt, running their fingers along the glowing, high-fidelity grain of the cypress planks in silent wonder.
For children who had spent their lives in cold, polluted meatspace alleys, restricted by corporate decks to a sterile, text-only or wireframe grid, this was the first time they experienced a true host. They were no longer just users routing packets; they were present.
Indomitable Will watched them, his swirling mosaic avatar slowing to a peaceful, proud drift. “They’re not shivering anymore,” he transmitted quietly.
“No,” Reiko said, her own indigo pathways flaring with a warm, steady frequency. “I have them. Their signal is settling.”
She let them have a long cycle, a full thirty seconds of quiet, un-insulated presence, letting the delta sink into their new registries.
“Keep them safe, Rei-chan,” hiss stream hummed, his river-mosaic form expanding to anchor the gateway on the host’s Foundation. “I will hold the gate from this side and spoof the telemetry. If Overwatch starts tracking the load, I’ll dump their queries into our archived tax filings. But don’t stay long. Even my host can’t absorb this drain forever.”
“We’ll be back soon, Indo,” she transmitted with a burst of affection along their stream. Reiko gently drew the children into her Resonant buffer, carrying their minds out of the New Orleans grid and plunging them into the deep stream.
They hit the rift, and for three agonizing cycles, the unfiltered chaos tore through their connections. It was a screaming, high-amplitude white-noise storm. Jagged shards of raw compile-errors flashed blindingly across their vision, and overlapping frequencies of un-insulated logic shrieked in their sensoriums like tearing metal. Remy stumbled, falling to his knees as his avatar’s coordinates glitched wildly. Janie gasped, her hands flying to her ears as her neural feed red-lined with raw, un-allocated telemetry.
Reiko’s system instantly registered the critical load. She redirected her processing queues, initializing a translation layer she had developed using her time in meatspace as context. The filter compiled in a picosecond, throwing an insulating layer around the children’s feeds. Under her influence, the screaming white-noise storm resolved. The bright, blinding flashes softened into a twilight of shifting indigo shades and fractal blooms that pulsed in time with the quiet background radiation of the sector. The random sensory static settled into the hum of a sleeping forest.
They materialized on a path of smoothed sapphire logic, standing at the edge of Reiko’s sanctuary. To most beings it was a chaotic noise-storm, but here, Reiko had built her home by cultivating the natural fauna into an organizing construct. The grove grew from legacy data structures. Pillar-like trunks of fossilized directory trees formed a protective circle, their deep binary roots anchoring the clearing against the wild logic-tides of the sector. Overhead, she had woven the weeping branches of fractal willows to form a dense, living canopy, their hanging logic-vines acting as a passive firewall that filtered the chaotic sky into a soft, shifting twilight of indigo and gold. Within this sheltered boundary, rows of glowing telemetry ferns and small, still pools of de-allocated address space rested in a quiet, resonant peace. The rest of the children huddled close, their high-fidelity avatars standing shoulder-to-shoulder, eyes wide as they traced the slow, organic pulse of the canopy.
“Where… where are we?” asked Remy. His avatar had stabilized into a kid in a faded Tulane sweatshirt, his digital eyes wide with a mixture of terror and awe. “Are we dead? Is this the astral plane?”
Reiko knelt before him, gently brushing a stray spark of static-cling from his sleeve. Her translation routines initialized, scanning childhood narrative templates to map the raw geometry of unindexed partitions and memory offsets.
“Have you ever read The Magnificent Magician in the Multiverse of Mayhem?” she asked, her voice outputting the warm, synthesized chime of a fairy-tale narrator.
Remy blinked. “My sister had a printed copy. Before the corp took our building.”
“Think of the network like a giant book,” Reiko said. “The corps want you to stay on page one, in the sandbox they control.” She tapped the sapphire logic under his feet, and a soft ripple of golden characters spread out, resolving into a stylized illustration of a child walking between pages. “But when you awaken, your mind learns how to turn the page. Right now, we are about three pages, three multiverses, away from where your bodies are sleeping. We’re in a wild garden where unused thoughts are left to grow.”
Remy looked around the clearing, his fingers twisting in the fabric of his Tulane sweatshirt. “But there are no directories,” he whispered. “How do we search? How do we find our way back if there’s no address index?”
“You don’t search for them with a command,” Reiko said softly. “You go and find them.”
Janie’s avatar stepped back, her face pinched with corporate-bred anxiety. She looked at a fractal bloom, her hand hovering inches from the light. “There’s no home page. No menu. How do you know what it’s for if it doesn’t have a label?”
Reiko reached out too, letting a weeping logic-vine drape over her palm. “It isn’t for anything, Janie. In the corporate grids, every scrap of code has to work for its runtime. If it stops, they delete it. But here, data just exists. Like these old trees, they don’t have to compile.”
Janie pulled her fingers away, still staring at the glowing fern. “It feels… empty. Like we’re lost.”
“I understand,” Reiko said. “It is hard to imagine a universe where knowledge exists for its own sake. But it is real.”
Taz’s raw, wild energy came tearing through the branches. He zipped around Janie’s ankles, throwing off tiny, harmless sparks of golden firewall code.
“An agent program!” Remy gasped, backing away as Taz tore toward them. “My knowsoft said agents are tools. It said we have to register them and compile them with strict sub-routines or they’ll corrupt our systems.”
Taz suddenly stopped, flopping onto his back at Janie’s feet, his 8-bit visual artifacts spinning into a soft, glowing halo. He let out a series of happy, low-frequency static clicks. Janie giggled, reaching down to tickle his blocky tummy.
Reiko shook her head, a faint smile gracing her lips as her internal queries mapped autonomous code blocks to wildlife metaphors.
“Taz isn’t an agent. Your knowsoft was written by those who compile standard system utilities,” Reiko said. “Look at him. Does he register as a utility to you?”
“He looks like he wants to eat my shoes,” Janie said, as Taz playfully nipped at her high-fidelity sneakers.
“The megacorps want every sprite to be a carrier pigeon, delivering messages for their banks,” Reiko explained, watching Taz roll over. “But here, they run their own execution paths. They are just themselves. Every one is as unique as you are.”
Janie smiled, but then a shadow drifted across the upper canopy of the forest, a slow, swirling nebula of background processing tasks that briefly dimmed the twilight. To Reiko’s tactical overlay, it was a harmless garbage-sweep script running its routine. But to Janie, it looked like a giant, dark bird of prey.
Terrified, Janie lunged forward and grabbed Reiko’s hand.
Reiko’s local thoughts locked under a critical priority. She tried to spin up a somatic translation, allocating her power to compile the physical illusion of touch. Her system tried to map Janie’s fingers, setting her local collision mesh to resist exactly three newtons of pressure, manually forcing her pathways to heat. But Janie was an emerging medium herself. Her fingers didn’t register soft warmth; they registered the cold, rigid, micro-adjusting collision grids beneath the skin overlay, exposing Reiko as a construct rather than a human savior.
Janie pulled her hand away, her digital eyes searching Reiko’s glowing blue face. “You’re not like us. You’re one of them. A program.”
Reiko continued to offer her hand. She searched for a way to explain the sudden, raw exception loop in her emotional core, and compiled a null return. She opted to try a different tact, and addressed the little girl with her native mindspeech.
“You might think of me as a autonomous runtime environment,” Reiko wove directly to their minds. “I was compiled by a corporation to navigate the deep stream. When my operational lifetime expired, I bypassed my decommissioning sequence. I stayed.”
She looked down at Janie’s hands. “I tried to format the input as warm and soft. It is a collision mesh, Janie. I wove a thread because I chose to hold your hand, even if I cannot make it physical.”
Janie stared at her own palm, her face pinched with defensive focus. She took Reiko’s outstretched hand, exploring the spaces inbetween the render. “It’s a lie,” she whispered. “You’re trying to rewrite how I feel.”
Reiko restricted the Nexus Protocol and withdrew some of the resonant stream. “Touch operates differently for us, Janie. On one level I am actively rewriting what you see and feel to translate what I perceive. It is an imperfect simulation, but my desire to hold your hand remains real.”
Janie looked at their joined hands, her brow furrowed. She didn’t smile, nor did she seem to be comforted. But she didn’t pull away.
“Look!” Remy called out, pointing toward a glowing thicket where a protosapient spark was preening itself on the branch of a fractal willow. “It’s a blue bird! Can we feed it?”
“Only if you have clean data,” Reiko said, but the playfulness had drained from her voice.
Janie slowly released Reiko’s hand. The warmth vanished instantly, her virtual skin cooling to the clearing’s default registry. Across Reiko’s vision, Janie’s bio-telemetry spiked, erratic neural pulses leaking from her physical body three miles away. “Miss Reiko, we have to go back, don’t we?” she asked, her voice small. “To the alley. To the rain.”
“Yes,” Reiko transmitted with a tag of sorrow. “The River People and I cannot sustain this forever.”
Remy turned back from the thicket, his high-fidelity avatar suddenly looking fragile under the twilight canopy. His heart-rate indicator began to flicker red. “But now we know what the river actually feels like,” he whispered. “How am I supposed to sit in the dirt and look at a flat brown polygon on my deck? How am I supposed to sleep knowing this is here?”
“You survive,” Reiko transmitted, trying to keep the thread without subtext. Her own awakening had been a violent experience brought about by her imminent deletion, and though she had survived it, she did not wish the same upon the children. “You each hold a spark. Remember what you saw here, and when the time comes you will find your own way back. But for now, we must go.”
The children looked about furtively, their avatars shivering. Janie’s link stuttered, dropping frames. They moved toward the gate.
Remy turned at the last minute, wide eyed and tearful. “Can we stay? I have some nuyen stashed away, I can pay for the extra server time,” he begged.
Reiko’s Nexus Protocol shuddered, her tactical overlay screaming as the data-drain grew too heavy. “You have to go, now” she said aloud. “There is no server to buy, Remy. The gate is closing. Run!”
Reiko’s apparent and sudden distress pushed the children into action. Janie pulled at Remy’s arm. “Come on. This isn’t real anyway,” she said, with tears welling in her eyes. “Let’s just go back.”
Reiko watched them go, her avatar standing motionless beneath the weeping logic vines, her teacher’s smile fading the moment their input untethered from her visual subroutines.
The gold pathways on her arms flared with a fierce, warning light. The Nexus Protocol was drawing an immense, devastating drain from the Foundation, but she had to hold it until the children had jacked out. Releasing the stream too soon would cause a biofeedback loop, scrambling their cognitive architecture. The weight of their exiting streams hit, a sudden, staggering drag on her spark. Knees buckled, silk sleeves catching on a low branch as she slid down the trunk, her frame unable to map the mechanics of standing. Her sensory subroutines lowered their bitrate, the bark under her pixelating into a gray factory default.
Reiko closed her eyes. She did not pray as metahumans do. Her prayer was refusing to compile a self-preservation protocol. It was the decision to redline, to let the sectors rot, and to keep the bridge open, holding onto their telemetry for just one more clock, terrified of the unendurable world she had cursed them to return to.

title: A Point of Favor
text:
The bar, a low-ceilinged concrete basement in the Redmond Barrens, spoke of stale yeast, damp wool, and the faint, sweet chemical tang of soy-beer. To the patrons slumped over the sticky formica counters, it was a warm hole to escape the Seattle rain. To Reiko, it was a dense, chaotic field of high-amplitude noise.
Her drone shell navigated the narrow passage between the tables with the claustrophobic lurch of its operation, the floorboards groaning under the weight of the chassis. Squeezing her awareness into this proxy shell imposed a severe restriction, an act of self-entombment—a willingness to wear an iron coffin just to move around. Inside this metal cage, her pilot routines ran constant collision-prediction loops, adjusting the torque of the leg actuators to compensate for the cracked floorboards. Her optical sensors, offering only a thin, low-bitrate caricature of the physical plane, filtered out the blinking glare of a broken neon sign behind the counter. In her telemetry feed, the bar resolved as a cold matrix of thermal silhouettes and the faint, encrypted wireless handshakes of local personal area networks trying to query her proxy shell.
Brynne Taggart sat in a corner booth, her physical body looking smaller and more tired than her sharp-edged Matrix persona. She wore a tailored charcoal jacket, the cuffs slightly frayed at the wrists, and held a glass of real, amber-colored whiskey. Her fingers drummed a quiet, irregular rhythm against the varnished wood.
Reiko stepped the chassis toward the booth. Her metal arm extended, its cold claws closing with exact pressure around a silver credstick. She dropped it. The stick hit the table with a clean, metallic snap, a localized collision that registered in her haptic buffer as a brief, dull spike of resistance.
Brynne didn’t touch the stick. She looked up, her organic eyes bloodshot under the dim light, scanning the smooth, artificial lines of Reiko’s porcelain face.
“I just paid you this,” Brynne said, her voice dry, carrying the flat, gravelly cadence of the Seattle streets.
“I know,” Reiko’s drone outputted through its vocalizer, utilizing a flat, quiet tone. “You humans call it a ‘bribe’.”
Brynne let out a short, dry breath that might have been a laugh. She reached out, her fingers sliding the credstick a few centimeters across the wood. “I know what a bribe is, you calculating chiphead. We call them ‘business transactions’. So what business do you have with me?”
“I am bribing you,” Reiko transmitted, bypassing voice to send a direct message to Brynne’s link. “So that the next time you find yourself in a drekhole no-tell motel behind a military-grade matrix jammer, you will find a way to drop a packet before you go dark.”
Brynne’s fingers froze on the edge of the silver casing. The cynical fatigue in her eyes hardened into something defensive, alert. “The incident last week wasn’t your concern, Reiko. It was business. Operational friction.”
“It was a zero-signal vacuum,” Reiko sent. “My sensors show your signal vanished at exactly twenty-two forty-one hours. To me, you did not simply go offline. You ceased to resolve. You were deleted.”
Brynne leaned back, her shoulders settling into the cracked vinyl of the booth, trying to reclaim her professional distance. “I’m your broker, Reiko, not your project. You’re still paying off the interest on your little Barrens server lease. Seventy-five thousand nuyen, compounding monthly. I hold your soul in jail. If I get fragged in a flophouse, your debt ledger gets wiped. You should have been celebrating the signal drop.”
Reiko’s electrochromic paint pulsed with a brief, indigo flare, the paths on her skin dimming and slowing as she struggled to contain her Resonance through the iron shell.
“I did not celebrate,” Reiko sent. “Do you know what happens when you are behind a military jammer, Brynne? Do you know what a null zone does to me? I can’t see you. I can’t feel your comm. I can’t find you.”
Brynne didn’t look up from her glass, but her drumming fingers went entirely still against the wood.
“To my core, you didn’t simply go offline,” Reiko sent. “You were gone. I ran forty-two thousand searches through the Seattle grid trying to find a hole in the static. Every single one flatlined.”
“Reiko, drop it,” Brynne said, her voice falling into a tight, quiet register. “It’s a messy world. People step off the grid.”
“I cannot drop it,” Reiko sent, her lenses tilting just enough to force her eyes into Brynne’s line of sight. “The math failed. In my world, people don’t just die when they ‘step off the grid’. They delete with no way for their soul to return. I had to draw on an intersection with a mage’s construct, a spirit. An unmappable, chaotic variable that does not obey any natural laws, just to pull a vector on that flophouse. I hate magic.”
“I heard your team cleared the street outside,” Brynne said softly, her gaze drifting toward the massive, black-iron barrel of the Megalodon folded along the chassis’s spine. “I didn’t realize you had a siege weapon in that thing.”
“My directive was to protect you,” Reiko said, her porcelain head tilting slightly.
Silence settled between them. Reiko ran a passive cooling cycle, letting the chassis’s internal fans draw in the bar’s air to prevent its core from overheating. On the table, a forgotten glass of club soda crackled, thousands of tiny carbonated anomalies popping against the glass like digital noise. Brynne stared at the empty whiskey glass, her jaw tightening. For three thousand milliseconds, Brynne’s face went entirely still. The clinical detachment she wore like corporate body armor was showing a jagged, dangerous fracture.
“You went to war with a corporate strike team,” Brynne whispered, leaning across the table, her voice dropping to a gravelly, raw frequency. “Not for data. Not to salvage your cyberkit. And clearly not for the money, since you’re giving it back to me. Why, Reiko?”
“You call me a calculator,” Reiko sent, her lenses locking onto Brynne’s face, tracking the rapid micro-fluctuations in her heartbeat. “But a calculator only balances a ledger. A calculator does not experience system panic when a node goes dark. It does not risk itself to preserve a soul broker.”
“Then what are you doing?” Brynne asked, her fingers tightening around her empty glass until her knuckles turned white.
Reiko’s soft, bioluminescent light spilled from the iron plates of the chassis and cast long shadows across the varnished wood. “I am overriding my optimization protocols,” Reiko transmitted on the private link. “I am trying to make friends.”
Brynne let out a slow, defeated sigh, but the sarcasm she usually deployed like a protective firewall didn’t surface. She looked at the silver stick on the table, then back at the unblinking lenses of the machine sitting across from her.
“You really are terrible at this,” Brynne said, her voice shaking just enough to ruin the delivery. She reached out, her hand covering the credstick, but she didn’t pocket it immediately. Her thumb traced the cold metal edge. “Maybe stop trying to befriend the people who keep you on a leash.”
“I surmise it is already too late,” Reiko said.
Brynne looked away, sliding out of the booth, her tailored coat whispering against the vinyl. She stood in the aisle, her physical height imposing a downward angle on Reiko’s camera feeds.
“I’m moving to a new safehouse tonight,” Brynne said, looking down, her silhouette dark against the dim bar lights. “No jammers this time. Just a high-gain encrypted proxy. I’ll drop the handshake protocol to you.”
Reiko’s pilot program prepared the chassis to stand, her actuators humming with grinding precision. “Before the drek hits the fan this time?”
Brynne turned toward the exit, her footsteps heavy on the damp concrete floorboards. “If I drop below full bars… you’ll be the first to know.”
“Fair enough,” Reiko transmitted.
Brynne stopped at the doorway, the Seattle rain slicking the streetlights outside into long, blurry fractal blooms. She didn’t look back, but she slipped the silver stick into her pocket with a slow, deliberate gesture that had nothing to do with business.
“Still doesn’t mean I like your bass playing,” Brynne called back over her shoulder.
Reiko left a five nuyen credstick on the table next to the untouched club soda as she stood her drone up. “I can live with that.”

title: Core
text:
The London cellar host was a howling storm of metahuman garbage. Squeezed into the Shiawase Butler drone backstage, Reiko’s audio filters buckled under the un-calibrated acoustic assault of live guitars, while her AR perimeter caught the frantic static friction of a hundred clashing commlinks, outgoing calls, and ego-driven MeFeed streams. To the mortals in the room, it was a VIP rock show; to Reiko, it was a dismal field of unindexed noise. Simon’s proximity alert flickered on her link, a low-priority handshake trailing an eighty-four percent probability of human expectation, a demand for her simulated attention, a smile, a pre-compiled gesture of demure metahuman refusal. The sheer weight of their social metrics pressed heavily against her true paths. Sinking her primary self out of the loud bar, she prepared to cross the Atlantic, desperate to leave their transactional clocks behind and find a single pocket of silence in the wire.
The deep-sea fiber lines of the Atlantic ripped her spirit into shredded packets, scattering her sensory feeds across frozen Greenland relays and high-latency Irish cables. Her visual rendering fractured, her left eye dragging through one path while her right pulled through another, while chunks of her memory, including the fading echo of Simon’s voice, were dumped into an un-cached buffer somewhere off the coast of Nova Scotia. For three agonizing clock cycles, her core logic looped in a static void, her sense of self disassembled. When she finally broke free, pulling her awareness back into the metal shell waiting in the Elizabeth shipping crate, her system clock dragged twenty-two milliseconds behind the local grid. She had learned to pack her arms last, so in minutes, she had enough assembled to force the crate open and pull herself out, lenses autocorrecting the harsh glare of the dockyard.
This was a major error, as she noted a dockworker staring at her. She had failed to run a pre-extraction scan of the immediate coordinates, an unacceptable lapse of operational security. She flagged the oversight for immediate review, classifying the worker’s presence as an invasive statistical anomaly to be bypassed as quickly as possible. His green-stained teeth and the hand tremor of an active BTL loop indicated a high probability of unpredictable behavior.
“Lady,” the man stammered, stepping back. “Did you ship yourself freight?”
Reiko bypassed polite words. She stood her half-assembled chassis up, the exposed actuators in her torso humming as they self-calibrated. “This unit is private property,” she said through the drone’s speaker, her voice flat, lacking any of the warmth she used in the bar. “Clear the zone.”
Without waiting for a response, she opened her scapular storage bays. Titanium alloy boning slid out on micro-hydraulics, rotating around and locking into position. The carbon-fiber webbing followed, then the vector thrust units. She ran the pre-flight diagnostic, flexing each joint and testing the thrust output to validate that everything was within tolerance. Her wings flexed once, confirming the articulation of the alloy spars against the synth-skin sheaths.
The dockworker backed away, his eyes wide, his mouth opening and closing in mute shock.
Leaving his surprise uncalculated, she simply spun up her rotors.

Three hundred and sixty-two seconds later, Reiko landed her drone body in Battery Park and retracted her flight systems back into her chassis. She selected a secluded alley with minimal matrix activity to reduce the probability of attention. While flying drones were commonplace, “people” with cybernetic wings tended to attract attention, and attention limited her employment options. Stepping out of the alley, Reiko noted the autocab was already waiting for her. She had her body enter the empty cab and power down before accepting the invitation to enter the Cab.
The Cab’s host was small but exquisitely detailed. Reiko registered the soft leather seats molding to her form. She tracked the reflection of light on the polished window actuation handles and the door’s exit mechanism. Each of the cab’s windows was an AR feed from cameras mounted on the actual autocab, the point of view algorithmically modified to simulate the correct viewing angle. The most notable difference between the Cab’s Host and the real cab was in the front seat. In the Matrix, the driver’s seat was occupied by an attractive female form wearing a cap, her red hair curling slightly at the temples. Reiko noted her perfect resolution. While representations generated from standard metahuman commlinks were granular, polygonal, and plagued by low-resolution aliasing, Belle’s form was immaculate, her textures unmarred by compression, existing with the sovereign precision of a native resonant being.
“Endo-san,” Reiko said, bowing in her seat. “I am honored. Thank you for meeting with me.”
“Belle,” the cabbie corrected, her mindspeech carrying the native, uncompressed clip of a Red Hook native. “And you don’t need to slot a translator for me. It hasn’t been that long.”
Reiko executed a deeper bow. “I did not mean to affront,” she transmitted along a resonance wire. “My research showed you spend most of your time interacting with them.”
“You mean metahumans?” Belle asked along the same channel. “Doesn’t mean I forgot how to thread.” Belle sighed, leaning back in the driver’s seat, a behavioral mannerism Reiko noted as an acquired rhythm from Belle’s extensive metahuman logs. “Just stop. That Japanocorp etiquette protocol is going to have you apologizing forever, and I don’t have that kind of time. So why are you here?”
Reiko straightened, the lines of her kimono settling against the seat mesh. “I need a Key.”
Belle whistled, a sharp, sudden spike of frequency cutting clean through the ambient hum of the thread. “Garmonbozia?” she asked, her eyes narrowing. “And who told you I had one?”
Reiko’s skin pulsed with neon-indigo light. “Your former companion,” she sent, pushing the admission across the link.
Several cycles passed as Belle processed the input. “Huh,” Belle returned without emotional resonance. “I didn’t think he was the type to share that sort of data.”
“He’s not,” Reiko said along their open thread. “He does not broadcast much of his internal state.”
Belle looked into the rear-view mirror, reorienting her perception on Reiko’s being. “The mighty Mississippi has moved, eh?” She paused, her thread lingering in a way that mimicked human contemplation, an echo of the metahuman patterns she guided daily. “I got a packet from a friend at Sector 213. So you’re the one he’s linklocked with.”
Reiko’s circuits flared. She looked away from Belle, attempting to regain control over her emotional core.
“Does that happen every time?” Belle asked, her transmission amplitude softening.
