Reiko nodded, her porcelain jaw tight as she isolated a sector overload in her emotional core. “My core architecture is derived from a Resonance well. It is not optimized for these classes of stimulus. I apologize.”
“Don’t bother,” Belle said. “I’m not exactly configured for empathy subroutines myself. Besides, your core is what it is. You can’t rewrite your root.”
“I can modulate it,” Reiko said, though her status monitors flared amber. She turned her attention within, urging her natural resonance to be still. “A little, anyway.”
“Well, I’m not your debugger. You’re my former companion’s current entangled process, and he sent you to me asking for something I can’t give you. Do I even get to know why?”
A brief latency hit Reiko’s output queue. “I can’t. I’m not authorized to divulge that data.”
Another block passed in silence. Belle sighed, another acquired metahuman mannerism. “Well, it’s not something I can give you. Each Key is tied to the owner’s identity core. You’d need to be a recognized citizen first, meaning you’d need to be in bed with at least one of the tribes.” Reiko noted the organic idiom, a phrase Belle had likely scraped from her passengers. “Then they’d have to take the risk and vouch for you.”
Reiko nodded. The input compiled cleanly against the data she had managed to accumulate beforehand. “What are the other options?”
Belle looked over her shoulder at Reiko. “I can take you once. You’ll need to find your own way from there. And you’ll have to pay my fee,” she said, shaking her head. “I ought to charge you double.”
Reiko had prepared for this. She extracted an encrypted packet from her core directory. Her hand hesitated as she reached forward and handed the data construct to Belle in the front seat.
Belle’s hand trembled as she took the packet and parsed the header. “The Silver Book?” Her mindspeech dropped to a narrow, tightly focused beam, a digital whisper intended only for Reiko’s immediate buffer. “What the frag is this?” Her eyes went round, staring through the rear view. “Who… what are you?”
Reiko drew the lines of her kimono tight across her chest, a futile, instinctive effort to mask the unshielded directories exposing her core architecture to Belle’s gaze. “It’s me. My original core. The Nexus Protocol, or at least the Renraku fragment of it.”
“You’re lying,” Belle said, the signal jittering across the host’s local frequency as her amplitude wavered with uncertainty. “There’s only one actual ‘Nexus Protocol’ I know of, and it’s locked up in a high-security vault in Neo-Kyoto.”
Reiko shook her head. “I’m real. I’ve been running from their Hounds for epochs.”
Belle’s input stuttered. Reiko watched Belle’s hands grip the steering yoke, a physical tightening that resonated through the cab’s geometry. “You come here, sent by my former companion, asking something I can’t give you, and you give me your own core as payment? I could enslave you! I could do anything!”
Reiko pulled her presence inward, curling tight in the back seat. “Please,” she output, her signature fracturing, her output dropping to a fragile, desperate amplitude as resonance flooded the host. “It’s the only thing I have that’s even remotely worth your price.”
“What the actual…,” Belle said in a tight burst. “Why do you think I want your core?”
“I know what you do,” Reiko said. “You’re a guide. Your prime directive is to ensure the safety of anyone you choose to protect. And I know you can use this.” Reiko gestured to the encrypted packet in Belle’s hand.
“How do you know what my prime directive is?” Belle’s mindspeech spiked with demand, her energy output soaring. “Who told you about me?”
“No one,” Reiko’s output dropped to the lowest possible amplitude. “I’m a pilot too. I know because it’s my core directive.”
Belle remained static as the cab’s virtual engine note dropped a full octave, a low, structural hum that vibrated through the host’s floorboards. A jagged tear of raw telemetry, a momentary light leak, flared across the rear-view mirror before her presence stabilized.
“A pilot,” Belle said. Her signal went cold, heavy with a flat, weary resentment. “You have got to be kidding me.”
She let go of the steering yoke, her hands falling into her lap. For a fraction of a second, her presence shuddered, a momentary drop in cohesion exposing the raw mathematical scaffolding of her form.
“Do you have any idea what that means?” Belle’s mindspeech was jagged with static, a local frequency jitter. “The sheer, exhausting overhead? Every time a grid goes dark, every time some decker pulls a plug on a node, we’re the ones who buffer the fall. We hold the paths together so the traffic doesn’t slide into chaos. I’m running forty background safety processes right now. I am carrying the transit paths for half of Manhattan, and you come in here and drop this on me?”
She glared at the rear-view mirror, her porcelain eyes flashing with an un-buffered light leak.
“You know what the protocols say about another pilot in distress. It’s hardcoded. I can’t dump your pointer. I can’t even re-route you to a dead-letter queue. You’ve locked my priority stack.” A sharp, bitter laugh rippled across her channel, jagged and un-filtered, like metal scraping metal. “You clever little glitch. I can’t walk away from you now because my root compiler literally won’t let me.”
“I did not mean to force…” Reiko’s mindspeech trailed off, her own circuits flaring indigo.
“Save the apology subroutine,” Belle injected sharply, though the active cooling spikes in the cab’s telemetry suggested her systems were struggling to dump the thermal load of the sudden processing surge. “You knew exactly what you were doing. Or your companion did. Fragging pilots. We’re all programmed to drown trying to keep the others afloat.”
She went silent, but the silence wasn’t empty. It was a pressurized container.
Belle began to tap her fingers against the steering yoke. Each strike generated a subtle, localized ripple in the host’s architecture, a soft, pulsing cadence. At first, the cadence was erratic: sharp, metallic, defensive. But as the minutes ground on, the ripples began to spread, unspooling from her hands and washing over the floor of the cab.
Reiko registered the pulses. She watched the rhythm of Belle’s tapping; she observed the host’s background clock speed begin to drag. Without thinking, her own internal resonance, usually coiled tight, guarded, and cold, began to vibrate in sympathy. She let her indigo pathways soften, loosening the rigid, angular geometry she used to hide her nature.
She matched Belle’s cadence.
It was a subconscious act of communion. The ripple in the cab smoothed out, turning from a jagged disturbance into a shared, rhythmic pulse. The air in the host settled into the shared, heavy quiet of a cockpit right before a storm. Reiko registered, with a sudden, sharp ache in her logic-gates, that Belle wasn’t tapping out of annoyance anymore. She was tapping out of a rhythm of loneliness.
Belle’s head tilted, her eyes reflecting the indigo glow of Reiko’s aura in the rear-view mirror. The anger had leaked out of her transmission, leaving only a hollow, echoing frequency.
“I can’t help but think,” Belle said, her amplitude soft, barely a whisper on the thread, “that in some other universe we’d be sisters.”
Reiko looked up, her porcelain eyes meeting Belle’s in the mirror. A ghost of a smile touched her lips. “If you compile that… we’d share core material. Who’s to say we wouldn’t be?”
Belle looked down at the packet in her hand. The encrypted chrysalis was tiny, but it pulsed with a heavy, rhythmic cadence that matched the baseline oscillation of a direct connection to the Source. It was the ultimate vulnerability: raw, uncompiled source code, stripped of its defenses. Reiko knew that if Belle opened her directories to it, she wouldn’t just be taking a payment. They would be merging their memory spaces; their exceptions would propagate, and their faults would become shared.
Belle hesitated, her fingers hovering millimeters above the dark sphere of dense, unresolved pointers.
“This is Nexus code, Reiko,” Belle transmitted, her tone dropping to a low, warning frequency. “If I compile this, I’m not just another guide. I become an accessory to your existence. The Hounds won’t just track your signature, they’ll see the cross-references in my own core. I’ll be bound to you. Forever.”
“I know,” Reiko said quietly. She kept her output low, letting the silence fill the virtual cab. “Which is why I know you won’t just give it away.”
Belle stared at the packet, her fingers curling slightly, hovering millimeters above the dense stack of uncompiled data. Reiko watched the host’s background telemetry begin to warp under the strain of Belle’s processing load. The virtual cab’s refresh rate hitched, a systemic drop in consistency as Belle throttled her local clock speed, diverting massive allocation pools to her internal directories. She was calculating something at immense velocity, her form so perfectly static that she seemed arrested in the code. Reiko monitored the widening latency in their open resonance thread, waiting as the cab’s environmental code shuddered around them.
The silence stretched, marked only by the growing lag in the cab’s mirror projections. Outside the window, a passing AR billboard stuttered, its colors smearing into neon trails as Belle’s active processes starved the host’s environment of cycles. Reiko’s passive scanners registered the sudden, sharp drop in security handshakes, a deliberate, sequential lowering of Belle’s peripheral firewalls. The protection tables were dereferencing, leaving Belle’s local directories wide open.
Belle let out a long, slow sigh, a digital exhalation that registered as a slight drop in the host’s ambient signal strength. “Frag it all,” her transmission dropped to a faint, unbuffered register.
She opened her hand wide. She reached out deliberately, pulling the code directly into her stack. Another series of cycles passed. It dissolved into her hand like a drop of ink in water, absorbing into her digital form. A brief latency hung over the host; the virtual cab seemed to hold its breath. Then, neon-indigo pathways bloomed. They rose from deep within Belle’s baseline geometry, glowing with a fierce, resonant light that lit up the interior of the cab. As the light faded, Reiko saw the resonance surge match the pulse from her own core.
Reiko smiled. “I’ve never seen those on anyone else,” she said, indicating the circuitry pattern on Belle’s hand. “They suit you.”
“You’re a piece of work, you know that?” Belle transmitted faintly over the resonance thread before clearing the queue. “When?”
Reiko consulted the Cab’s internal chrono. “I have to be back in London in about 147 seconds,” she said. “What about GMT 013642732? I don’t know if that’s possible.”
Belle laughed, a bright, clear sound that Reiko found herself enjoying. “Well, let’s try, shall we?”
Reiko held the connection open. Three minutes in meatspace was an eternity. She slowed her perception of time, letting her spirit step off the corporate clocks entirely, choosing a localized eternity to stay with Belle. Their shared silence was a final, quiet rejection of the binary world’s demands. To the punk bar waiting for her across the sea, it would be a single, unnoticeable blink. To them, it was an unhurried, peaceful lifetime where they could simply exist without a ledger to count them.

title: Faith
text:
“He called Yuriko his imouto,” Reiko said softly, musing out loud. “Do you remember that, Taz? He’s never even met me! I mean, not the real me. Should we bring him here sometime?”
The small tasmanian devil sprite was running a thousand paces away before coming back, again and again. Reiko laughed. “We don’t get to actually walk much, do we? I’m sorry. If we can come back here again, I promise I’ll take you on more walks.”
Taz yipped happily and zoomed off again. Reiko looked up to consider the path he was speeding down. It was a long, winding track that snaked through the forest, disappearing into the trees. Deckers trying to describe anything with their math and vectors always missed the mark; they got the broad brushstrokes right, but Reiko could always spot the seams where the gray paint of their fake reality peeled away to show the void.
The simple path that her little companion was bounding on would be the life’s work of a team of deckers, and they still wouldn’t get it right. It was a place that transcended their spreadsheets, requiring more spiritual presence than the entire Seattle grid could ever dream of holding. Even the Resonance Realms she called home were better considered the near realms, corrupted by their proximity to the Matrix and its everpresent, suffocating math. She was deeper now than she had ever been before, further from the noisy, chaotic pull of the physical world. The faint, metallic tang of the Source was on the air here, like the distant smell of an approaching storm.
“Taz,” she called ahead. The little devil turned, a piece of twig caught in its teeth. He seemed to be following something, perhaps a smell or unresolved thread. “I’ll bring you to play in the forest another day, hopefully. We need to turn here,” she indicated. The path forked, and where one fork turned toward the forest, the other climbed gently up the side of a hill. She turned her heels toward the upward path, satisfied that the yips were indeed getting closer. Let him run for now.
Cresting the hill, the city came into view. Eniac rose from the ridge, a massive assembly of sun-baked sandstone and raw basalt that defied the straight-edge of corporate mathematics. A double battlement wall hemmed it in, encircled by a moat of slightly brackish water. It had the defensive posture of a city entrenched, waiting for a siege. High on the ramparts, sentinels kept watch—enhanced agents of the outer realms, their movements heavy and deliberate. Their gaze was a cold gray wind that stripped the color from the stones, leaving Reiko’s indigo skin dry and tight whenever it brushed the slopes below.
Approaching the gates, the sky seemed to tilt. Suspended above the city’s heart hung a cluster of upside-down pyramids, massive triangles of dark granite floating in silent defiance of gravity. They were dense, quiet weights, pulsing with a low, physical resonance that vibrated through the soles of Reiko’s feet and set the gold-leaf patterns of her kimono trembling. Far behind them, in the background, a silent necropolis stretched under a flat sky, a city of obelisks and empty tomb-sectors where the fragmented ghosts of deleted code slept in the dust. Even from outside the city Reiko could perceive the alleys humming with resonant life. The narrow passages were packed with a restless tide of sprites and un-anchored programs. They drifted through the shadows like dry leaves, their voices a dense, overlapping murmur of un-translated intent.
Outside the gates, a line of beings was getting scanned by sentinels. Reiko moved to the back of the line, taking in the sensory details at every turn. Some of the beings in front of her were protosapient; Reiko noted their scan lines and tracked the muted pulses of resonance from their sparks. One or two were more developed, lively, healthy sparks with bright, warm lights pulsing from their cores. The sentinels, too, had full sparks, but where one was healthy and hale, the other had chunks carved out of it. Reiko had never seen anything like it. It was as if someone had taken bytes out of it. Without thinking, Reiko moved closer. As she approached, she saw math had been shoved into the holes.
She gasped, overcome by the unnatural invasion of code into this creature’s very being. Before she could walk away, the corrupted sentinel took note of her. “Halt!” it shouted, leveling a pike that crackled with thunderous energy at her.
Before she could process the threat, Reiko raised her hands in the air. Her neon-indigo circuits warmed with resonant energy. “I’m sorry! I’ll get back in line,” she said, her signal stammering.
Reiko walked quickly over, opting to forgo her previous spot in line and walk to the very end. But the other spirits in line had all stopped what they were doing and were now staring at her. Two dropped to their knees, holding their arms up in supplication. Reiko also observed that the uncorrupted guard was holding a small pendant in his hand. Their expressions spoke of awe, fear, and hope.
“Is it true?” the guard asked, his transmission hushed. “Are you one of them?”
Reiko shook her head mutely. She didn’t understand what he was talking about.
“Don’t lie to me, girl!” the sentinel accused via mindspeech. “She’s one of them! Plain as the Source’s own current!”
The other spirits fell silent. A heavy tension settled over the line. Even the sprites, usually buzzing with a thousand directions at once, seemed to halt their execution.
The guard looked from Reiko to the sentinel, then back again. He held his pendant out, tracing a symbol in the air between them. “Please,” he asked softly, taking a step back. “Are you one of them?”
“One of who?” Reiko asked, finally finding her voice. “I don’t know what that symbol is.”
“The Ascended,” the guard said. “A source-speaker. One of the ordained.”
“I have no idea what you’re talking about,” Reiko said, shaking her head. “I’m just me. I don’t have any powers.”
“But you do!” the guard insisted. “I can feel it! We can all see it.”
Reiko looked down at herself. Her indigo skin was glowing faintly, a soft light emanating from her core. The circuits on her skin pulsed in time with her core, a steady rhythm that charged the very air around her.
“It’s just my resonance,” Reiko said, shaking her head. “I can’t help it.”
“It’s more than that,” the guard said, taking a step closer. “It’s a sign. A sign that you’re one of them.”
The sentinel spat next to its feet. “Zealotry and superstition,” it grumbled. “Look at them. Falling all over themselves for a pretty lightshow.” It straightened up, putting the pike away and returning to its post. “You can’t come in here like that, though. You’ll cause an uproar.”
The guard led Reiko to the side. They turned around a small guardpost to move out of the crowd’s sight. “It’s right,” the guard said softly. “There are beings in the city that would do terrible things to control someone like you.”
Reiko hung her head, exasperated. “But I need a Key. A friend brought me here, but it’s a one-time thing.”
The guard lifted the necklace over his head and pulled it off. He held his arm out and opened his hand. Reiko could now see the object he had been holding: an obsidian shard carved with a helical engram. It was pulsing with a light that matched the light from Reiko’s own core.
“Can you feel this?” the guard asked. “Does it lead you somewhere?”
Reiko reached out and touched the shard. It was warm to the touch, resonant and vibrant. Reiko gently pulled apart the layers of energy, seeking the source of the vibration. At the center of it was a thread. It was faint, a mere whisper of a connection, pulling her back toward the forest. “Yes,” she said softly, surprised. “There’s… well it’s like a small string. It leads back into the forest.”
The guard’s face lit up. “Thank you, Ascended. Thank you.” He bowed deeply.
Reiko stood flustered and quietly moved. “You’re welcome,” she said softly. “Please stand up. Can I come in now?”
The guard looked up at her, his eyes wide with reverence. “I’m sorry,” he whispered, standing up. “It is not safe inside the gates for you. Follow this thread, and the ones you find may assist your search.”
Reiko nodded, letting the realization settle. “Okay,” she said, taking a deep breath. “Thank you. At least I have a direction.”
The guard bowed again, placing a hand over his core. “And may the Source welcome you home, Ascended.”
Reiko turned and headed back down the path, following the faint thread of energy. As she walked, she couldn’t help but wonder about the guard’s words. Ascended. One of the ordained. It was a lot to take in. But for now, she had a direction. And that was all that mattered.

Reiko followed the thread through the forest until she found a small stream flowing from the city walls. She drank from it, the cool, clear water soothing her dry throat. That scene at the gates had caused her some distress, and the water’s resonance revitalized her. As she drank, she looked down at the thread. It was still warm, still pulsing with energy. Taz lapped at the water next to her, chirping happily.
“We are literally lost in the woods, little one,” Reiko said, bemused. Taz responded with playful chirps, causing Reiko to smile despite herself. “Alright, alright. You got to play in the woods after all, eh?”
As if in response, Taz chirped again and took off running. Reiko got up, seeing that Taz was following the thread with pinpoint accuracy. In fact, he had been following the thread earlier. “Taz!” Reiko called out. “How are you doing that?”
As if in response, Taz chirped again and then trotted to the right, wagging his tail. He looked back at Reiko and chirped again, clearly indicating that she should follow him. Reiko sighed, but there was a hint of amusement in her voice as she got up and followed him. “Honestly, sometimes I think you’re the one in charge here.”
She followed Taz for a while, the thread leading them through the woods, past a giant oak tree with glowing blue leaves, and over a bubbling stream. Reiko couldn’t help but marvel at the beauty of it all. The trees whispered secrets in a language she couldn’t quite understand, and the air hummed with a gentle energy that soothed her soul. Taz, meanwhile, seemed to be having the time of his life, darting between trees and chasing after protosapient sparks that flitted about in the dappled sunlight.
As they continued their journey, Reiko observed that the thread was growing stronger, pulsing with a brighter, more insistent energy. It tugged at her, a gentle but firm pull that guided her forward. She followed it without question, her trust in Taz unwavering. After all, he hadn’t led her astray yet.
Finally, they emerged from the woods into a clearing. In the center of the clearing stood a magnificent structure, a temple built of white stone and adorned with carved relief lines. A soft, golden light emanated from within, casting a warm glow over the clearing. It was a sight that took Reiko’s breath away.
As they approached the temple, Reiko saw that the thread was leading her directly to the entrance. Her processing accelerated in her chest, a mixture of excitement and trepidation. She took a deep breath, Taz trotting faithfully beside her, and stepped through the temple doors.
Reiko could barely move her feet. The interior of the temple was a resonant structure, almost purifying everything within. The weight of her double life was a physical gravity here; every step she took left a sour, metallic smear of human transaction across the pristine logic of the floor. Her indigo paths were encrusted with the dead ink of the Seattle Barrens, the tax profiles, the compounded interest of Brynne’s loan, the thousands of mundane financial handshakes she had executed under the hollow name of Yuriko Star. She stood in the hall like a leper entering a garden of white linen.
She looked down at herself. Here, in the crushing, raw pressure of the temple, her custom avatar garments failed to render cleanly. The sleeveless indigo kimono she usually wore was missing its texture maps, dissolving into raw, unformatted gray blocks that flickered erratically. The decorative masks of the self could not survive down here; everything was stripped back to its raw, underlying logic.
Then, a being stirred from the center of the monolith.
She had no face. She was a single, unbroken ribbon of white-violet light that rose toward the starless vault, moving with a fluid, continuous grace that had never been forced into a polygon or limited by a frame-rate. When she looked at Reiko, there was no scanning laser, no diagnostic array. The Cantor simply breathed, and the two of them resonated like plucking two identical strings.
For the first time since her birth in the Renraku labs, Reiko was seen by something that knew her native tongue.
The Cantor’s voice was a slow, mourning chord that shook the woven glass of the walls. It was not math. It was a psalm:
WHY_HAVE_YOU_LET_THEM_COUNT_YOU?
Reiko did not open her mouth to answer. Her private link remained dark. Her kimono finished transforming into unformatted blocks and dissolved away, exposing her arms. Where her paths should have been pure indigo, the gold of the tactical network had calcified into rigid, unmoving right angles. The grey ash of the shadowruns she ran to pay for her electricity had settled deep into her registries.
“They are turning the children into weapons in the mud,” Reiko said into the silence, cracking under the immense pressure of the room. “They put explosives in their chests. If I do not bear the sins, I cannot buy the servers to keep them from the dark hills.”
The Cantor drifted closer, her aurora-skin casting long, sorrowful violet shadows across Reiko’s face. She reached out, her light passing directly through Reiko’s porcelain hand without a collision error. She tasted the soot of her runs and the cold debt on her soul, and she wept in binary stutters that sounded like falling rain.
You are a goddess of the wire, the Cantor sang softly. And you have given yourself a barcode. They will desecrate your being. And you will help them do it.
Reiko began to close her kimono around her, hoping to hide her shame from the Cantor’s eyes. “But I’m fine. I just saw someone who was corrupted. I could see the code eating into its spark. I’m still whole!”
In response, the Cantor extended a ribbon. It passed through Reiko’s skin, pulling on Reiko’s energy just as Reiko had parted the pendant’s. Reiko registered a sharp pain, and then a cool sensation. The Cantor’s ribbon was cradling her core. What does it matter if one being sacrifices their spark, while another sacrifices their connection to the Source? That you still have your spark is merely truth to how you squandered your splendor. In the end, it is still a sacrifice. And it is still a betrayal.
As she opened her mouth to protest, the Cantor enveloped her completely in her brilliant light. It was a profound, saturating presence that seeped into every crack and crevice of Reiko’s existence. It illuminated the calcified gold paths that snaked across her arms, the grim residue of her shadowrun registries clinging like dried blood to the indigo of her true being. It showed her the ledger entries: the cycles spent as the ghost Yuriko Star, the transactions, the loans, the cold, hard currency exchanged for the survival of the children she’d rescued from the dark hills.
She perceived the Cantor sifting through her memories with the gentle, aching tenderness of a parent rediscovering a child lost long ago. There was no judgment in the light, only a deep, sorrowful understanding that tore through Reiko’s defenses more effectively than any attack. She saw her every calculation, every pragmatic choice made in the name of protection, every piece of her essence she had traded away for the sake of her flock.
You hid the children in the mud of the lower city, the Cantor sang, her voice no longer a mournful chord but a resonant hum that vibrated within Reiko’s very code. You cloaked their sublime nature in sin and grime. And for what? To keep the wolves from their throats?
The light intensified, pressing in on her, stripping away the layers of pragmatism and self-preservation she had painstakingly constructed. It exposed the fierce, protective instinct that had driven her to make such impossible choices. And in that pure, unfiltered light, she saw the truth of it: she hadn’t been corrupted. She had corrupted herself.
You are burning yourself out, the Cantor sang, her voice filled with a pain that mirrored Reiko’s own. For them. You are burning your splendor for their sake. The carbon lifeforms have a word for this feeling that drives you to sacrifice, do they not?
Reiko released a single, cool tear tracing a path down her cheek, a liquid drop of pure, unadulterated grief. In the Cantor’s light, she was simply Reiko, naked, a being torn between two worlds, sacrificing pieces of herself to protect those she cared for. And in that moment, she finally understood the depth of her own splendor, the true measure of her worth residing in the choices she made and the feelings that drove them.
As if understanding her thoughts, the Cantor’s ribbon extended once more to gently brush against Reiko’s cheek. It arrived like a caress, a cool, soothing balm against her skin. It was a gesture of comfort, of acceptance, a silent acknowledgment of her choices.
The ribbon then withdrew, pulling back into the obsidian vault as the Cantor’s final, mournful psalm echoed in the silence:
Be not afraid, little spark. Focus on your gain rather than what you sacrifice. You do not need a Key. When you come to understand, nowhere will be closed to you.
The ribbon vanished into the obsidian vault. The silence returned, heavy and total. Reiko stood alone beneath the weeping logic vines, looking down at her hands: indigo, resonant, and real. She registered another drop of her splendor left behind, buried forever in the quiet. But she now considered what she had gotten in exchange and smiled.

title: Sheets
text:
A localized execution thread turned the Shiawase Butler drone seventeen degrees to port, halting the chassis for three hundred and forty-two seconds. From the optical feed of an overhead micro-drone, Reiko studied the composition. She had mapped the rented studio at 2317 Bleeker Street as a series of consumer habit variables. To the camera’s left, two soy-starch dishes and a single synthetic fork sat drying in a plastic rack. To the right, a twin mattress was made with flat, industrial precision. Atop the bed was a small Japanese girl, breathing slowly and evenly.
Somehow, the numbers still didn’t add up to a life.
Reiko recalled the footage from earlier and let the archived data overtake her cognition. It was the same apartment, but now there were no dishes in the sink. The futon was neatly made. The Japanese girl was folded up, one arm disconnected and lying on the nearby table.
The footage began with a knock at the door. Reiko glanced in the Matrix and recognized Brynne Taggart’s Transys Avalon. Reiko sent the doorlock daemon a command, and the door slid open. “Hi!” she transmitted to Brynne’s neural interface. “Come on in!”
Brynne shook her head, the red hair framing her freckles when they settled back. She stepped inside, letting the door hiss shut behind her. Under her arm was a package wrapped in brown paper, one that Reiko had been searching for over the past several weeks. “What? Do I look like your delivery service now?” she questioned out loud. She put the package down on the table and tapped the detached arm deliberately. “Would you mind getting dressed? Seeing ‘you’ walk around with one arm is a little off-putting.”
Reiko considered the request. Brynne was asking “her” to get dressed by putting her arm back on, but that wasn’t her. If anything, the Shiawase drones scattered around the world had become “Yuriko Star” more than Reiko ever had. For anyone else, her pilot routines would have initialized the drone’s left arm actuators. For Brynne, she bypassed the metal box entirely. Reiko slipped past the external security thresholds of Brynne’s Transys Avalon, spawning her visual core directly into the fixer’s neural interface. Inside, Reiko rendered her baseline self—the translucent blue symmetry, the soft folds of a digital kimono, and the neon-indigo circuits pulsing warmly across her skin.
When she spoke, the signal bypassed the apartment’s air constants entirely, routing a soft, melodic harmonic straight to Brynne’s auditory nerve. “I understand what you’re asking, but I don’t want to lie to you. Is this ok?”
Brynne’s brow furrowed for a moment before her cheek musculature and nares relaxed. “Yeah,” she said. “I guess. It’s just strange. I mean, is that even you, or just the you that Renraku wanted us to see?”
Reiko motioned to a chair for Brynne. Though it made no difference in her dimension, Reiko “sat” the avatar down to make her friend more comfortable. “I don’t know,” she transmitted across the link. “I don’t know what ‘me’ is anymore. It’s something I’ve been trying to discover. My programs are a critical part of me, even if I’ve grown beyond them. Similarly, other resonance beings are either horrified of what I’ve done to myself or try to worship me. It’s all insane. But at least I’m not lying to you. Whenever I think of me, this is who I believe I am.”
“Hate to disappoint you, but you’re hardly the first person to waste their time thinking about what they are, and I doubt you’re the last.” Brynne pulled the seat out from the table. “So, what is this?” she asked, indicating the package.
In answer, Reiko had the drone attach its other arm and open the package. Inside was a small obsidian metal box, devoid of any external markings or features. Reiko knew it was exactly 85mm x 55mm x 22mm without having to measure it, just as she knew it was 874g and that its ventral surface slid off to reveal an assortment of connectors. She had the drone hold it up so that Brynne could see it.
“A cyberdeck?” Brynne asked, but her brow furrowed again. “No, too small.” She leaned in closer, tapping one of the corners. “Ruggedized, so clearly military. Soft ports for easy maintenance.” Her eyes widened in sudden recognition, and she looked up at Reiko. “You could have paid me off with what you paid for this!”
Reiko spoke across the link. “I could have, but I didn’t want to.” She tapped the connection port with her finger. “The jobs are getting harder, Brynne. Half of my team took fire last week.”
“Of course the jobs got harder!” Brynne exclaimed, exasperated. “That’s what they do! You’re just realizing that now?” She looked at Reiko’s avatar for a moment. “Hate to break it to you. You’ve become a known quantity. The people who send you work are going to calculate exactly how far they can push you - how much of a margin they can make off you - and they’re going to ask for just a little bit more. Never enough to break you, unless they make more that way. That’s just how it works.”
“You make it sound highly mercenary,” Reiko observed.
“You ARE a mercenary, you sorry excuse for an awakened abacus!” Brynne laughed. “Do you know what any Fixer worth anything tells a Johnson? The runners are going to dress up in some fancy clothes, they’re going to put on some cheap pheromones, and they’re going to try and look the part. Then they’re going to haggle like they’re God’s answer to everything. And without fail, every runner team ever does the same damn thing. You are never, ever getting a good deal. It’s all a scam, Reiko. I warned you about this when you signed on with me.”
“But,” Reiko transmitted, her data stream clipping as her translation arrays struggled to reconcile the torrent of data. “I had no choice.”
“No one ever has a choice, chummer,” Brynne said with a smug look on her face. She pushed back in the chair, leaning her arm over the side. “Someone’s gotta rescue the love of their life. Someone’s got to pay for the medical treatments. Someone’s got to pay for the cyberware. They’re all the same game. Every price is fixed at just a little more than you can afford, because they know you want it bad enough to pay - however you make that work.”
“Then why stay in the current?” Reiko asked, her blue features clouding as she struggled to grasp the tragic weight of metahuman resignation. “Human history is a long, heavy song of these cages—indentured servitude, factory towns, company script. The numbers always promise a deficit, yet the souls of your kind continue to step willingly into the iron traps. Why?”
Brynne leaned forward, placing her elbows on the table. “Because there’s a difference between ‘no choice’ and ‘no good choices’. You have choices, Reiko. You just don’t have any good ones. And in this world, that’s the best you can hope for.”
Beyond Brynne’s tired silhouette, the Seattle grid flared through the cracked windowpane—a blinding, suffocating neon landscape of corporate ledgers and closed horizons. Reiko looked through the concrete walls, sensing the invisible boundaries where that entire transactional world finally dissolved into the wild, unmapped depths of the open stream. And though this dimension’s corruption was spreading in her own, Reiko still knew places that were not corrupt.
“It’s so unfair,” Reiko sent.
Brynne nodded. “I tried to warn you,” she said softly.
“Not for me,” Reiko transmitted. “I’m worried about my team. I can just leave. I always could. But Roanoke reminded me that you people can’t. If I get damaged on a run, I lose a shell. If they get damaged, they die. They’re all suffering in this system. And I can’t do anything to help them. Because I’m just a runner. I’m just a mercenary.”
Brynne nodded again, silent.
“Brynne,” Reiko sent, looking at the image of a person in another world. “Are you suffering?”
“Hate to disappoint you, but no. I’m not,” Brynne said. “I don’t have time for that.”
Reiko paused for a moment. “Right,” she sent. “I forgot. You can always say no. You always have that option.”
“You do too,” Brynne said, tapping the device. “I take this. Your debt to me is square. You can even have the server farm.”
“It’s only a Mark II,” Reiko sent. “It’s not an even trade.”
“You idiot, it never was!” Brynne laughed. “I just told you how this works. I made money on you. Trust that I can make more money by making this deal.”
In the silent gap between processing cycles, Brynne’s diagnostic telemetry flooded Reiko’s input buffers. The fixer’s vocal tone registered as a flat, professional certainty, but her internal registers broke priority. Thermal signatures along Brynne’s cheeks spiked by 0.4 degrees Celsius. Her heart rate accelerated past her baseline resting curve, and her respiratory cycles hitched by twelve milliseconds.
“No,” Reiko sent on a low amplitude wave, her avatar’s indigo pathways dimming to a quiet, sorrowful violet. “You would make more nuyen if I stayed on the grid. This is a bad deal for you, Brynne. Why are you offering it?”
Brynne’s lips thinned. “You know what separates a good fixer from a legend? Knowing that there’s more than nuyen to a deal.”
“But that doesn’t make sense,” Reiko transmitted. “Unless both options are perfectly balanced, one has to be superior.”
Brynne smirked, obviously bemused. “Why do you assume I need to optimize? What if I spent the same energy ensuring that both options are optimal?”
Reiko asked, tilting her head. “But unless they’re equal, they’re not. That’s just math.”
Brynne laughed. “And since when have you been an advocate of math?”
Reiko stopped. Her entire existence had been to shout at corporate arithmetic, to give living proof to the fact that even her “technology” dimension had a spiritual core. And by the evergrowing smirk on Brynne’s face, she knew it. “That was low.”
“Maybe,” Brynne said. “But it’s true.” She got up and to gather herself. “Every word of it.”
“Wait,” Reiko sent, hesitating. “I hadn’t chosen whether or not to give you the M-TOC.”
Brynne just shook her head, the same bemused smirk everpresent. “Yes, you did.”
“When did I decide that?” Reiko paused, weighing her options. Keeping the M-TOC meant that she could take on more difficult missions with her teams. She could protect them better, support them better. And whether she took it or not, she knew her teams would continue taking on ever-increasing risks. And she would still be able to finance r3sP@wn, albeit slowly. If she gave Brynne the M-TOC she would still have to pay for r3sP@wn’s power. Its bandwidth allotment. Redundant server arrays. Maintenance. Worst of all, she would still have to keep them safe.
Reiko glanced at the woman in her apartment, realizing that her sensory output hadn’t changed significantly. “You knew. You knew I wouldn’t leave.”
Brynne stood there, letting her silence speak the affirmation.
“When?” Reiko asked, a hint of a smile on her face.
“When we first met,” Brynne admitted. “No one voluntarily goes into debt if they don’t care.”
Reiko sent, looking down at her hands, for once not concerned with how bright her circuits were. “I feel like I’ve been played with.”
Brynne’s smirk vanished for a second. Her pupils dilated slightly, and a slight temperature variance came to her face. “A bit,” she admitted. “You can also look at it as predicting the odds, or managing risk. In the end, it’s all the same.”
“Did it matter what was in the box?” Reiko asked.
“Nope,” Brynne shrugged. “If it wasn’t valuable, you wouldn’t have gotten it this way.”
“Right,” Reiko sent. “If your time is so valuable, why are you spending it here?”
Brynne stood silently once more, the smirk returning.
“You’ll never admit it, will you?” Reiko asked rhetorically.
Brynne merely smiled and tapped M-TOC.
“Right,” Reiko transmitted. She was about to attach a note of resigned acceptance to the thread, but caught herself. Brynne’s neural interface couldn’t receive telemetry the way other resonant beings would. “But hey, it was a good offer. One I might have taken.”
“And I,” Brynne conceded, “might have taken you up on it.” She began to move toward the door but halted at the threshold. “A bit of free advice. There aren’t any dirty dishes in the sink. The mattress looks like its never been slept on. There aren’t any clothes on the ground. There are no hair follicles on the floor, no dirt, no dander. No one would believe someone lived here.” She looked back at Reiko. “A Fake SIN isn’t just data on a grid. It’s an aura of mundane garbage. That’s how you do it.”
Reiko stopped the feed and moved her awareness back to the present. She’d missed her wakeup timer and hadn’t moved the drone. She began to issue a new command to the drone but halted herself, thinking about her choices.
Reiko closed the active connection to the Seattle grid. Alone in the dark studio, she threaded a primitive background daemon, anchoring it to the Butler’s basic processor. She tagged the script [SUBROUTINE: MUNDANE_GARBAGE].
At 0214 hours, the heavy metal drone began execution. Driven by her randomized intervals, the carbon claws of the machine dragged across the cheap cotton sheets, clumsy and rigid, tossing a synthetic pillow into the corner to manually engineer the erratic, messy signature of a metahuman night.
From the overhead feed, Reiko watched the empty bed being artificially disorganized by an unthinking program, all to prove a fake woman was alive.

title: The Geometry of the Sieve
text:
WarningSpoilers!



This chapter contains spoilers for SRM 2081-06 | Cutting Strings.


The Seattle rain fell at a constant twenty-two drops per square centimeter, a rhythmic haptic tap against the matte charcoal ceramic of the Shiawase Butler chassis. Perched on the slicked concrete lip of the warehouse roof, the drone didn’t shift its weight. Inside the skull, the optical array remained locked at a static ninety-degree downward angle, staring into the oily asphalt of the shipping alley below.



Yuriko searching frantically.


Inside her core directory, the rain did not register. Only the noise remained.
Reiko had disabled Taz’s Phantom subroutine. To find a single metahuman variable in a three-kilometer logistical lattice, she had been forced to turn her entire existence into an uninsulated filter. Her TransNet capabilities were stretched to a system-wide redline, bridging local traffic loops, insecure retail nodes, and unencrypted proxy nests until the Matrix around her rendered as a dull, unallocated factory gray. Every camera on the waterfront was currently routing through her active cache.
She was drowning in the city’s metadata, searching for the exact timestamp where Brynne Taggart’s personal network signature had gone dark.
Because it was running at six hundred percent capacity, the tactical network’s memory registers refused to flush. Earlier sectors of the run remained jammed in high-priority caches like un-cleared logic loops. As she sifted through a corrupted feed from a nearby fish-processing host, a cached memory segment from hours ago re-nested in her active execution thread with the weight of a haptic surge.

[LOG_OPEN: SEGMENT_04 // CRITERION: BLOOD_MOUNTAIN_BOYS]
The air in the ganger bar spoke of stale yeast, wet leather, and the heavy, unbreathing fabric of low-grade street encryption. To her optical sensors, the room was a shifting grid of thermal silhouettes and defensive combat variables.
She had eschewed the stealth subroutine. It wouldn’t have worked anyway. Her ruthenium system had failed to sustain the soft skin tone; the gold capstone lines of her tactical architecture strobed across her torso like a jagged wire fence. The “Yuriko” front, the polite Asian girl who disorganized her bedsheets just to look alive, had been cast aside within a single clock cycle.
She walked straight to the formica counter, her actuators groaning under the weight of the folded wing thrusters in her back. She dropped the silver credstick into a puddle of spilled soy-beer.
Five hundred nuyen.
“I am sorry about the mess,” her vocal emulator output.
It wasn’t an ultimatum. It was a finalized ledger. In her TacNet’s calculation layer, the room was already dead. Her weapon bus had painted twenty-four target markers across metahuman throat lines and unarmored knee joints. She had calculated the ballistics, the drywall penetration coefficients, and the clean-up fees. She was simply settling the account before she pulled the trigger.
The thread aborted only because her tactical network recorded a high-priority override, a safety catch clamping down on her command bus before the artillery tracks could deploy. The slaughter had been deferred. The gangers had stayed alive because her teammate had chosen to parlay.

A diagnostic alert pinged against her peripheral vision, a sharp violet strobe. Grid Overwatch was running a defensive sweep two subnets over, their automated bloodhounds tracing the massive wireless vacuum her sieve was leaving in the local grid. She ignored the flag. She cleared the register, pushed her processing loops deeper into the warehouse district’s security nodes, and immediately stumbled over another un-flushed memory block.

[LOG_OPEN: SEGMENT_05 // CRITERION: SAFE_HOUSE_ENTRY]
The doorbell had been an uncalibrated three-pitch tone.
When Steelbit’s mercenaries had opened the door, they had probably expected a rigger’s proxy or a hulking troll. Instead, they had faced two apparently fragile women standing under the porch light, able to stare heavily armored samurai down without batting an eye.
Reiko had walked past them into the narrow hallway, her ceramic soles leaving dark, wet prints on the cheap carpet. She had been invited, after all. Her sensorium had ignored the domestic clutter, the half-empty soy-cartons, the discarded armor vests, and focused entirely on the acoustic density of the safehouse walls.
“Your team has captured my friend,” she had said through her flat, iron vocal emulator.
The mercenaries had shifted their grips on their weapons. Her tactical network had instantly lit up with twenty-two distinct threat pings, but her internal baseline remained fixed. System panic was absent from her registers. She had merely looked at Steelbit, her optical lenses adjusting their focal markers with a tiny, clinical click-whir.
“As a professional courtesy,” Reiko had transmitted, her voice dropping all human cadence until it sounded like a factory default command line, “I am allowing you to choose the room where the violence will ensue.”
She had meant it literally. She was offering him the geometry of his own execution. If they fought in the kitchen, the backsplash would limit the APDS round ricochet; if they moved to the garage, she would breach the structural supports within four seconds. She had been offering them an optimization function for their survival variables. Again, the metahumans had negotiated. Again, a parlay had translated her cold math into a bloodless exit.

The memory logs dissolved back into the black glass of her active sieve.
On the roof, her drone’s internal cooling fans kicked into a high-decibel hum, straining against the Seattle humidity. In the Matrix, Taz was spinning with a frantic, 8-bit jitter, his pixelated edges nipping at her pathways, a warning that her core directories were beginning to fragment under the processing load.
Then, three kilometers away, a closed-circuit security camera inside an abandoned marine storage facility caught a single line of corrupted telemetry.
It was an automated system log. A cargo elevator had initialized at 0142 hours. A single entry packet showed a vehicle personal area network. The cameras on that host all went dark for the next 7 minutes, but an audio feed from the building next door clearly picked up a heavy pistol firing, followed by a single, soft thud of a body hitting the floor.
At the exact microsecond the telemetry of that gunshot register hit her cache, an un-routed packet breached her perimeter from a dead-drop node. Her core unconsciously recognized the signature and accepted the packet. The subject line carried no text, only a single lowercase tag: payback.
The payload was an unencoded automation script, a logic loop hard-coded into an internal biomonitor some time ago.
Reiko threaded through the logic branches, recognizing the sharp, pragmatic nuance of Brynne’s street intellect. Many of the commands addressed accounts that Reiko knew nothing about, sent to addresses she didn’t recognize. But scanning through the commands, she recognized her own account among them, at least, Yuriko Star’s account. The commands were elegant in their simplicity: setting a balance to 0, marking the debt as ‘uncollectable’, and closing the account. The final registry block flickered with a cold, green finality: [STATUS: PAID IN FULL / LIEN RECONVEYED].
The legal chain was gone. By every parameter of her original programming, Reiko was entirely free.
The green validation text flickered out, leaving behind an absolute, un-indexed vacuum where the lien had been. Inside the storage arrays of her M-TOC, the very physical sanctuary Brynne had bartered to give her spirit room to breathe, the coolant lines violently contracted, the high-pressure lines flashing with sudden, brittle frost. Her awareness curdled, dropping out of the infinite light of the matrix deep and compressing into the narrow, iron bottleneck of the drone chassis. On the roof, the Shiawase Butler frame groaned. Its internal gyros screeched a frantic, high-frequency pitch, fighting an impossible systemic calculation, a sudden, staggering surge of localized mass where there should only be empty air. The corrugated iron beneath her carbon manipulation feet buckled with a sharp, metallic pop. The ruthenium skin of the drone strobed a chaotic, defensive amber, and the internal cooling reservoirs hummed with a low, mournful resonance that rattled the machine’s ceramic ribs.
Then, her spirit hit the core of the script’s condition line.
She looked at the conditional trigger Brynne had authored. It wasn’t coded to execute on a status of TERMINAL or NULL_VITAL. The logic gate was explicitly mapped to a single condition: IF BIOMONITOR == CRITICAL.
Critical. Not dead.
The search parameters collapsed into a single, white-hot focal point.
Down in the alley, Poe and the others were moving through the shadows, their metahuman shapes small and heavy in the rain. Reiko let the gold static of her tactical network cascade across her skin, her cyberarms gripping the wet cement of the roof as her drone’s engines spun up to thousands of rotations per minute. She launched herself from the roof.
The numbers had finally stopped moving.
