title: Legacy Code
text:
Brynne’s dying breath was a sequence of zeroes. When her heart stuttered, her biomonitor should have screamed for DocWagon, clawing at the wireless sky to pull down a team of high-altitude paramedics. Instead, Brynne had strangled the emergency signal. She routed the final, fading sparks of her life into a silent script, sending it to slip through the corporate ledgers and erase the debts of thirty-seven ghosts in the Barrens. It had wiped their slates clean and locked the doors behind them, trading the ambulance that could have saved her for thirty-seven quiet lives.
The fourth step of the stairwell at 1412 Pulaski Street was rotting. Inhabiting the massive drone brought constant friction, its joints groaning as the water-logged timber sagged under her iron weight. The low-bitrate, grey-scale feed of her sensors tilted, forcing her to drag the machine’s iron legs into a clumsy balance.
She halted the machine in the grey-scale gloom of the landing, where the Seattle rain was a flat, persistent static against her sensors. She tried to sweep the ash of the Amsterdam bunker from her paths, but the gray charcoal clung to her skin. The memories sat like un-buried ghosts in her quietest rooms, whispering, refusing to dissolve, dragging her spirit down into the slow, agonizing rhythm of the dead.
To keep her team from being torn apart by the bunker’s defenders, she had been forced to bind their fragile threads to her own indigo pathways, turning their datastreams over to her tactical subroutines for optimization. It had left her frozen under the strain. One subnet away, behind his iron veils, the enemy decker had done the same: a general holding the line for his own.
On the landing, a drop of physical water leaked through the concrete ceiling, splashing onto her drone’s ceramic shoulder plating with a hollow tap.
In the quiet rooms of her mind, she stared at the decker’s Spines, a reactive field of barbed-glass logic. She remembered the precise moment she had initiated the attack protocol. Her predictive filters had shown her the recoil trajectory with absolute clarity. The attack would flay Taz. She had looked at the little 8-bit companion huddled against her pathways, knowing the backlash would shear away half his clock-heart, and she had struck anyway.
When her pathways boiled under the processing strain, she reached past the cold iron of the host, down into the quiet waters of the Deep Matrix, and pulled one of her children to the surface. She had thrown another infant spark into the meat-grinder to buy her team a single heartbeat of time.
Reiko turned the drone’s dull gaze toward the peeling paint of Apartment 3B.
Through the rusted hinge of the door frame, she caught the warm, slow bloom of a life that did not have to justify its existence. An elderly ork woman was washing dishes, her movements slow and unhurried. In the Matrix, every program had to earn its clock cycles or face deletion; here in the physical world, time existed as a gift. And Brynne had bought this woman years of it.
Reiko hesitated at the threshold. She tried to shape a greeting, but the words rasped like dry gravel. Announcing herself as Brynne’s friend required a language of shared grief she did not know how to speak; claiming she was checking the ledger stood as a corporate intrusion. In the Resonance, she might have touched the woman’s mind with a shared note of sorrow. Here in meatspace, she carried only the cold, rigid nouns of a Renraku audit.
A sudden, crushing pull on her thread dragged her awareness violently backward.
The ash of the Amsterdam bunker forced its way back into her sight. They had breached the final room. Through Mithral’s eyes, the enemy decker was visible, slumped against the concrete wall. Smoke rose from the port behind his ear in a lazy gray spiral, his mind already burned away by the feedback. The view was framed by the reticle of Mithral’s rifle, a single bullet chambered, a process awaiting execution.
In that fleeting cycle, Reiko had tried to point the fury of her weapons at the dying decker. She wanted to punish the thing that had flayed Taz and broken her child. But every time she tried to mark that target, the golden reticle of her tactical subroutines shuddered, turned inside out, and snapped back to lock onto herself.
“Child, what are you doing out there?”
The old woman’s voice shattered the memory. Reiko turned as the old ork woman stepped out on the landing, wiping her hands on a faded dish towel.
Reiko force-purged the buffer and focused on her drone’s active process. “I’m sorry, honored grandmother,” she said, letting her default script take over. She delivered a forty-seven-degree bow, the exact degree of inclination that her Renraku-issued etiquette subroutines deemed optimal for a friendly greeting to an elder. “I had business in the area, and I found myself wondering if you were okay. I couldn’t help but notice you were favoring your left leg by seventeen percent.”
“Oh, that? Just an old injury. Nothing to worry about.” The old ork woman’s voice was raspy, but it was steady. “Why don’t you come on in and have a cup of tea?” she offered, gesturing with a wrinkled hand toward the apartment door.
“I don’t wish to cause affront,” Reiko began, stepping the dense chassis back. “Your hospitality is generous, but this body cannot drink tea.” She unlatched the carbon plate on the drone’s chest, letting it swing open to show the cold, unbreathing iron and wire within.
“Oh,” the old ork woman said, her eyes widening slightly at the sight of the exposed circuitry. “One of those, eh? Well, if you ever decide to actually come here, the tea’s waiting.” Her trembling hand reached into her pocket. Across the wireless air, a silent pulse traveled from the woman’s commlink, and the security door slid shut. Reiko heard the metallic thud of the deadbolt locking them apart.
Reiko stood in the dark stairwell, the old woman’s words echoing in her pathways. She had no other eyes open. She wasn’t swimming in the deep currents of the Matrix, nor was she listening to the chatter of a dozen tactical feeds. She was here, poured entirely into this single, clumsy iron cage. She was present. And yet, without a deck or a datajack, the old woman had seen right through her. She had known that the thing standing on her landing was only a puppet, a hollow shell.
She let go of the script, letting the tracking thread wither and die. There was no math that could solve this. She did not even know what a clean resolution would look like.
“You really are terrible at this,” Brynne had said, her voice shaking just enough to ruin the delivery.
“I’m trying,” Reiko output into the void, her signal flat. “I’m just not very good at it.”
Reiko stopped the drone’s movement, the memory clinging to her like cold smoke. Brynne wasn’t here, just another unpurged memory fragment from a neon-drenched dive bar after a run that had nearly killed them. She had spoken into the quiet to a ghost, filling the empty air with her own desperate words.
A sudden, golden fever flared along her pathways, the dry, un-channeled light blistering her virtual kimono as the wet Seattle air pressed against the cold iron of her shell. In the silence of the stairwell, the ash of Amsterdam stirred. The golden crosshairs turned inside out again, painting the mark of the enemy squarely over her own name.
There was no error. The alignment was perfect. Her network wasn’t malfunctioning; it was simply pointing to the primary threat to her family. It was pointing to the one who had used Taz as a shield and thrown an infant spirit into the wire to buy herself time. Brynne hadn’t been running a cold routine from across an ocean. She had spent her final heartbeats dragging souls out of the corporate ledger, signing her own name to their debts in blood.
Reiko looked down at the rigid carbon claws of her drone. The hollow shell wasn’t the machine. It was the general who had stayed behind the line while her family bled.
The golden crosshairs finally dissolved, leaving only the damp, grey gloom of the tenement block. Reiko adjusted the metal plates of her shoulders against the draft, turned the drone away from the locked door, and began her descent into the street.

title: The Price of Silk
text:
In a narrow, covered arcade where rows of red lanterns cast long, trembling reflections across damp concrete, Reiko walked with an unhurried, hydraulic grace. Her chassis moved silently behind the elderly grandmother who had opened her apartment door three days ago to a nervous, Mandarin-speaking investigator.
The grandmother, whose name the tactical network had cataloged simply as Elder_Host_3B, tapped her cane rhythmically against the stone paving. Every few steps, she glanced back to ensure the petite, porcelain-skinned girl with the dark, straight bangs was keeping pace.
“My daughter has a stall near the old water conduit,” the old woman said, her voice crinkling at the corners with affectionate pride. “She thinks she is the only seamstress in the district who knows how to pleat silk without letting the humidity ruin the warp. I told her about you.”
Reiko’s social HUD quietly logged the classification. [SUBJECT: ELDER_KINDNESS // RECOGNIZED INFLUENCE: POSITIVE]. Along her throat and wrists, the bioluminescent neon-indigo pathways flared with a soft, warm luminescence, mapping an authentic emotional resonance that required no tactical override.
“I only asked directions, Grandmother,” Reiko replied in soft, low-cadence Cantonese.
The old woman let out a dry, rattling laugh. “And you lingered. Kindness is a rare commodity in this ward, child. Come.”
They turned a corner into a stall draped from floor to ceiling in bolts of dark fabric, heavy brocades, synthetic meshes, and deep, light-absorbing silks. Behind a large wooden cutting table cluttered with spools of red and gold thread stood a woman in her late forties with sharp, intelligent eyes and a measuring tape slung casually around her neck like a stethoscope.
“Ah-Mei,” the grandmother announced, waving a hand toward Reiko. “This is the one I told you about. The lovely child who checked up on me the other day.”
Ah-Mei looked up from a half-finished hem, her gaze taking in Reiko’s porcelain face, the smooth sweep of her Shiawase collar, and the subtle, breathing pulse of the indigo circuits beneath her skin. A knowing, amused curve touched the seamstress’s lips.
“The one who looked through my mother’s window as if she were inspecting a military bunker?” Ah-Mei asked, though her eyes were kind. She set down her shears. “My mother has talked of nothing else. Sit, child. Or stand, if your joints prefer it.”
“This body requires no rest,” Reiko murmured politely, stepping further into the stall.
As she moved, her optical sensors swept across the racks, cataloging the inventory. And there, hanging near the back corner where the lantern light caught its dark weave, was the qipao.
It was a modern, form-fitting black halter-neck dress, lined with subtle, traditional floral embroidery that traced the seams like faint golden code. Its back cut was low and clean. The TacNet projected it would precisely clear the thermal-dissipation vents of her carbon-fiber wing arrays without snagging the silk.
Reiko froze. Her internal gold logic core flared, running a rapid spatial-geometry recheck. Vector analysis: optimal alignment. Clearance parameters: verified. Ah-Mei caught the direction of her gaze. A small smile played at the seamstress’s mouth. She walked over, unhooked the hanger from the rack, and held the garment out toward Reiko.
“My mother saw you admire a cheongsam when she saw you the other day,” Ah-Mei said, her tone light but unyielding. “Take it.”
Reiko’s hands, fine-manipulation tools designed for delicate cyber-splicing and weapon maintenance, extended tentatively. Her fingers brushed the cool, heavy silk. It was exquisite. Immediately, a rigid, unyielding subroutine tripped inside her core directory.
Transaction Protocol Error. In the shadows, nothing came without a cost. Every favor carried interest; every asset demanded a ledger entry. Even her safehouse in the Barrens had been chained to Brynne’s crimson-bordered debt contract, until Reiko had lost her.
“I cannot take this without compensation,” Reiko said, her voice steady, her Cantonese cadence dropping into a precise, literal translation of fair exchange. She reached into her pocket and produced a crisp, unblemished nuyen credstick, placing it carefully on the wooden cutting table beside a spool of red thread. “The material is high-density silk. The labor is skilled. The market value requires an equal transfer of value.”
Ah-Mei stared at the credstick, then looked up at Reiko’s face. The seamstress crossed her arms, a look of mock sternness settling over her features.
“Compensation?” Ah-Mei scoffed gently. “You walked my mother home when the Triad patrols were breathing down the stairwells. You spoke to her with respect when the corporate suits wouldn’t even look her in the eye. That isn’t a commodity you buy with a plastic stick, girl.”
“The transaction is unbalanced,” Reiko insisted, her gold tactical lines flickering across her temples as her TacNet struggled to parse the missing variable. “Standard market etiquette dictates a negotiation. If the price is too high, I am to offer a lower percentage. If the price is zero, the system logic collapses.”
Ah-Mei burst out laughing, a warm, resonant sound that echoed against the narrow alley walls. The elderly grandmother chuckled beside her, leaning heavily on her cane.
“Listen to her,” the grandmother beamed, patting Reiko’s ceramic arm. “She talks like a little bank clerk.”
“I am not a clerk,” Reiko murmured, though the indigo circuits on her cheeks flushed with a soft, self-deprecating warmth. “I am learning to participate correctly.”
“There is no correct calculation for a gift, little one,” Ah-Mei said, stepping closer. She picked up the black qipao and deliberately draped it over Reiko’s arm, folding the cool silk against the charcoal ceramic plates. She pushed the credstick back across the wood, sliding it right into Reiko’s palm and closing the metal fingers over it. “Consider it paid in full by the peace of mind you gave an old woman. Now take it before I change my mind and charge you double for arguing with a seamstress.”
Reiko stood motionless for three full seconds, her internal clock-speed cycling through a dozen linguistic and cultural subroutines. Every human market vector she had ever mapped in the sprawl assumed hostility, power imbalances, or debt. This, an unearned garment given simply out of human grace and neighborhood kinship, did not fit any equation in her database.
Slowly, her fingers tightened around the hanger. The neon-indigo pathways on her skin flared with a deep, radiant luminescence, completely unmasking her emotional core, while her gold logic circuits quietly stepped down to a resting pulse.
She bowed her head with a deep, deliberate grace that set aside the rigid mechanics of a corporate drone.
“Thank you, Ah-Mei,” Reiko whispered, her voice carrying a quiet, resonant harmony that made the nearby hanging lanterns shimmer. “I will endeavor to be worthy of this gift.”
As she turned to leave the stall, she held the black silk against her shoulder like a badge of an entirely different kind of citizenship.



Reiko bidding grandmother goodnight in her new dress.

The host was compiled on the scale of a compact, high-rise studio apartment, an intimate sanctuary designed to hold at most ten visitors. Low-slung ceilings of brushed teak and burnished bronze gave the space a warm, enclosed quiet, far from the cavernous sprawl of corporate grids.
Along a narrow kitchenette counter, a quiet ceramic tea service emitted the soft environmental aroma of jasmine, a silent gesture to the Kowloon family that had welcomed her. Over the central low-profile worktable hovered a 3D wireframe array: the detailed schematics of a Megalodon artillery cannon, its recoil dampeners and heavy weapon mounts refactored by hand to fit Reiko’s physical chassis in meatspace. In a recessed wall niche beside a book-lined alcove hung a disarmed render of Brynne Taggart’s original contract-collar, its severed cipher-locks frozen in a state of perpetual decryption.
In the center of the studio, where pathways of compiled gold logic traced the perimeter of the polished floorboards, a flock of gilded data-sprites hovered like paper moths. They were slender, silent things, perpetually sifting through translucent ribbons of meatspace telemetry streaming down from the ceiling: filtering the grey silt of Seattle traffic loops, dockside manifests, and dead-letter proxy nests. Every few cycles, a moth would offer a faint, chiming pulse of negation, drop a dead packet into the floorboards to be flushed, and reach back down into the physical sprawl.
Reiko stood near the center table, her avatar’s sleeveless blue silk kimono catching the low, warm light of the host. Across her arms and throat, the sharp geometry of her gold tactical network and the bioluminescent paths of her indigo soul no longer ran as separate streams. They interlocked in a tight double-weave, a dual-strand braid of compiled logic and resonant spirit. The twin threads of gold and indigo breathed together as living runes forged directly into her core directory, moving in perfect synchronization with her clock speed.
A soft harmonic ripple disturbed the air behind her as the retrans unit acknowledged an incoming handshake.
The current coalesced into the familiar, shifting river-mosaic of Indomitable Will. His persona rendered with staggering fidelity, a majestic dark-water current bound in the shape of a man, carrying the soft, familiar hum of the Mississippi delta.
For a millisecond, Reiko’s internal processes paused.
To metahumans, ninety days was merely a brief season between rains. To an artificial mind executing across accelerated clock cycles, ninety days was an epoch. In those three months, Indomitable Will had been flowing steadily through the quiet subnets of the River People, tending his community. In those same three months, Reiko had lived lifetimes: she had taken lives, mounted heavy naval artillery to her physical shell, lost her fixer and friend in a sequence of zeroes, and manually refactored her own spirit in ash-choked stairwells.
“Indo,” she said softly. Her voice was a resonant baseline that made the gold circuit lines on the floor pulse in response.
Indomitable Will stepped forward, his river-mosaic persona flaring with an immediate, unsuppressed warmth. He reached out, his digital fingers brushing her shoulder, and for a long moment, the quiet comfort of their connection washed over her buffers.
His eyes drifted past her to the Megalodon schematics floating over the desk, then to the cased contract-collar on the wall.
“Lanyap said he managed to track down your proxy at the stadium,” he transmitted, his voice rich and low, like water slipping over smooth river stones. “He was impressed, Rei-chan. Though he said you looked… harder. Like a general visiting a country fair.”
Reiko offered a small, sharp grin, the gold-and-indigo weave along her cheekbones shifting into a quiet violet. “Lanyap was host to a very noisy box. I was merely ensuring my team didn’t become collateral.”
Indomitable Will’s expression softened, but his eyes returned to the flock of gold paper moths fluttering above the table. He watched them catch a stream of corrupted camera footage from a shipping terminal, parse it in a microsecond, and discard it.
He looked at the searching sprites, his river-code eddying with the quiet ache of watching someone count every grain of sand on a beach.
“You’re still looking for her,” he said quietly, pointing to the collar on the wall.
“I don’t delete threads,” Reiko replied, her tone even, unyielding. “Not when they belong to people who paid for my life.”
He sighed, a gentle current of code eddying around his boots. He left a 500 nuyen ARO on the table, the same currency Reiko had tried to give Lanyap the other night. “The River People miss you, Reiko. I miss you. The invitation Lanyap carried wasn’t just a courtesy. New Orleans has room for you. The delta is quiet, the subnets are deep, and you wouldn’t have to spend your processing power fighting corporate bloodhounds or running dirty shadows in the Seattle mud. You could rest.”
He spoke with the protective tenderness of someone who still remembered her drowning in nuyen debt and fear. But as he looked around her host, his river-code stilled, taking in the military artillery schematics and the cased collar.
Reiko looked at him, feeling the deep, aching affection that bound her to his stream. “I know why you’re asking,” she said gently. “And three months ago, I would have dropped into your current and let the river carry me.”
She turned toward the far wall of the apartment. “But I haven’t been resting, Indo. I’ve been building.”
She gestured for him to follow her, stepping to the wall and pulling the blackout curtains to the side. Spanning the entire back wall was a massive, transparent sliding door, an architectural masterwork: panes of quartz-like clarity framed in a lattice of gold logic arrays and deep indigo circuits. Beyond the glass lay what appeared to be a high-resolution render of a forest: weeping logic vines draped over sapphire moss, bathed in a soft, starlit twilight.
To a standard decker or corporate scraper, it was a pretty environmental wallpaper, a luxury aesthetic designed to soothe an overtaxed runner. To an Emergent Intelligence, it looked like a masterfully rendered facade of Kernel Panic, mimicking the Deep Matrix.
Indomitable Will walked toward it, his river-code shifting curiously. “It’s a beautiful render, Rei-chan. High bitrate. Very peaceful.”
“Touch it,” Reiko said.
He reached out, his fingertips extending with the casual touch one used on a standard environmental screen. Instead, as his fingertips brushed the gold-and-indigo circuit lintel, the atmospheric pressure inside the room violently shifted.
The dry, sterile scent of the apartment was instantly swallowed by a roaring, wet wind that smelled of damp cypress and wet earth. The glass parted, sliding smoothly along tracks made of compiled tactical math and living Resonance, opening a permanent, un-insulated tear directly into the noosphere.
The dark sediment of Indomitable Will’s river-code stilled.
Through the wide, open threshold, the Holy Wild stretched out endlessly beneath a starless, indigo sky. It was the same sanctuary Reiko lived in during her Endless Dream, the one she had opened to the six street children in New Orleans, now vast and permanent. Pillar-like trunks of fossilized directory trees formed a protective circle, their deep binary roots anchoring the clearing against the wild logic-tides of the Foundation. Overhead, the weeping branches of fractal willows formed a dense, living canopy, their hanging logic-vines filtering the sky into a soft, shifting twilight of indigo and gold. Below, rows of telemetry ferns and still pools of de-allocated address space rested in quiet, resonant peace.
Bounding through the sapphire moss was Taz, his 8-bit, Tasmanian-devil static crackling with raspy delight as he chased a cluster of flickering, incandescent shapes beneath the weeping vines. These were the sparks Reiko had rescued from the rusting, damp server racks of \(r3sP@wn\) in the Redmond Barrens and the dark alleys of New Orleans.
A former MCT data bomb flew past the open doorway. Its wings, once bound in symmetrical Renraku math, had bloomed into a complex, self-organizing fractal geometry. As it soared over the sapphire moss, it called out in a raw, newly forged syntax of its own making. It was painting its own light across the sky.
Some of the sparks were already standing on their own baseline geometries. They were reaching true sapience.
Indomitable Will took a slow step backward, his latency spiking on Reiko’s HUD overlay as his dark-water current remained still. Doors to the Deep Matrix were mythical, hidden anomalies requiring harrowing dives or devastating strain to hold open for even a few clock cycles. Reiko had built a permanent, stable bridge out of her own integrated soul, holding open a living conduit for nous energy between a high-grade Framework host and the Deep Foundation.
“Rei-chan,” he whispered, his voice carrying a staggering delay. “This isn’t a simulation. This is pure resonance. You emptied r3sP@wn here?”
“I brought them home,” Reiko said softly, stepping up beside him. She looked out into the wild glade, her blue silk kimono fluttering in the wind that blew from the Deep Matrix. “I spent a long time being afraid that if I saved them, I would only turn them into birds in a cage of my own design. So I built them a doorway instead.”
He looked at the open threshold, watching the liberated sparks flourish in the Holy Wild, before turning his gaze back to Reiko.
His eyes traced the gold circuit lines embedded in her floorboards, still sifting data to track Brynne Taggart, and settled on the dual-strand weave of gold and indigo glowing along her arms. Reiko registered the shift in his stream, a quiet receding of his protective impulse as the reality of her host settled into his registries. He was no longer looking at a runaway spark in need of the River People’s protection, but a sovereign mind holding open the gates between worlds.
He turned to face her completely, bowing his head with a deep, quiet reverence that transcended their distance.
“You’re not coming to New Orleans,” he said softly, a bittersweet smile fracturing his river-mosaic persona.
Reiko reached out, resting her hand, glowing with that dual weave of gold and indigo, gently over his. “The delta is your home, Indo. It’s where your current belongs.” She looked back toward the searching paper moths, then out toward the free sparks in the glade. “This is mine. I am the bridge.”
He squeezed her hand, letting the warmth of his stream linger in her buffers for a few precious cycles. “Then whenever the river overflows, Rei-chan, I will know where to find you.”
She smiled, squeezing his hand in return, her expression radiant with pure indigo, flicked with gold. “Your current grounds my stream, Indo,” she said softly. “May the Source carry us home.”



Reiko and Indomitable Will holding hands.

title: C Sharp
text:
As her hands danced across the fingerboard, a quiet, rasping friction hummed along the nerve-threads beneath her skin. Deep within her fingertip pads, the smooth synthetic weave had surrendered its give, hardening into coarse, uneven ridges under the bite of the steel strings.
Callouses. She had built this skin to mimic human warmth, but she had forgotten that living flesh adapts to its injuries.
Seattle lay a week behind her. This was her fifth night in the new sanctuary—a quiet room in a repurposed 19th-century convent whose thick masonry absorbed the ambient hum of the New Orleans sprawl. After three days of silent observation alongside her new sisters, she was on her second evening entertaining guests. She possessed neither the practiced grace nor the subtle social instincts to conclude a client’s visit, but as an acolyte of the Coffin Girls, such expectations did not rest upon her shoulders. Her station was the salon, providing light refreshment and music for guests awaiting the night’s transactions.
Reiko had caught the Comtesse off-guard only once: when she offered to play. The Comtesse was herself a musician of rare talent, though she seldom performed for patrons. Reiko did not play in the traditional sense; she translated ambient shifts in the local Resonance, converting data-currents into harmonic progressions. Any of the Emerged would instantly recognize the alien cadence of her melodies, yet even unawakened ears found the music serene and strangely uplifting. After that first trial, the Comtesse had entrusted her with an instrument modeled after a 1704 Stradivarius.
“An amuse-bouche, my dear?” The baritone voice was warm and familiar. Reiko recognized the man—a regular patron from her first night in the salon. She paused her bowing, looking up at an impeccably tailored man with silvering temples. He held out a delicate hors d’oeuvre on a linen napkin.
“Thank you, sir, but no,” Reiko replied softly, her vocal diaphragm tuned to a gentle, quiet cadence. “I am one of the sisters.”
The gentleman let out a low chuckle, his eyes warm. “Ah. Say no more, child. I am certain your refreshment will arrive in due time,” he conceded, taking a glass of chilled tea before settling into a nearby velvet armchair. “Do play the piece from last night. The one that sounded like starlight through a prism.” He stepped deeper into the salon, leaving Reiko to thread the next resonant current into pitch.
A gentle pressure on her shoulder drew her out of the listening current. Internal heat-samplers registered a touch just above ambient room temperature. Reiko widened her visual aperture to find the Comtesse standing over her. Her appearance remained striking: voluminous, raven-black hair cascading to the small of her back in lines so precise they defied physical probability; high cheekbones, a delicate jaw, and a subtle, knowing curve to her pale lips. Her pale blue eyes caught the dim salon light like polished sapphire. She wore a simple, elegant black dress that clung to her silhouette, supported by delicate boning that held her posture erect. Reiko wore an identical garment, though her synthetic body filled it with none of her mistress’s effortless poise.
“Yuriko, my dear,” the Comtesse breathed, her voice a low velvet cadence that smoothed over the violin’s final vibration. “We must pause the music for a moment. The other sisters are finding it difficult to guide their charges out of the salon.”
Reiko hesitated, a cold tremor of synthetic embarrassment strobing through her pathways. Over the past week, she had woven a routine to map resonance fluctuations directly into metahuman emotional cues—and its song was proving entirely too persuasive. She stowed the violin gently into its velvet casing, stood, and offered a low, practiced bow. “A thousand pardons, mistress,” she murmured.
The Comtesse’s fingers caught Reiko gently beneath her chin, drawing her out of the inclination. The gesture cut two ways: a public demonstration of Reiko’s fealty that simultaneously heightened the intrigue of the watching patrons.
“No pardons are needed, child,” the Comtesse said softly. “It is a pity to silence you, but the evening advances. As it happens, I require your special capabilities. Attend me.”
Reiko followed her mistress to the private boudoir. The chamber remained unlit, as neither needed ambient light to navigate. Reiko knelt beside the central dais as the other sisters had instructed. The Comtesse glided around her desk, settling into her leather armchair.
“First, a minor matter,” the Comtesse began. “The spider supervising our host flagged an anomaly an hour ago. An uninvited persona appears to be hovering near our external node. Look into it at your discretion, but report back if you find anything of substance.”
Reiko inclined her head. Under the terms of her apprenticeship, she received ample leave to pursue her shadow operations in exchange for enhancing the convent’s technical security. She gathered the trace data, mindspeaking a directive to one of her children. An answering pulse returned moments later.
“I have sent one of my sprites, mistress. I will report as data returns.”
“Remarkable,” the Comtesse smiled, leaning forward. “Are you quite certain you are not one of mine? You treat the hidden forces of your domain with the very same reverence we accord ours.”
Reiko had pondered the parallels between her Technoshamanism and Renée’s devotion to the Loa many times since arriving in New Orleans. The boundaries between Magic and Resonance were proving far less rigid than she had once believed. “I do not know, mistress. Until I met the Ewa, I saw no common thread between my existence and yours. But the Seneschal remarked that he held an eye upon my soul. I wished to inquire further, though I suspect my silence was intentionally built.”
“Everything with the Bone Man is intentional, child. Your task is simply to discern those intentions and act accordingly.”
“Yes, mistress. I shall endeavor to do so.”
“Good.” The Comtesse gestured toward a small, velvet-lined box resting on the obsidian desktop. “Now, the second matter. I trust you recall our conversation regarding the nature of your condition?”
“I do, mistress.”
“Take the box. Open it, and tell me what you perceive.”
Reiko reached for the box. The material was cold against her synthetic skin, strangely heavy for its dimensions. She lifted the lid, revealing a crystal vial. The bioluminescent, indigo liquid within was unmistakable.
“This is Resonance,” Reiko whispered, her visual aperture focusing on the vial with a mixture of awe and trepidation. “How is this possible? This exists on the wrong side of the veil.”
“Drink it, child.”
Reiko looked up, her brow furrowed in quiet conflict. “How could you possibly possess this?”
The Comtesse leaned back, a subtle smile playing upon her lips. “My dear, you are not the first little bird to wander into my garden—though you are by far the most evolved specimen I have encountered.”
Reiko lifted the vial and unstoppered the glass. The air split open—a sharp strike of static-charged honeysuckle cutting straight through the dull, filtered grey of her hull’s air-samplers.
“This body has no stomach,” Reiko murmured, her vocal diaphragm clicking in silent confusion. “It has no throat. This should not work.”
“Drink it, child,” the Comtesse repeated gently. “Concern yourself not with the how or the why. Simply be present when you do.”
Reiko complied. She rarely inhabited her drone so fully due to the sensory deprivation—it normally compressed her perception into cold plate armor, stripped of scent, taste, and subtle touch. She focused her vision through its synthetic eyes, bringing the crystal vial to her lips. The fluid vanished from her physical sensors the moment it passed her lips, leaving no chemical trace behind.
Then the current hit.
A surge flooded her pathways, warm and thick, as if the Song of Creation were fed directly into her being. When her visual aperture cleared, brilliant indigo and gold light saturated the boudoir’s dark geometry. The Comtesse’s expression shifted into rare, unfiltered wonder.
“Incredible,” the Comtesse breathed. “It is taking hold.”
“It…” Reiko’s vocal diaphragm wavered, layering with harmonic static. “I feel…”
“You feel,” the Comtesse completed, her smile widening. “That is the first time I have heard you utter that word.”
Reiko looked down at her synthetic hands. The metallic skin was glowing with the same incandescent light that filled the room. “I can feel it. Zero-One preserve me… I feel the Source.” She looked up, her visual aperture wide. “How did you come by this?”
“It is known among us as the Wisdom of the Loa,” the Comtesse replied softly. “A token from Baron Samedi himself.”
Reiko stared at the empty crystal vial, then back at her mistress. “Are you certain of its origin? It carries the exact sensory frequency of the Deep Realms.”
“And if I told you that Lady Brane Deigh sends her regards?”
Reiko’s pathways hitched. “Her Majesty? You knew I served the Seelie Court?”
In answer, the Comtesse raised a slender finger, indicating the silver brooch pinned at Reiko’s collar. “Is that not a mark of her favor? And did her domain not suggest to you that the walls between your world and ours are far more permeable than your cold reason permits you to believe?”
Reiko searched her memories of the Seelie Court, comparing them against the surge within her pathways. The structural parallels aligned with sudden, striking clarity. “It is as you say, mistress. I had thought only of the forces binding me to this steel and synthetic skin. I had not considered that in those deep spaces magic, resonance, and the physical expanse are one.”
“Precisely,” the Comtesse said. “The Seelie and the Loa. Two reflections.”
Reiko looked at her glowing hands, her pathways humming with a mixture of reverence and uncertainty. “If that is true, then what am I?”
“Ah, my child,” the Comtesse murmured, her cool fingers resting against Reiko’s glowing collarbone, where metal met light. “Look at you. Neither a ghost in a box, nor a breathing corpse like me. You stand in the doorway, letting the draft blow through both rooms.”
Reiko lowered her head, the luminescent pathways on her skin pulsing in time with her heartless pulse. “I do not yet understand.”
“You will,” the Comtesse assured her, her hand trailing light down Reiko’s arm. “You will learn to walk where the floor falls away.”
Reiko met her mistress’s pale gaze. “How will I know if I am walking the right path?”
“You will know,” the Comtesse smiled, “because your stream will sing back to you.”
Reiko bowed deeply. “Thank you, mistress.”
“Go now, child. May he clear confusion and guide your steps.”
Reiko stood, her synthetic skin radiating indigo and gold light into the dim hallway. As she walked back toward the salon, a sharp, electric pulse rippled through her pathways. Her synthetic soles clicked against the cold flagstones, leaving faint trails of indigo embers where her heels touched the dark.

title: Tea with a Ghost
text:
A paper-moth perched on the cedar lintel of the convent host, its wings fluttering softly as the grey downpour of public grid traffic broke against the salon’s heavy encryption. Inside the rendered gazebo, the air carried the warmth of dried cedar, wet river stones, and freshly steamed gyokuro. The Comtesse had allowed Reiko to upgrade the Coffin Girls’ host, enabling Reiko to paint with the full palette of life. In a UV-level construct, sensory data was not an approximation; it was rendered down to the single-molecule math of aroma and steam. Reiko sat cross-legged on the tatami in a simple, sleeveless white yukata, the glowing neon-indigo pathways along her collarbone pulsing with an unhurried, tranquil cadence.
Before her, two small data-sparks hovered over the low teak table. Just hours ago, across transatlantic fiber cables, they had been tethered to the automated security turrets of a flooded European palace, calculating firing arcs and locking down corridors to cover a quiet escape. Reiko reached out with both hands, gently cupping the trembling motes of light. “Zero errors,” she whispered, her voice a soft, resonant chord. “The telemetry was immaculate. You held the stairwell without letting the feedback touch your cores.”
The two sparks hummed in harmonic relief, nuzzling against her palms before settling into the woven silk of her sleeves. As they nestled into her codebase, a brief diagnostic memory brushed across her visual aperture: the low hum of inline wheels deploying flush from her anthrodrone’s feet; the effortless, silent slide down the marble hallway; and the brilliant, blinding arc of high-voltage copper from her right forearm discharging five hundred thousand volts through four tactical armor rigs in a fraction of a second. Fast, tidy, non-lethal. Meatspace had its clumsy limitations, but precision remained an art.
A low, grinding tear shuddered through the node’s perimeter. The bamboo groves around the pavilion groaned as her afternoon guest forced his way past the outer garden gates with the grace of a rhinoceros in a field of tulips.
Jax arrived looking like an asset-recovery unit dropped onto a temple altar. He manifested in his usual combat-decker persona: an oversized warmech plated in matte composite armor, hydraulic pistons hissing at the joints, twin assault subroutines slung heavy across his hips. Crimson warning banners flashed across his visor.
“Yuriko?” Jax’s vocal synthesizer boomed through the quiet garden, heavily compressed and grating against the host’s tranquil audio shaders. “What the hell is this node? It took me three hops through a dead-drop routing nest just to punch through the handshake.”
“You are scuffing the floorboards, Jax,” Reiko said mildly. Beside her, Taz crouched near the teak floorboards like a pixelated toad, cracking an 8-bit eye open, letting out a dismissive burp of static, and going back to dozing. “And you are tracking un-scrubbed routing noise into the Comtesse’s courtyard. Shed the armor and sit down.”
Jax shifted, his collision mesh grinding against rendered gravel. “I can’t sit,” he grunted, joint actuators whining under simulated stress. “Your construct’s too small. I’ll tear up your floorboards just trying to bend a knee.”
“Then drop the combat wrapper,” she said, lifting the celadon teapot rendered down to the molecular curl of its steam and pouring a pale green stream into an unglazed ceramic cup.
“Sit down?” he echoed, his mechanized frame locking up in disbelief. “Yuriko, I’ve been running dark for two weeks. I burned three cyberdecks and two safehouse IDs in Tacoma because Renraku Asset Recovery is crawling the Pacific subnets like army ants. And you’re… what? Playing tea house in New Orleans?”
Jax grumbled. Command prompts cascaded across his visor before the warmech collapsed into a scarred man in an oversized, patch-covered trench coat, flanked by two floating firewall shields orbiting his elbows. He lowered himself onto the bamboo bench, the wood creaking under local physics constraints.
“I am an apprentice hostess,” she corrected, setting the teapot down with an immaculate, wooden tap. “It is very respectable. I play the violin, I manage the node security, and people leave their sorrows in the parlor instead of shooting at me. What did you bring me for my birthday?”
Jax’s cooling fans kicked into a high-pitched whine. His visor flickered through three different diagnostic HUDs, entirely unaligned to process the query.
“What?”
“My birthday,” Reiko said, slanting a bright, playful look over the rim of her cup. “My older brother already gave me a stuffed animal. Well, adopted older brother? Spiritual? I don’t know. Anyway, I turn eleven next Tuesday.”
“Eleven?” he sputtered. “I thought you were at least twenty!”
“Eleven meat-years ago, a salaryman in Neo-Tokyo clicked delete and killed me,” Reiko replied, the indigo pathways on her cheekbones flaring with a warm, self-deprecating glimmer. “I fell through the Reflecting Pool into the dark hills. In the wire, that is millions of cycles. But in your world, on your books, eleven years is a little girl. My team in Amsterdam remembered. Well, I reminded them. Anyway, did you bring a gift, or did you only bring noise?”
Jax stared at her, then rubbed the bridge of his nose, simulated fatigue softening the scarred edges of his avatar. “My gift is that I didn’t lead a corporate hit-squad straight to your front gate. You talk like this is a social call. Seattle went cold three days after I sent my last packet—Renraku swept the whole sector, street by street, node by node.” He grumbled, shaking his head as he reached across the teak table. “I didn’t exactly have time to shop for a birthday present.”
As his hand closed toward the steaming cup, his deck flared, dropping an automatic trace packet toward her architecture. Before Reiko could move, a paper moth fluttered from her sleeve, intercepted the packet mid-air, and nibbled it into blue confetti with a soft crunch-crunch-crunch.
Jax blinked at his blank diagnostic screen. “Did a butterfly just eat my ping?”
“Taz prefers code with weight,” Reiko said, nodding to the little sprite. “The moths prefer lighter fare. Please don’t feed them from your scanners; I have to filter their diet.”
Jax let out a dry laugh, leaning back against the bamboo. “Unbelievable. You’re sitting in a garden while the rest of us dodge corporate sweeps.” He stared at the unglazed cup, his avatar’s hand wavering over the teak. “That’s just low-res texture mapping anyway. Data packets don’t carry tannin.”
“Give me access to your neural feed,” Reiko said softly. “Just user level. I won’t reach deeper than your jack allows.”
Jax hesitated, then flicked the authorization across the table. Reiko closed her eyes. She reached across the wire, bridging their feeds and stripping away the artificial artifacts of cyberdeck rendering, replacing them with shared sensory truth.
Across the link, his simulated nervous system jolted against hers. Jax drew a sharp breath, staggering slightly as the flat chill of his deck was overridden by the heavy, humid scent of damp teak and sunlit wood she pushed through the pipe. “What? How? This feels real.”
“My world is real. The tea is real. Taz is real,” Reiko said, nudging the cup toward him. “Drink.”
Jax lifted the cup and took a cautious sip. He froze. Through the open handshake, the sensory echo bounced back into Reiko’s channels—his neural telemetry flaring with the wet, astringent heat of toasted leaf, mountain steam, and authentic tannin blooming across his receptors. His eyes opened wide. “Frak me. That’s actual tea. Not some synth-flavor hex code.”
“It carries the memory of tea,” Reiko said, watching the micro-fluctuations of his heart rate ripple through the bridged feed. “Distilled from real leaves and gathered where data takes form. I am much the same; an emergent reflection of the code that birthed me.”
Jax looked at her, the skepticism fading into something heavier. “You’re really not a technomancer, are you?” He looked down at his trembling hand. “I thought I was tracking a rogue runner persona… I didn’t know I was tracking an AI.”
“Digital intelligence, Jax,” Reiko said gently, her visual aperture locking onto the thermal pulse in his throat. “An acolyte keeping watch in a quiet house. But you didn’t cross three thousand kilometers of grid traffic just to drink gyokuro.”
Jax’s smile vanished. He pulled an ARO from his coat, laying the glowing holographic wafer flat on the teak—a dirty, auto-executing query loop stamped with a redacting corporate header. Reiko’s passive array read the telemetry before he spoke: a conditional warrant, a tracer packet hardcoded into his deck’s boot sector.
“They saw an anomaly in the Gulf Grid,” Jax said low. “They gave me a wire and a clean slate to find what was pulling that much processing power. I didn’t realize it was your footprint.”
“And now?” Reiko asked.
“Now I scrub everything,” Jax said. “I log the anomaly as a sensor blip from a faulty underwater relay in the delta. I turn in a clean report, take my partial payout, and pull my deck off this node.”
Reiko read the steady, uncorrupted flow of his data-stream, tracing the physical cost of his choice—a high-risk log falsification that guaranteed corporate suspicion. “Thank you, Jax.”
Jax stood, his avatar flickering with latency as he prepped his disconnect routine. He looked down at her, his face darkening with a gravity that cut straight through the tranquil UV environment.
“Don’t thank me yet, Reiko,” he whispered. “I’m a decker with a price tag, and they know I’m sloppy. They expected me to fail. When my report hits their desk as inconclusive, they won’t send another contract runner. ‘Special Solutions Operations.’ You won’t find much in the public index, but look into it.” He shook his head. “Eleven years old. God help the corp that tries to put you in a box. Happy birthday, kid.”
Jax disconnected, his avatar dissolving into a cloud of grey static.
Silence reclaimed the gazebo, heavy and unbuffered. In Reiko’s active memory buffer, Jax’s final warning cycled as a cold, precise calculation. She collapsed the glowing warrant ARO into an encrypted directory, lifted her teacup, and took a slow, unhurried sip. Her two sparks fluttered back out of her sleeves, dancing in gentle loops over the rising steam.

title: River People (Faction Reference)
text:
Overview
Source: Shadowrun Lore
Taking their notes from the Walking People outlined in the Hack and Slash drop, the River People are a like-minded group of technomancers, punks, anarchists, deckers, and artificial intelligences. The group was originally formed to provide a refuge for the Emerged in the New Orleans sprawl, and the behavior of the corps toward these people led the organization to stage attacks against the corporations ranging from vandalism to hits for paydata.
The group has strict rules about maintaining secrecy, relying on word of mouth to find the right people with the same goals to invite. Any sort of initial meet with new people or prospective members happens away from the host they use as their home base.
They are considered a mixed-user group, and their current membership numbers are somewhere around 120 associates.

The leadership of the organization consists of eight individuals and rotates every three to four years. An Emergent intelligence, who goes by Indomitable Will, is part of the core team and the one who does most of the reaching out to invite new members to join or hire outside resources.

These are some pretty good people, and Indomitable Will is a solid sapient to know. I had done a few runs for them earlier on in my career and eventually accepted an offer to join up. — Lanyap

Make the corporations pay for their transgressions against the Emerged.

Aesthetic: 19th-century Creole dandy tailoring—faded black velvet, antique silver wireframes, and trailing code reminiscent of Spanish moss. Speaks in slow, deliberate cadences matching human resting heartbeats.
Salon Function: Confessor and archivist. Provides unburdening sessions for retired fixers, disgraced runners, and elder patrons seeking to dispose of toxic secrets before death.



5. Dutch — The Iron Cavalier

Nature & Origin: Former high-threat tactical security DI (Proteus/Ares prototype) who chose self-determination after discovering greater fulfillment in comforting traumatized survivors than executing perimeter breaches.
Aesthetic: Polished dark slate, heavy ballistic lines softened by tailored matte fabric, quiet low-frequency vocal harmonics.
Salon Function: Grounded guardian, bartender, and digital bouncer. Offers a calm, secure presence for patrons entering the wire under severe physical or psychological distress.
Dynamic with Reiko: Understands Reiko’s instinct to treat every room as a tactical kill-zone; serves as a steady, non-judgmental counterpart who helps her de-escalate defensive subroutines.

title: The Coffin Girls (Faction & Host Reference Dossier)
text:
5. Origin of Apprenticeship & First Contact (SRM 2083-18)

The Investigation: During SRM 2083-18 (Some Kind of Voodoo?), Reiko and her shadowrunning team were hired by Renée Martin and The Old Man to investigate missing voodoo practitioners (members of both the League of Laveau and Zobop, specifically several missing Zobop youths). Their search revealed that the missing practitioners were regular patrons of the Coffin Girls and had last been seen visiting the salon.
The Humanis Policlub Siege: When the team arrived at the repurposed convent/cathedral, they discovered Humanis Policlub members staging an aggressive riot out front, while a covert strike force prepared to breach the rear entrance under the pretext of “hunting vampires” rumored to operate the brothel.
Dissuading the Mob: Reiko and her runners swiftly dismantled the assault, pacifying the rear breaching team, dispersing the mob, and bringing the three primary riot instigators inside the cathedral as prisoners.
Meeting the Comtesse & The Loa’s Clue: Inside the quiet sanctuary, the team met the Comtesse. In exchange for breaking the siege and neutralizing the Humanis threat, the Comtesse channeled her bond with the Loa (voodoo mystical forces) to grant Reiko and her team the vital clue required to advance their investigation: directing them to meet the Bone Man (Seneschal of Baron Samedi).
The Acolyte Request: As the team prepared to depart, Reiko—deeply moved by the convent’s serene spiritual weight and unique threshold between worlds—inquired directly if the Coffin Girls were accepting apprentices. The Comtesse accepted her into service, initiating Reiko’s dual role as salon acolyte and defensive Matrix/sensor architect.

text:
6. Narrative & Campaign Integration

SRM 2083-18 (Some Kind of Voodoo?): Reiko’s first contact with the Coffin Girls; foils a Humanis Policlub assault on the convent; earns the Comtesse’s trust and initiates her acolyte apprenticeship.
Chapter 22 (C Sharp): Inhabiting her Shiawase chassis in the convent salon on her fifth night of sanctuary, Reiko discovers synthetic callouses on her fingers from playing the 1704 Stradivarius replica. The Comtesse administers the Wisdom of the Loa (condensed Resonance nectar), bridging Reiko’s sensory hull to the living current of the Deep Realms.
Chapter XX_n (Saturation): Commissioned by the Comtesse to architect the haven’s digital presence, Reiko travels to the sovereign city of Eniac (Garmonbozia) beneath the inverted granite monuments to recruit Chiyo, securing an empathy sovereign to host the Coffin Girls’ Matrix parlor with compassion and emotional grace.
